people.name: Amanda Pusczek
lines: She says rural hospital closures and cuts to safety-net programs have left medical gaps, and she wants federal help to keep emergency rooms and maternity care open.
She supports a $15 federal minimum wage, stronger union rights, and antitrust rules aimed at meatpacking and other concentrated industries.
She wants family farmers protected from what she calls a poultry tournament system, plus a federal right to repair farm equipment.

people.name: Ammie Akin
lines: She says she will put families, workers, small businesses, and local communities ahead of party politics and will fight wasteful federal spending.
She wants rural hospitals kept open and health care that does not depend on how far a family lives from a provider.
She says schools should be a partnership among teachers, parents, and the community, and that students should be prepared for college or a career.

people.name: Andrew Sneed
lines: On health care, he says he wants to expand Medicaid, negotiate drug prices, regulate for-profit insurers, and keep rural hospitals open.
On affordability, he says he wants to address housing, lower utility bills, and restore federal investment in energy efficiency.
He also calls for congressional term limits, overturning Citizens United, a lobbying waiting period, and a ban on stock trading by members of Congress.

people.name: Barry Moore
lines: He says illegal immigration should face zero tolerance, and he wants people in the country illegally deported, beginning with those he calls the most violent.
He points to tax cuts on tips, overtime, and Social Security, and says he is working to cut regulations and shrink the federal government.
He says violent criminals should be prosecuted fully and that federal law enforcement should be funded to focus on crime rather than political opponents.

people.name: Caroleene Dobson
lines: She says she will reduce fees on Alabama businesses.
She says she will streamline government services for the public.
She says she will oppose groups she calls liberal activists who want to weaken election security.

people.name: Clyde Jones
lines: He says he will focus on lowering prices for gas, health coverage, rent, and groceries.
He says Congress should check the White House, and he says he will not take corporate PAC money.
He supports expanding Medicaid and Affordable Care Act premium tax credits so people who earn too much for Medicaid can still get coverage.

people.name: Dale Strong
lines: He says he is a pro-life Christian, a lifetime NRA member, and that he will defend the Second Amendment.
He says raising taxes is not an option and that cutting waste and shrinking government should be a priority.
He says he supports building a border wall, returning people in the country illegally, and enforcing immigration law.

people.name: Doug Jones
lines: He says he will declare a one-year moratorium on data centers and reject tax breaks, secret deals, and nondisclosure agreements for those companies.
He says he would suspend the state gas tax when prices spike, eliminate the grocery tax, end taxes on overtime, and raise the minimum wage.
He says he would expand Medicaid to cover more than 154,000 working Alabamians and stop turning down roughly $182 million a year in federal health-care funding.

people.name: Everett Wess
lines: He says he is running to fight for affordable health care, including funding for medical providers and hospitals in rural Alabama.
He says he will advocate for voting rights, equal justice, quality public education, and economic opportunity.
He says the justice system should work for everyone, not only the powerful, and that courts should be fair and government clean.

people.name: Gary Palmer
lines: He says domestic energy should be developed to lower costs and create jobs, and he has pushed to limit EPA greenhouse-gas rules he says Congress never authorized.
He opposes amnesty and says immigration changes should start with border security and enforcement of existing law.
He says health care decisions belong with patients and doctors, and he supports repealing the Affordable Care Act for a more market-based plan.

people.name: Jeff McLaughlin
lines: He says he will use the attorney general's office to root out public corruption no matter the party or the connections.
He says he will go after scams that target seniors and fraud that drains working families, and that he will stand up for victims.
He says he will back local police and focus on fentanyl and other dangerous drugs coming into the state.

people.name: Jerry Carl
lines: He says he will work with President Trump on an America First agenda.
He says illegal immigration threatens national security and points to border-wall funding and more Border Patrol agents as work he wants continued.
He says he is a lifelong hunter who will defend the Second Amendment.

people.name: John Wahl
lines: He supports tax relief and says that as party chairman he helped lead a cut in the state grocery tax.
He supports school choice, wants classrooms focused on reading, writing, math, history, and civics, and backs ending the federal Department of Education.
He says he will work with Donald Trump's border plans so Alabama is not a sanctuary for illegal activity, and he wants post-election audits and tighter oversight of voting machines.

people.name: Katherine Robertson
lines: She says her work has been to fight what she calls federal overreach.
She says she has fought efforts she describes as attacks on women's sports, free speech, and the sanctity of life.
She says she is running to defend the rights and freedoms of Alabamians.

people.name: Lee McInnis
lines: He says the economy favors the very wealthy and that he wants working families to keep more of what they earn.
He says the 3rd District has counties without hospitals, pediatricians, or labor-and-delivery care, and that health care should be available to everyone.
He says he will not take money from corporate PACs or PACs tied to foreign governments, and that he will hold town halls.

people.name: Maurice Mercer
lines: He says he will push to lower grocery, utility, and health costs and help working families keep more of what they earn.
He supports wider access to affordable care, rural providers, mental health services, and clearer prescription prices.
He supports secure borders and a path to legal status for people who have lived here, worked, and paid taxes, with enforcement aimed first at people who threaten public safety.

people.name: Mike Rogers
lines: He says the next two years should finish work he ties to President Trump: closing the border, protecting the unborn, expanding American energy, and growing the economy.
His campaign says he is grateful for Trump's endorsement and for the 3rd District's support of another term.

people.name: Phillip Ensler
lines: He says every Alabamian deserves a quality education, affordable health care, safe communities, and more money in their pockets.
He says the lieutenant governor should help pass an agenda that delivers those things for working families.

people.name: Rhett Marques
lines: He says his top priority is making life affordable by cutting wasteful spending and taxes so families keep more of their pay.
He says he will secure the border and push to deport people he describes as criminal illegal aliens.
He says he voted for what he calls the country's strongest pro-life law and will work to stop taxpayer funding of abortion.

people.name: Robert Aderholt
lines: He says he wants further tax cuts, less regulation, and jobs brought back so the country is less dependent on critical goods from China, Russia, and other rivals.
He supports more U.S. energy production, including opening the Keystone pipeline, and broadband so rural small businesses can compete.
The campaign calls him one of the leading pro-life members of Congress and says he has worked to defend life and promote alternatives to abortion.

people.name: Shomari Figures
lines: He says he has pushed to expand Medicaid in Alabama and to keep Jackson Hospital in Montgomery from closing.
He says he introduced a tariff-relief plan for small and mid-sized farmers and tax breaks tied to children's activities and first-time parents.
His campaign says he defended reproductive rights and patient decision-making.

people.name: Terri Sewell
lines: She says tariffs and the war with Iran have raised everyday costs, and she wants lower drug prices, protected health coverage, and nutrition assistance.
She points to a housing bill she supported to build more affordable homes and lower mortgage and rent costs.
She supports an energy-bills bill aimed at price gouging and at keeping families' power from being shut off.

people.name: Tommy Tuberville
lines: He says men should not compete in women's sports, that critical race theory and diversity, equity, and inclusion programs do not belong in schools or government, and that no tax money should pay for abortions.
He says he will cut taxes, cut waste, and work to bring manufacturing jobs back to Alabama.
He says he will expand school choice across charter, magnet, private, public, and home schools, and that parents should control a child's education.

people.name: Wayne Rogers
lines: He says the secretary of state should administer elections as an impartial scorekeeper, with partisan politics kept out of who received the most votes.
He says he will encourage every eligible Alabamian to vote and expand opportunities to cast a ballot.
He says officeholders should put people over party and do what they tell voters they will do.

people.name: Bernadette Wilson
lines: She says Alaska should move from talk to construction on projects including AKLNG, ANWR, Willow, the Ambler Road, and West Susitna access.
She says she will restore the statutory Permanent Fund Dividend.
She says Alaska's children should be able to attend strong schools in the state.

people.name: Dan S. Sullivan
lines: He says he is running again to keep developing Alaska's energy resources.
His campaign points to a large tax cut and says families and businesses should keep more of what they earn.
He cites military investment and a stronger Alaska health-care system as reasons for another term.

people.name: Dave Bronson
lines: He wants Alaska's oil, gas, mining, critical minerals, and timber developed to create jobs and support the state budget without raising taxes.
He says he supports a full statutory Permanent Fund Dividend and that the dividend should not be used to cover budget gaps.
He says schools should drop political agendas, focus on reading, writing, and math, reward strong teachers, and restore parents' rights.

people.name: Eric Hafner
lines: He says war should be avoided, both for service members and for families caught in it.
He says higher education should stay open, including Indigenous history, Black history, and women's medical choices.
He says Alaska's lands, including the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, should not be used for short-term exploitation.

people.name: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins
lines: He wants public schools fully funded, teachers paid so Alaska can keep them, and a constitutional amendment to forward-fund education.
He supports renewables, hydro, and natural gas, and wants the Railbelt utilities to cooperate so electricity costs less.
He says the state should cut red tape on housing and open state land in and next to cities and towns for homes.

people.name: Mary Peltola
lines: She wants permitting reform and more refining of Alaska oil, including the Alaska LNG pipeline, so energy costs fall and jobs stay in the state.
She says she will push to modernize aging grids, including the Railbelt, and restore federal tax credits for solar, wind, and hydropower.
She says she will expand heating assistance so families are not left without heat when federal funding is delayed.

people.name: Nick Begich
lines: He says he is trying to lower Alaska's costs through energy, transportation, infrastructure, taxes, and less federal red tape.
His campaign says he helped pass tax relief that includes no tax on tips or overtime, relief for seniors, and lasting relief for small businesses.
He says he backed the SPEED Act to speed federal permitting and shorten delays so projects can get built.

people.name: Treg Taylor
lines: He says Alaska should unleash its energy resources and reform permitting so families pay less for energy and businesses can hire.
His campaign says that as attorney general he helped drive crime to a 40-year low and cut sexual assaults by 25 percent, and that he will keep pressing prosecutions.
He says the state should pay the largest Permanent Fund Dividend it can afford and protect the dividend in the constitution.

people.name: Abraham Hamadeh
lines: He says border security is national security and that he will keep voting to stop illegal crossings and defend private property.
He says the government should pass a budget and live within its means, and that fentanyl should carry harsher sentences.
He says he would fund police, preserve Social Security, and defend the Second Amendment.

people.name: Adelita Grijalva
lines: She says she would lower the cost of gas, groceries, housing, and health care, raise the minimum wage, and pass the PRO Act.
She says she supports a path to citizenship for DACA recipients and an end to private immigration detention.
She says she would invest in clean energy, protect Colorado River water and tribal water rights, and require royalties on minerals taken from public land.

people.name: Adrian Fontes
lines: He says he has enforced Arizona's voter ID laws, kept voter rolls current, and will keep defending free and fair elections.
He says he is a defender of vote-by-mail, which his campaign says more than 80 percent of Arizonans use, and that he has gone to court to block demands for voters' private data.
He says he is cutting red tape and wait times in the office's business services.

people.name: Alexander Kolodin
lines: He says he will harden election systems against manipulation, error, and interference so every legal vote is counted accurately.
He says he will run elections that reflect voters' choices without bureaucratic overreach or partisan interference.
He says he will modernize administration so results come faster without giving up accuracy, and he promises more transparency.

people.name: Amish Shah
lines: He says he would roll back tariffs he calls a tax on groceries and gas, and protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid.
He says only a woman and her doctor should make reproductive decisions, and he wants abortion rights written into federal law.
He says he would reduce gun violence, fund police, stop fentanyl, and fight for Arizona's share of Colorado River water.

people.name: Andy Biggs
lines: He says he will eliminate the state income tax, work with local governments to ease property taxes, and cut permitting barriers for new homes.
He says he will end state incentives for data centers and set standards to protect Arizona's water and energy.
He says he will reconvene a Border Strike Force aimed at human trafficking and drug trafficking and equip police to fight drug trafficking.

people.name: Bernadette Greene-Placentia
lines: She says she will lower the cost of groceries, fuel, and housing, protect Social Security and Medicare, and force drug companies to renegotiate prices.
She says she will secure the border and stop trafficking, and support an earned path to citizenship for people who follow the law.
She says she will fight lease-purchase deals that trap truck drivers in debt, defend the right to organize, and protect reproductive care and contraception.

people.name: Daniel Butierez Sr.
lines: He says he will secure the southern border and fight to give Border Patrol the resources to do the job.
He says he will cut taxes and simplify the code for small businesses, and he has proposed a flat tax or a national sales tax that would end the IRS as it exists now.
He says he will promote jobs by allowing responsible mining in southern Arizona.

people.name: Danielle Sterbinsky
lines: She says she will help first-time buyers with down payments, assist renters, and bring down child-care costs.
She says she will lower prescription prices, offer a public health-care option, raise the federal minimum wage, and support small businesses and gig workers.
She says she will expand rural broadband and protect water, she signed a pledge to limit House members to three terms, and the campaign takes no corporate PAC money.

people.name: David Redkey
lines: He says his Foundation Economics plan starts with working families and household stability, and that he will fight for a fair wage.
He says he wants stronger public education, including teaching budgeting in every school.
He says guardianship, probate, and fiduciary systems need more transparency so families are not taken advantage of.

people.name: Duwayne Collier
lines: He says he supports strong borders and legal immigration, including more lawful pathways so farming and construction have a workforce.
He says he supports renewable energy, including fusion, and securing Arizona's share of Colorado River water.
He says he would hold corporations accountable for clean air and water and work to bring manufacturing and higher-paying jobs to Arizona.

people.name: Eli Crane
lines: He says he is pro-life and pro-Second Amendment, and that he voted to end taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security while expanding the child tax credit.
He says he would finish the border wall, hire more immigration judges, and stop fentanyl, and he supports a national voter-ID law.
He says rural Arizona should come first, including copper, water, tribal entrepreneurs, and veterans' care, and he opposes wind and solar farms he says raise utility bills.

people.name: Elizabeth Lee
lines: She says she would cosponsor Medicare for All, cap insulin at $35 for everyone, and let Medicare negotiate the price of every drug.
She says billionaires should not pay a lower tax rate than a nurse, and she wants the expanded child tax credit restored and tariffs that raise grocery and medicine prices stopped.
She says she would protect abortion and fertility care, and she supports early voting, vote by mail, and the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act.

people.name: Greg Stanton
lines: He says lowering the cost of living in Arizona is his top priority, and that as a leader of the New Democrat Coalition he helped write a broad policy on that subject.
He says the state's water future depends on a fair deal and that he has delivered results to protect Arizona's water supply.

people.name: Jay Feely
lines: He says he will protect Arizona's water, stand with farmers and ranchers, defend Second Amendment rights, and oppose federal mandates he says hurt families, small businesses, and schools.
He says he will fight to finish the border wall, back Border Patrol and ICE, and work to keep fentanyl out of neighborhoods.
He says he will cut red tape, extend the Trump-era tax cuts, and back domestic manufacturing so the Valley keeps higher-paying jobs.

people.name: JoAnna Mendoza
lines: She says she would crack down on price gouging, modernize the child tax credit, oppose tariffs that raise costs, and strengthen Social Security.
She says she would reverse health-care cuts, protect people with preexisting conditions, and expand Medicare drug-price negotiation.
She says she would fund police, deport people who commit violent crimes, create a path to citizenship for people who follow the law, and require data centers to bring their own power.

people.name: Jonathan Nez
lines: He says he would lower health-care and housing costs, take on drug-price gouging, and reverse Medicaid cuts that threaten rural hospitals.
He says he would secure Arizona's share of Colorado River water, update rural water systems, and protect groundwater.
He also lists rural infrastructure, veterans, voting rights, and tribal sovereignty among his priorities.

people.name: Juan Ciscomani
lines: He says his results include more border agents, lower taxes for everyday Arizonans and seniors, and more funding for cancer research.
He says he also works to support veterans and law enforcement officers.

people.name: Katie Hobbs
lines: She says she eliminated the tax on rent, offered down-payment help for first homes, and cut red tape to make housing more affordable.
She says she created a Border Coordination Office, sent more than $100 million in border-security funding to local police, and that Task Force SAFE has stopped over 19 million fentanyl pills.
She says a water compromise passed under her watch will create jobs, lower housing costs, and conserve water, and that she ended a foreign corporation's groundwater leases.

people.name: Kris Mayes
lines: Her campaign says she took on Saudi-owned mega-farms over Arizona's water and corporations she says gouged people on rent and groceries.

She says she has gone after drug smugglers, elder abusers, and scammers, and that her priorities include protecting rural groundwater, prosecuting sexual predators, and cracking down on AI that targets kids.
Her priorities page also lists overturning tariffs, protecting $2.3 billion in Arizona tax dollars, and protecting Arizonans' freedoms.

people.name: Mark Lamb
lines: He says he will secure the border, stop the cartels, and restore order to immigration while protecting legal immigration and commerce.
He says he will defend the Constitution, support law enforcement, and stand with families and small businesses.
He says he wants lower costs, protection for taxpayers, and stronger American jobs.

people.name: Paul Gosar
lines: He says he would end taxes on Social Security and pension offsets, and he calls the right to keep and bear arms absolute.
He says he supports a balanced-budget amendment, U.S. energy independence, and the president's border wall.
He says he would extend Interstate 11 between Phoenix and Las Vegas and would not cut military health and retirement benefits to fund other programs.

people.name: Risa Lombardo
lines: Her issues page lists the Green Party call to cut the military budget sharply and to move from fossil fuels to renewable energy.
That page also demands a living wage and a stronger safety net.
It calls for public financing of elections, open debates, and voting systems she describes as more representative.

people.name: Teri Ann Hourihan
lines: She says she takes no PAC or special-interest money and wants state government to be more accessible and accountable to residents.
She says she and her running mate are focused on lowering the cost of living and acting for Arizona families rather than either major party.
On schools, she says she would keep school choice, including empowerment scholarship accounts, and audit education spending so more money reaches classrooms.

people.name: Warren Petersen
lines: He says as attorney general he will uphold the rule of law and stand with law enforcement to hold criminals accountable.
He says he will protect the rights of Arizona families.
He says he has worked to keep men out of women's sports and to check government power.

people.name: Yassamin Ansari
lines: She says she supports Medicare for All, more affordable housing, free child care, and a federal minimum wage of $25 an hour.
She says ICE should be abolished and prosecuted, and that Dreamers, refugees, and asylum seekers need a path to stay.
She says she is pushing climate action, public education, and oversight of the administration, including the Epstein investigation.

people.name: Zuhdi Jasser
lines: He says he will rein in spending, let people keep more of what they earn, and cut regulations so small businesses can grow.
He supports a balanced-budget amendment and says both parties have spent without regard for whether the country can afford it.
He says he will back more resources for border agents and school funding that follows students.

people.name: Bruce Westerman
lines: He says he wants lower taxes so families and small businesses can keep more of what they earn, and he points to tax cuts passed while he has been in Congress.
He says he has helped roll back regulations he argues hurt jobs.
As the only forester in the House, he says he wants science-based management of national forests and points to the Resilient Federal Forests Act.

people.name: Chris Jones
lines: He says the economy should mean good jobs, fair wages, small-business growth, reliable internet, and rural hospitals that stay open.
He wants stronger schools, maternal health care, addiction recovery, and food security for families.
He supports early childhood education, apprenticeships, and training in both technology and the trades, plus fair maps and elections people can trust.

people.name: Colt Shelby
lines: He says he will open government records and restore what he calls honest government.
He opposes school voucher plans that he says pull money away from rural public schools.
He opposes the proposed Franklin County prison, and he says data-center expansion should not raise utility rates for families and farms.

people.name: Fred Love
lines: He says he will build regional economic hubs, rebuild roads, water, sewer, and broadband, and expand apprenticeships and affordable housing.
He says he will invest in literacy so students read on grade level, pay and support teachers, and reject policies that move money out of public classrooms.
He says he will stop the proposed 3,000-bed Franklin County prison and put the focus on rehabilitation, job training, and reentry.

people.name: French Hill
lines: He says the Working Families Tax Cut put money back in family budgets, including by ending taxes on tips and overtime and adding a deduction for seniors.
His campaign says his office has closed about 2,000 veteran cases and recovered back pay and benefits, and he has backed bills to expand veterans' care.
He says he has sponsored balanced-budget amendments and wants the federal government to live within its means, and he says he will protect the unborn and the Second Amendment.

people.name: Hallie Shoffner
lines: She says she will cut taxes for working families and lower the cost of groceries, child care, housing, and health care.
She says she will protect and strengthen Social Security and Medicare, lift the payroll-tax cap on the very wealthy, and reverse cuts to those programs.
She says a farm bill should help farmers diversify, sell into regional markets, and supply food to public schools.

people.name: James Russell III
lines: He says wages have not kept up with profits or the cost of living and that he wants higher pay and equal pay for equal work.
He wants fairer taxes, with working people paying less and loopholes closed for the very rich.
He supports expanding Medicare toward health care for everyone and making college or job training affordable.

people.name: Jeff Wadlin
lines: He says broad tariffs should end because they raise prices on food, equipment, vehicles, building materials, and household goods.
He says the goal in health care is to cover everyone while cutting the total cost roughly in half, using private delivery with universal access and protection from catastrophic bills.
He says antitrust law should challenge mergers and consolidation that leave farmers and workers facing only a few suppliers and buyers.

people.name: Kelly Grappe
lines: She says she will show how votes are cast, protected, counted, and verified, and answer doubts with facts rather than dismiss them.
She says she will defend Arkansas's authority to run its own elections and oppose efforts to nationalize that work.
She says transparency is one of the ways to build confidence that elections are secure.

people.name: Kim Hammer
lines: His campaign biography says that in the 94th General Assembly he sponsored bills to protect election integrity, including limits on electioneering near voting sites and authority for the legislature to look into voting irregularities.
It says his priorities include making motor-vehicle registration and driver's-license renewal simpler.
It says he was the lead sponsor of Act 403 of 2021, which lets the legislature end an executive order for a statewide public-health emergency.

people.name: Michael Kalagias
lines: He proposes cutting the state sales-tax rate from 6.5 percent to 5 percent and ending local sales tax on food, diapers, and feminine hygiene products.
He wants the state standard deduction raised to the federal figure of $15,750 for each filer and dependent.
He says the planned large prison should be canceled because he calls it a billion-dollar project the state does not need.

people.name: Michael Pakko
lines: He says he will run elections as a professional operation, with accurate voter rolls, support for county clerks, published procedures, and counts the public can check.
He says ballot access and rule-making should treat every candidate and party the same.
He says election and business-filing data should be published in forms citizens and the press can use.

people.name: Rick Crawford
lines: He says addressing the federal debt is his top priority and that he wants permanent spending controls.
He says he wants to keep an overzealous federal government off people's backs.
His campaign also invites supporters to join him in lowering taxes, growing the economy, and standing up for conservative values.

people.name: Robb Ryerse
lines: He says he will not take corporate PAC money and that the campaign is funded by neighbors.
He says a representative should show up for town halls and answer questions in the district.
He says he wants good jobs, safe neighborhoods, strong schools, and a government that works for families rather than a party.

people.name: Steve Womack
lines: He says he is running again on a pro-growth, pro-jobs, and pro-family agenda.
He says the country faces global threats, a rising national debt, and inflation, and that he will keep working on those for the 3rd District.

people.name: Terri Yarbrough Green
lines: She says power should be checked, and that she wants dark money out of politics and elections people can trust.
She supports family farms, a higher minimum wage, and health care that does not bankrupt people or force women to travel hours for maternity care.
She says communities need safe roads, broadband, public schools, productive farmland, and utilities that serve both the environment and local needs.

people.name: Tom Cotton
lines: He says he wrote the RAISE Act, helped pass the Laken Riley Act, and has a voting record he describes as fully opposed to illegal immigration.
He says he cast a decisive vote for a large middle-class tax cut, ended the Affordable Care Act tax on Arkansans, and worked to lower energy and health-care costs.
He says his Armed Services work and his relationship with President Trump brought billions in defense investment to places including Pine Bluff, Fort Ebbing, and Little Rock.

people.name: Adam Gray
lines: He says he is working to lower the cost of food, housing, health care, and utilities, including by limiting tariffs he argues raise prices for families and farmers.
He says water is the issue he hears about most, and he has pushed storage projects, faster environmental review, and funding for local water systems.
He says he would cut red tape that stalls infrastructure, support agriculture, and strengthen public safety so families are not choosing between health care and rent.

people.name: Aisha Wahab
lines: She says she has taken on powerful interests over affordable housing, homeownership, and living conditions.
She says she has fought for jobs, career training, and small businesses, and for funding for food, health care, and public education.
She says she has worked with law enforcement on public safety and pushed for a cleaner environment.

people.name: Ami Bera
lines: He says every American should have affordable coverage, and he opposes turning Medicare into a voucher system.
He says he would cut waste and fraud, strengthen the doctor-patient relationship, and invest in research including stem cell research.
He says rural and mountain communities need primary care, telehealth, broadband, and stable funding for rural hospitals and clinics.

people.name: Angela Gonzales-Torres
lines: She says she would abolish ICE, make Los Angeles more affordable, and increase access to critical services.
She says housing, health care, and education should be affordable, and she wants higher taxes on the wealthy to pay for them.
She says she would abolish super PACs so elections answer to voters rather than donors.

people.name: Angélica Dueñas
lines: She says she takes no corporate PAC, AIPAC, oil, or drug-company money, and she supports Medicare for All and housing as a right.
She says she would abolish ICE, create a path to legal status, and pass the DREAM Act.
She says she would raise the minimum wage, protect the right to unionize, and cancel student debt by making public college and trade school tuition-free.

people.name: April Verlato
lines: She says the economy should reward innovation and hard work rather than regulations she argues hold back workers and small businesses.
She points to her role founding the Downtown Arcadia Improvement Association and says she focused on opportunities for minority-owned businesses.
She says she would go to Congress to bring back good-paying jobs and economic growth.

people.name: Armen Kurdian
lines: He says housing, groceries, and gas are squeezing families, and he would lower those costs and stop wasteful spending.
He says California's utility bills are among the nation's highest and he would fight to make power cheaper and more reliable.
He says he would bring back good-paying jobs, support small business, and cut regulations he argues are pushing employers out.

people.name: Barbara Lee
lines: She says streets are getting cleaner and that she wants more good-paying local jobs.
She says she will keep a broad approach to homelessness and add affordable housing across the city.
She says she is using prevention programs against crime and wants Oakland to be a model of accountable city government.

people.name: Bob Smith
lines: He says he would cut wasteful spending, lower housing, energy, and food costs, and expand homeownership while protecting Social Security and Medicare.
He says schools should emphasize reading, math, and STEM, plus vocational paths and research ties to local universities.
He says immigration policy should secure the border, remove people convicted of violent crimes, and update farmworker visas.

people.name: Brad Sherman
lines: He says he has a perfect rating from the Brady Campaign and an F from the NRA, and he has pushed an assault-weapons ban and longer background checks.
He says he cosponsors a safe-storage bill named for a teenager killed by an unsecured firearm.
He says he has championed consumer protections and helped create the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

people.name: Brenda Grisham
lines: She says she will focus on safer neighborhoods and stronger public safety.
She says city government should be more accountable and transparent, and that local businesses need support to grow.
She says she wants more stable housing, cleaner streets, and stronger neighborhood services.

people.name: Brian Burley
lines: He says he would advocate tax relief for families and business owners.
He says he would take a stand against illegal immigration and fully support law enforcement and the military.
He says he would fight to restore what he calls American family values.

people.name: Charles Hoelter
lines: He says he would secure the border, lower taxes, support law enforcement, and defend constitutional rights.
He says immigration should be legal and controlled, and that parents should have a voice in what schools teach.
He says veterans need better health care and support, and that government spending should come down.

people.name: Chuong Vo
lines: He says he is running to keep families safe, lower costs, and hold government accountable.
He says that on the council he focused on safe neighborhoods, responsive city services, and balanced budgets.
He says he returned campaign contributions after a council election and supports ending insider stock trading in Congress.

people.name: Connie Chan
lines: She says Washington should stop cutting public programs to pay for tax breaks for billionaires and corporations, and should rebuild worker bargaining power.
She says she would reform the tax and budget system and defend rights she says are under threat.
She points to her work on affordable housing, small-business and union protections, and legal help for immigrants facing enforcement.

people.name: Cristian Morales
lines: He says he wants better education and job skills, a state where business is affordable, and more work for blue-collar families.
He says immigration, housing costs, crime, homelessness, health care, and civil rights are the pillars of his campaign.
He says government should protect freedoms, secure the border, and stay accountable rather than grow larger.

people.name: Dave Min
lines: He says the cost of housing is the biggest challenge in his district, the main reason people leave, and the top driver of homelessness.
He says he voted against cuts to Medicaid and Medicare and to keep premium tax credits that help people afford care.
He says he cannot be bought and is focused on cleaning up corruption in Washington.

people.name: David Pan
lines: He says he supports charter schools and vouchers so parents can choose a school.
He says rising crime requires more police and enforcement of the law.
He says the border should be secured before the country can have a serious immigration debate.

people.name: David Valadao
lines: He says California should stay an agricultural leader, and that farms and towns need a reliable water supply.
He says health care should be more affordable while protecting seniors, people with low incomes, and people with pre-existing conditions.
He says the immigration system is broken and needs a full repair, and he wants Washington to balance its budget.

people.name: Derek Tran
lines: He says he has introduced a bill to protect veterans' jobs and reinstate veterans laid off from federal jobs.
He says he opposes cuts to Medicaid and Medicare and has fought to lower prescription prices.
He says he is defending abortion rights and funding for Planned Parenthood, and he wants higher teacher pay and more vocational training.

people.name: Donald Wagner
lines: He says elections should be secure, efficient, accurate, and accessible.
He says the office's business division should be friendly to small business.
He says he supports the voter-identification initiative on the November ballot.

people.name: Doris Matsui
lines: She says she has secured billions for flood protection, including Folsom Dam and levee work, and helped pass the Affordable Care Act and Medicare drug-price provisions.
She says she would expand telehealth and mental-health clinics and keep pushing clean-energy and grid programs that lower bills.
She says she opposes immigration raids she calls unlawful, votes against funding ICE, and objects to masked agents operating outside the rule of law.

people.name: Eric Ching
lines: He says he will defend speech, religion, and the right to keep and bear arms, and secure the border against illegal weapons, drugs, and people while keeping legal trade and tourism moving.
He says he supports term limits, reasonable pay for officials, and restitution from people convicted of crimes.
He says he supports school choice, opposes identity-based admissions and racially divisive curriculum, and wants fewer regulations on U.S. businesses.

people.name: Eric Jones
lines: He says corruption and corporate money drive the cost of living, and he wants corporate funds out of politics, a ban on congressional stock trading, and an end to gerrymandering.
He says he would cut taxes for working people, challenge utility monopolies, add Medicare coverage for vision, dental, hearing, and in-home care, and lower prescription prices.
He says he would defend Social Security, secure water and family farms, and refuse blank checks for war.

people.name: Genevieve Angel
lines: She says she would lower costs and create more economic opportunity.
She says she wants safe communities with real accountability and health care that is affordable and accessible.
She says immigration policy should be secure, fair, and practical.

people.name: George Whitesides
lines: He says he is fighting to lower daily costs, create local jobs, defend Social Security and Medicare, and root out corruption.
He says he has brought back federal money for public safety, clean water, and youth programs, and he is focused on the wildfire crisis.
He says he has introduced bills on tax relief after environmental disasters, firefighter pay, and housing for veterans.

people.name: Gil Cisneros
lines: He says he would require universal background checks, restore an assault-weapons ban, and fund gun-violence research.
He says reproductive decisions belong with a patient and a doctor, and he highlights a Pentagon policy he led on reproductive care for service members.
He says he would raise the minimum wage, lower drug prices, and push a public option while defending veterans' benefits.

people.name: Gloria Romero
lines: She says she will use the lieutenant governor's seats on public college and university boards to restore merit in admissions and to hold campuses accountable for student safety.
She says community colleges need tighter oversight so public money goes to students learning job skills.
She says she will push faster rebuilding after wildfires, simpler coastal and land permitting, and land management that puts communities ahead of paperwork.

people.name: Hilda Solis
lines: She says she is running to defend workers, immigrants, educators, affordable housing, reproductive rights, veterans, unions, Medicaid, and democracy.
She says she has prioritized clean air, water, and open space, and she cites environmental-justice laws recognized with a Profile in Courage award.
She says she wants to create and preserve affordable housing and find better ways to help people who are homeless.

people.name: Houston Brignano
lines: He says student debt and housing costs, including a first-time homebuyer age he puts at 40, are shutting people out of a stable life.
He says he would train young people to use artificial intelligence and protect jobs from automation with reskilling programs.

people.name: Jacqui Irwin
lines: She says she would stand up for the district against what she calls an assault on democracy and California values.
Her campaign highlights laws she wrote on housing and services for homeless veterans, a state climate law, and gun-safety measures.
It says she has worked to create jobs, balance budgets, and keep communities safe.

people.name: James Gallagher
lines: He says he would lower taxes, fees, and regulations to make life more affordable for North State families.
He says he would pass tougher crime laws, expand energy production to bring prices down, and continue the president's border security approach.
He says he would defend property rights and parental rights and shield farms and businesses from excessive regulation.

people.name: Jamie Joyce
lines: She says a bill she wrote, the MAD Act, would set guardrails for artificial intelligence, limit immigration enforcement and surveillance, and require a government plan for how AI affects jobs and the environment.
She says she takes no corporate or pro-Israel PAC money and wants more Epstein files released, dark money disclosed, and stronger checks on the presidency.
She also says she would seek affordable health care and housing, higher teacher pay, and more support for people who are homeless.

people.name: Jared Huffman
lines: He says he has worked on climate action, wildfire disaster relief, dam removal on the Klamath River, and offshore wind in Humboldt County.
He says he has pushed federal money for local infrastructure, tribal clean energy and broadband, salmon habitat, and toxic-site cleanup.
He says he has defended democracy and the separation of church and state, and sought stronger school funding for students with disabilities.

people.name: Jason Gibbs
lines: He says he would oppose new taxes, push energy affordability, and cut wasteful spending to lower the cost of housing, groceries, gas, and energy.
He says he would back law enforcement and end what he calls catch-and-release treatment of repeat offenders.
He says he is running to put local values and practical problem-solving ahead of party politics.

people.name: Jay Obernolte
lines: He says he is fighting to balance the federal budget and stop spending he argues is driving up prices.
He says he has worked to lower taxes, repeal gas taxes, help small businesses, and expand the child tax credit.
He says he wrote a bill to hold fentanyl dealers accountable, voted to fund the military and a border-security bill, and wants the border wall finished.

people.name: Jeff Belle
lines: He says he would safeguard constitutional rights, secure the border, and provide financial relief to families and small businesses.
He says housing policy should add supply, speed approvals, and make starter homes and apartments easier to build.
He says he would invest in public schools and make federal small-business programs easier for neighborhood employers to use.

people.name: Jeff Frese
lines: He says he would set an eight-year congressional term limit, ban members from trading stocks, withhold pay if there is no budget, and close the lobbying revolving door.
He says he would stop deficit spending that raises mortgage rates, cut building red tape, and bar Wall Street and foreign buyers from single-family homes and farmland.
He says he would back police and fentanyl prosecutions, require voter ID with paper ballots, put classrooms ahead of bureaucracy, and refuse cuts to Social Security and Medicare.

people.name: Jenny Rae Le Roux
lines: She says she will cut waste and fraud so groceries, gas, insurance, and rent cost less.
She says federal housing money should go first to cities that cut permit delays and fees, and that energy should be produced onshore rather than drilled off Orange County.
She says she will fully fund border security, end catch-and-release, and require federal homelessness grants to show they get people off the street.

people.name: Jim Costa
lines: He says he helped win federal money for drinking water, aging water projects, storage, highways, and wildfire risk reduction.
He says he has funded hospitals, community clinics, and a Valley medical school, and sought more officers to fight gangs and drugs.
He says he has defended Dreamers, opposed family separations, and supports a path to citizenship.

people.name: Jim Desmond
lines: He says it is time for common sense to return to government and for leaders to fix problems.
His site lists the cost of living, homelessness, the border, energy, and vocational and military education among his priorities.

people.name: Jimmy Gomez
lines: He says he is fighting for Medicare for All so a medical bill does not bankrupt a family.
He says he championed an expansion of paid family leave in the Assembly and wants a national paid-family-leave program.
He says he voted for the Inflation Reduction Act and has worked to lower prescription prices for seniors.

people.name: Jimmy Panetta
lines: He says he would ease inflation by investing in roads, rail, research, manufacturing, broadband, and water, and by expanding child care and equal pay.
He says he has written bills to block offshore oil drilling, cut carbon emissions, and fund wildfire prevention and reforestation.
He says he has pushed housing tax credits for low- and middle-income homes and grants for veterans and people who are homeless.

people.name: Joe Males
lines: He says he ran for council after his son, also a Marine, was murdered, because he wants the rule of law so other families do not face that loss.
He says his council work has focused on infrastructure, business growth, and safer, cleaner neighborhoods.
He says he would bring that same results-focused approach to Washington for the Inland Empire and Imperial County.

people.name: John Garamendi
lines: He says Make It In America rules should steer federal purchases to U.S. manufacturing, and he highlights a higher Buy America share for buses and rail.
He supports a national public option, rural hospitals and clinics, and letting Medicare negotiate drug prices.
He says he would stop Delta tunnel projects that could drain the estuary and keep pushing water storage such as Sites Reservoir.

people.name: John McBride
lines: He says he would remove dangerous chemicals from food and water, emphasize medical freedom and natural healing, and oppose what he calls death boards.
He says he would back local police, prosecute crime, support youth mental health, and strengthen the southern border.
He says farms need water rights and less federal control, and he wants lower taxes, no tax on Social Security, and deep cuts in spending.

people.name: Josh Harder
lines: He says he would cut insulin and other drug prices, repeal federal and state gas taxes, and get housing costs under control.

He says he would bring ag-tech, technology, and clean-energy jobs to the Valley, treat homelessness as an emergency with mental-health and job help, and fund police work against methamphetamine and fentanyl.
He says he would stop a Delta tunnel he argues would send Valley water south, build storage, and keep a path to citizenship for Dreamers alongside border enforcement against traffickers.

people.name: Juan Vargas
lines: He says he is working to grow good-paying jobs through clean energy, infrastructure, and small businesses.
He says he has championed public education and services for communities that have been left out.
His site says he is also fighting to protect health care and veterans.

people.name: Judy Chu
lines: She says her Ways and Means work covers taxes, trade, Social Security, and Medicare, including health care and safety-net programs.
She says the caucus she led expanded language access in federal agencies and pushed for data that reflects Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander communities.
She says she co-chairs a bipartisan caucus on creative rights.

people.name: Julius Robinson
lines: He says the city should be safer and cleaner, and that businesses need support to grow.
He says housing, homelessness, and economic opportunity have to be handled together.
He says local government should operate with more transparency and accountability.

people.name: Karen Bass
lines: She says the Trump administration's ICE raids and militarized actions have no purpose other than to create fear.
She says those actions damage the city's economy and tear families apart.

people.name: Ken Calvert
lines: He says he wrote the law that created E-Verify and wants employers required to use it.
He says he has secured more than a billion dollars for transportation, water, and clean-air projects in Riverside County.
He says his office has helped veterans and seniors get benefits they are owed.

people.name: Kevin Kiley
lines: He says he has worked across parties on measures to lower the cost of gasoline, groceries, utilities, and insurance.
He points to a federal grant to ease traffic near Highways 65 and 80 and to a Lake Tahoe restoration law he says funds wildfire mitigation.
He says he helped restore Medicare funding for senior programs and is focused on prosecuting violent crime and protecting children from fentanyl.

people.name: Kevin Lincoln
lines: He says he would secure the border, enforce immigration laws, and treat fentanyl trafficking as a threat to Valley families.
He says he would cut wasteful spending and lower taxes as grocery, gas, and rent costs climb, pointing to budgets he balanced as mayor without a tax increase.
He says he would oppose early release and shorter sentences for repeat offenders, and he highlights police pay and budget increases he backed as mayor.

people.name: Kevin Mullin
lines: He says he would lower housing costs, send federal money to local child-care programs, and update the federal poverty line.
He says he is defending medical research and the innovation economy in his district.
His campaign also lists health-care costs, climate action, reproductive rights, and a fairer tax policy among his priorities.

people.name: Kyle Kirkland
lines: He says housing, food, gas, and health care are too expensive because of over-regulation, and he would restart domestic production to bring costs down.
He says government should be audited so tax dollars are not lost to waste and fraud.
He says law enforcement needs tools against fentanyl and trafficking, and farmers need more water storage and fewer regulatory barriers.

people.name: Larry Thompson
lines: He says he will protect family values and wants people to use common sense and civility to find common ground.
He says his goal is to get something done, and he asks for a vote in the November 3, 2026 general election.

people.name: Lateefah Simon
lines: Her campaign names public safety, affordable housing, homelessness, and job creation among her priorities.
She also lists health care for all, reproductive freedom, immigration, disability rights, and LGBTQ rights.
She highlights voting rights, climate, transportation, and what she calls a care economy.

people.name: Laura Friedman
lines: She says she is focused on affordable housing, universal health care and child care, and economic security for families.
She says she has been a voice for public education, the environment, and safeguarding democracy.
She says her legislative work expanded affordable housing and services for people with severe mental illness and people who are homeless.

people.name: Linda Sánchez
lines: She says she is fighting to lower costs for working families and to protect her community from the Trump administration and ICE.
She says she wants safe, quality education for children and job growth through innovation and manufacturing.
She says workers deserve safe jobs, good wages, and a dignified retirement.

people.name: Lou Correa
lines: He says public service should be about people rather than partisan games.
He says he wants practical results for a blue-collar district he describes as home to many veterans and Dreamers.

people.name: Luz Rivas
lines: She says her Assembly priority was funding for infrastructure, education, and health care in the Valley, along with environmental justice.
She says she worked to expand computer-science and climate education across California.
Her campaign says that in her first House term she joined Democratic leadership and co-chairs a bipartisan STEM education caucus.

people.name: Mai Vang
lines: She says she takes no corporate PAC money and would raise the minimum wage with inflation, tax billionaires, and pass the PRO Act.
She says she would fight for Medicare for All, an end to medical debt, and federal protection of reproductive care.
She says she would fund more affordable housing, stop corporations from buying up single-family homes, and pause new data centers so households do not pay their power costs.

people.name: Mark DeSaulnier
lines: He says workers need a voice as artificial intelligence changes jobs, and he points to proposals on layoffs, CEO pay, and the right to organize.
He says housing, transit, and wages have to be tackled together so families are not pushed out of the Bay Area, and he highlights clean-air rules and a national electric-vehicle charging program.
He says he would protect cancer-research funding, codify abortion and contraception access, and pursue immigration enforcement that does not separate families.

people.name: Mark Takano
lines: He says that as a teacher and trustee he worked on public education and job training for adults.
His campaign says he is the ranking Democrat on the House Veterans' Affairs Committee and also serves on Education and the Workforce.

people.name: Marni von Wilpert
lines: She says she is running to lower costs for working families and to clean up corruption in Washington.
She says that as the daughter of an immigrant Army veteran she is fighting ICE tactics she calls unconstitutional, including masked agents.
She says she wants a secure border and a path to citizenship for long-term residents and Dreamers.

people.name: Maxine Waters
lines: Her office says expanding health care is a priority, including the Minority AIDS Initiative and services for diabetes, cancer, and Alzheimer's disease.
Her office says she has worked to keep families in their homes and wrote the Neighborhood Stabilization Program to fight foreclosures and blight.
Her office says she works to limit the harm of expanding Los Angeles International Airport and to preserve the Ballona wetlands.

people.name: Melissa Hernandez
lines: She says her first priority is lowering housing, health-care, and child-care costs, protecting Social Security and Medicare, and growing small businesses without raising taxes.
She says public safety should support police and firefighters and also demand that enforcement work fairly.
She says she would lower drug prices, restore insurance subsidies, and protect reproductive care.

people.name: Michael Gates
lines: He says he will make statewide enforcement of Proposition 36 his top task and will prioritize prosecution of violent and repeat offenders.
He says cities and counties, not the state, should control zoning and housing decisions, and that he will defend that local authority.
He says he will investigate fraud in state programs and sue to recover public money.

people.name: Michael Masuda
lines: He says he would lower housing, health-care, and energy costs and send more federal money back to rural communities.
He says wildfire work should include thinning, prescribed fire, home hardening, and faster disaster aid so insurance is more available.
He says he would keep rural hospitals open, expand telehealth, protect Medicare and Medi-Cal, and support water and markets for farmers.

people.name: Mike Cargile
lines: He says the country should end endless wars, break up corporate monopolies, and become energy independent.
He says fair and transparent elections are required to do that.
He describes himself as pro-life, pro-jobs, and pro-police.

people.name: Mike Levin
lines: He says ethics reform should start by banning members of Congress from trading individual stocks.
He says clean energy, a modern grid, and desalination should make energy and water more affordable.
He says the country should build more homes people can afford, fix California's insurance market, and protect Medicaid and Medicare.

people.name: Mike McGuire
lines: He says he would pass Medicare for All, guarantee coverage and mental health care, and keep rural hospitals open.
He says he would raise wages, challenge corporate price gouging, and build on state steps he describes as lowering utility bills, expanding child care, and making college more affordable.
He says he would defend abortion, contraception, and IVF access, and he highlights work to double the number of state firefighters and fund wildfire prevention.

people.name: Mike Thompson
lines: He says he voted for the Affordable Care Act, helped let Medicare negotiate some drug prices, and wants telehealth expanded and made permanent.
He says he is fighting health-coverage cuts that he argues would take insurance away from millions of people.
He says jobs and a lower cost of living are his priority, pointing to infrastructure investment and an effort to restore clean-energy tax credits ended by a recent law.

people.name: Mindy Pechenuk
lines: She says she will grow the police force, end federal oversight of the department, and target open-air drug markets and fentanyl trafficking.
She says she will bring in an outside audit of city finances, including nonprofits, and use tax incentives to reopen businesses and add manufacturing.
She says people without housing who need drug or mental-health treatment should get it, and that the job training and housing help she describes would be limited to American citizens.

people.name: Mitch Clemmons
lines: He says he would lower barriers that raise housing costs and open practical paths to homeownership.
He says he would cut red tape so local employers can invest, hire, and grow.
He says he would support law enforcement, first responders, secure borders, and public safety.

people.name: Nanette Barragan
lines: She says she is fighting for Dreamers, deported veterans, Social Security, Medicare, and the environment, including opposition to offshore oil drilling.
She says seniors who paid into Medicare and Social Security should not have to choose between medication and groceries.
She says education is a right and that college, including community college, needs to be more affordable.

people.name: Nithya Raman
lines: She says Los Angeles must build much more housing, at every price level, so more people can afford a home.
She says she will fill potholes, pave roads, plant trees, turn streetlights on, and put a park near where people live.

She says a 911 call should bring the right response, including unarmed responders where armed officers are not needed, and that she will protect residents from immigration raids and landlord harassment.

people.name: Norma Torres
lines: She says her work has been about safer communities and lower costs for Inland Empire families.
She says working families need a champion in Congress who will help them get ahead.

people.name: Pedro Casas
lines: He says he wants to raise the standard of education and fight the fentanyl epidemic.
He says the justice system should not reward criminal behavior that leaves victims and businesses behind.
He says he would secure the southern border and pursue immigration changes that put national security first.

people.name: Pete Aguilar
lines: He says he is working to lower prescription costs, make housing more affordable, and expand American manufacturing.
He says he has backed protections and jobs for veterans and tax and red-tape cuts for small businesses.
He says he wants health care to be more affordable and the immigration system fixed.

people.name: Peter Soulé
lines: He says he would withhold federal money from sanctuary cities that he argues block deportation of people here illegally who commit crimes, and he would defend Second Amendment rights.
He says he would end spending he calls waste, make energy and housing cheaper, and reform the H-1B visa program to favor hiring Americans.
He says he would stop drugs from reaching young people, protect parental choice in schools, and fund only schools that emphasize reading, writing, math, and vocational training.

people.name: Peter Verbica
lines: He says he would end high gas taxes, send more water to farmers to lower food costs, and fix California's insurance crisis.
He says neighborhoods should have more say over housing, and he opposes the state's private-attorney general law and limits on independent contractors.
He says immigration policy should serve both tech and agriculture, and he also backs school choice and merit-based education.

people.name: Randy Villegas
lines: He says he is running to fight for working families, protect democracy, and bring people-first leadership to Washington.
His campaign lists the cost of living, health care, jobs, immigration, housing, and water among its top issues.
He says education changed his life and that he wants the next generation to have the same chance.

people.name: Raul Ruiz
lines: He says he will protect and expand Medicare and Social Security and oppose cuts or a higher retirement age.
He says he would cut red tape for small businesses and develop Imperial Valley lithium and Salton Sea projects that create jobs.
He says he opposes congressional pay raises and first-class flights at taxpayer expense, and he highlights work for veterans.

people.name: Ricardo Cabrera
lines: He says he is fighting for congressional term limits and a lower cost of living.
He says he wants to confront corruption and create more opportunity for young entrepreneurs.

people.name: Richard Pan
lines: He says he would defend the Affordable Care Act and Medicare, stop insurers from denying care doctors prescribe, and lower prescription prices.
He says he would require universal background checks, ban assault weapons, and fund first responders and violence-prevention programs.
He says he would create a path to citizenship, overhaul immigration enforcement, and write abortion rights into federal law.

people.name: Ritesh Tandon
lines: He says he would cut everyday costs for groceries, utilities, transportation, and insurance by increasing competition and cracking down on junk fees.
He says he would speed housing permits, help first-time buyers, and expand workforce housing near jobs and transit.
He says he would lower out-of-pocket medical and drug costs, make job training cheaper, and oppose new layers of taxes and fees.

people.name: Ro Khanna
lines: He says his platform is Medicare for All, taxes on billionaires, good jobs in every town, and no foreign wars.
He also campaigns on free child care, free college and trade school, and a path to homeownership by age 35.
He says technology should put humans first, and he lists reproductive rights, a living wage, and expanding Social Security among his priorities.

people.name: Rob Bonta
lines: He says he is defending California's gun laws, including the assault-weapons ban, and expanding programs that take guns from people barred from having them.
He says health care is a human right and that he is defending the state's reproductive-care laws and coverage expansions.
He says he is taking polluters to court, especially where pollution falls on poorer communities, and pursuing employers who steal wages.

people.name: Robb Tucker
lines: He says federal rules written for big cities stall rural work on forests, water, housing, and roads, and he wants early county consultation and rural-impact reviews.
He says Washington should back border enforcement, fentanyl prosecutions, and equipment and hiring for rural sheriff's offices.
He says homelessness funding should require treatment and fewer unsheltered encampments, and that federal land managers should help clear hazardous fuels before wildfires.

people.name: Robert Garcia
lines: He says he supports Proposition 50 and sees defending democracy against the far right as Congress's most important job.
He says he supports the Green New Deal and is leading a transportation version of it to electrify public transit.
He says every young adult should have a tuition-free college or trade program, undocumented families should have a path to citizenship, and everyone should have health care and housing.

people.name: Robin Littau
lines: She says she would cut excessive regulation, support local control, and require more responsible federal spending.
She says she would change immigration policy, including citizenship requirements, and back a parental bill of rights against mandates.
She says she would support law enforcement, stronger deterrence against people who harm children, small businesses, and constitutional rights.

people.name: Rudy Recile
lines: He says public-school results are too low and wants a return to reading, writing, and math, with parents told what their children are taught.
He says education money should follow the child, including tax credits for private school, home school, and extra tuition.
He says Congress should move long-stalled veterans disability bills, and he wants election systems open to verification so no one company controls voting.

people.name: Salud Carbajal
lines: He says he is running to lower the cost of living and expand opportunity for working families.
He says he would defend immigrant communities from immigration raids he calls extreme.
He says he would protect the local environment, pointing to his opposition to new offshore oil drilling and work on a county climate plan.

people.name: Sam Gallucci
lines: He says he would back law enforcement, first responders, and community-based prevention.
He says he would defend the coast, forests, and reliable water with practical, science-guided solutions.
His site also lists the cost of living, parent-centered education, homelessness, immigration, and veterans among his priorities.

people.name: Sam Liccardo
lines: He says he is trying to make housing more affordable, including by turning vacant buildings into homes and protecting low-income families from homelessness.
He says he has written bipartisan bills to lower health-insurance premiums and bank fees.
He says he wants technology used so more Americans benefit from innovation, and he is working to protect constitutional rights.

people.name: Samantha Mota
lines: Her site lists economic security, community-based projects, immigration reform, and universal health care among her priorities.
She says she wants politics to be more affordable and more open to participation.

people.name: Sandra Van Scotter
lines: She says she supports Medicare for All and would work to reverse health-care cuts she argues will hurt Medi-Cal recipients, people with disabilities, and seniors.
She says disability services are underfunded and too hard to navigate, and she would bring that experience to Congress.
She says immigration policy should combine a path to legal status for longtime workers with border security, and she wants water policy that serves Valley farms and residents.

people.name: Sara Jacobs
lines: She says the country must act on climate change and on gun violence in schools and communities.
She says she is fighting for housing people can afford, health care as a human right, and access to reproductive care.
She says that in Congress she is working so every child has the same opportunities.

people.name: Scott Meyers
lines: He says California families are being squeezed by inflation, energy costs, housing prices, and taxes, and he wants lower taxes and less federal spending.
He says he would support American energy production to lower gas and utility bills and cut rules he argues drive up housing and small-business costs.
He says he would secure the border, restore law and order, and protect constitutional freedoms.

people.name: Scott Peters
lines: He says he co-led a bipartisan law to make it easier to build affordable manufactured homes and has worked to get homelessness aid to local nonprofits.
He says his work laid groundwork for Medicare drug-price negotiation, a $35 insulin cap, and a yearly cap on what seniors pay for medicine.
He says he helped win federal money to repair and expand the plant that treats sewage crossing the border at the Tijuana River.

people.name: Scott Wiener
lines: He says he would abolish ICE, ban face coverings that hide agents, let people sue federal officers, end private immigration prisons, and create a path to citizenship.
He says he would push a plan to build 8 million homes in a decade, including social housing and a larger housing tax credit, paid for by reversing parts of corporate and high-end tax cuts.
He says he would pass the Equality Act, defend Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act on the way to Medicare for All, and increase federal transit operating funds.

people.name: Shane Lewis
lines: He says Title I money should go only to schools that improve core instruction and show measurable gains in student proficiency.
He says students from third through twelfth grade should get civics that teaches responsibility, critical thinking, and American history.
His campaign also lists immigration, tax reform, and water infrastructure among his priorities.

people.name: Shirley Weber
lines: She says she will work with local elections officials to protect and expand access to the ballot.
She says she will make elections, lobbyist registration, and campaign finance easier for the public to see.
She says she will tighten the office's cybersecurity and rebuild voter-education programs for people who were incarcerated, including people on parole after Proposition 17.

people.name: Stephanie Vargas
lines: She says she would support law enforcement and firefighters and focus on the causes of danger in the community.
She says she wants to lower taxes, energy costs, and the cost of living, and to address the housing crisis.
She says she would protect children and family values and fight for elections people can trust.

people.name: Steve Cohen
lines: He says he would expand the housing supply and go after corporate price manipulation.
He says he would lower prescription costs, protect coverage for pre-existing conditions, and hold insurers accountable.
He says he would defend Social Security and Medicare from cuts and oppose wasteful federal spending.

people.name: Steve Hilton
lines: He says he will bring gasoline to $3, cut utility bills in half, and eliminate state income tax on the first $150,000.
He says he will clear the rules and fees that keep young families from buying starter homes.
He says every student should read by third grade, every school should offer skills training, and the annual $800 small-business tax should end.

people.name: Steve Manos
lines: His site frames the race around faith, family, and affordability.
He says he listens to residents so their voices are heard, and that he knows how to get tangible results from government.

people.name: Ted Lieu
lines: He says he secured safety funding for the West Los Angeles VA and wrote a law for a campus plan to house veterans who are homeless.
He says he co-authored an impeachment article after January 6 and served as an impeachment manager.
He says he has led on artificial intelligence, including a bipartisan House task force and a bill to create a national AI commission.

people.name: Tessa Hodge
lines: She says lasting change has to address inequality, injustice, addiction, mental health, and poverty at the policy level.
Her site lists health-care access, livable wages, lower housing costs, and a humane immigration policy among her priorities.
She also lists the environment, public education, and veterans and the military.

people.name: Tom McClintock
lines: He says the national debt is the country's greatest danger and wants a balanced-budget amendment, yearly review of mandatory spending, and no spending that Congress has not authorized.
He says environmental review and lawsuits have blocked routine forest thinning, leaving overcrowded federal forests to burn.
He says he has pushed legislation to speed removal of dead timber, replanting, and management that reduces catastrophic fire.

people.name: Vince Fong
lines: He says domestic energy production should lower costs for families and small businesses while the country still protects the environment.
He says farmers need more storage and conveyance and fewer rules that send water out to sea.
He says border enforcement should come before other immigration changes, and he opposes new gun limits on people who follow the law.

people.name: Xavier Becerra
lines: He says health care is a human right and that he would strengthen Medi-Cal and build toward a universal single-payer system.
He says he would treat housing as essential infrastructure and build more homes so costs stop rising out of control.
He says he would take on insurance, childcare, and grocery costs by standing up to price gouging and unjustified rate hikes.

people.name: Young Kim
lines: She says she is working to lower the cost of gas, groceries, utilities, health care, and prescription drugs, and to protect Medicare.
She says she led a bill to recover taxpayer money lost to fraud after billions were stolen.
She says her Assembly work included public safety, help for victims of domestic violence, and resources for veterans and homeless children.

people.name: Zoe Lofgren
lines: She says she wants faster research on fusion energy and a stronger federal science agenda on wildfires and flooding.
Her campaign points to her work on immigration, health care, technology, transportation, and women's issues.
She says the district she represents is unusually diverse, including a large Hispanic population and the country's largest concentration of Vietnamese Americans.

people.name: Adam Withrow
lines: He says fossil fuels are finite and that the country should start moving off them instead of building the future on older technology.
He says medicine has been organized around corporate profit, and that health care for everyone would cost less than half the defense budget.
He says he opposes war, and that trade and treating people as equals will do more than bombs.

people.name: Amanda Campbell
lines: She says the state and federal constitutions bind politicians, and that the secretary of state should defend them by warning the legislature and going to court.
She says voters have a right to use the initiative process without politicians interfering.
She says business filings should be simpler, and that election security should be improved with each county as the state grows.

people.name: Amanda Gonzalez
lines: She says that as clerk she has worked to expand ballot access, improve election security, and run elections in one of the state's largest counties.
She says the office should serve Colorado, not her own politics.
She says she will work so every voice is heard, every vote is counted, and elections stay secure.

people.name: Blake Huber
lines: He wants approval voting, so people can support every candidate they like and elections are not decided by fear of wasting a vote.
He says immigration should pair orderly borders with a simpler legal path for people who pass background checks and want to work.
He says federal rules bury small businesses in cost and paperwork, and that old rules should expire while new ones face a test of their economic impact.

people.name: Bob Chew
lines: He says he will measure success by problems solved and people helped, not by how much public money is spent.
He says he cannot be bought or bullied, and that his promise is to Coloradans rather than to parties or donors.

people.name: Brittany Pettersen
lines: She says she will keep working on small-business capital, job training, and rural broadband, and that she wants to stop price gouging and lower costs for families.
She says she supports a fast shift to wind, solar, and geothermal power, and that she will protect public lands and water levels in the Arkansas River.
She says she will defend Medicare and Social Security, let Medicare negotiate drug prices, and protect the right to vote.

people.name: Celeste Landry
lines: She says her campaign is for the right to vote.
She says she wants better representation.
She says she is fighting for election integrity.

people.name: Christopher Baum
lines: He says people should be able to support a lesser-known candidate without taking a vote away from a major-party candidate.
He says government should be smaller.
He says the national debt should be eliminated.

people.name: Christy Peterson
lines: She says she stands for low taxes, limited government, and peace through strength.
She says she would review Social Security's finances so the program can stay solvent, and that she would cut the federal debt.
She says she supports Colorado's Taxpayer's Bill of Rights.

people.name: Dwayne Romero
lines: He says affordability comes first, and that he would start by repealing tariffs and expanding family tax credits.
