He says he would pass a farm bill, keep foreign buyers out of Colorado water and farmland, and defend the district's water.
He says the district should keep using the energy it already produces while newer sources come online, and that rural hospitals and public-land staff need to be protected.

people.name: Eileen Laubacher
lines: She says lowering costs comes first, including ending tariffs that raise prices, a middle-class tax cut, and making data centers pay for the power and infrastructure they use.
She says she would fight for rural hospitals, pass a long-term farm bill, and build water supplies so farms are not sold off and dried up.
She says she takes no corporate PAC money and supports term limits, a ban on members trading stocks, a secure border, and a path to citizenship.

people.name: Eric Mulder
lines: He says programs should be judged by the results they deliver, not by how many dollars they spend, and that communities closest to a problem should be free to solve it.

He proposes a one-year break from the state sales tax for places in economic distress, with local voters deciding whether to replace it with a local tax for schools, roads, water, emergency services, or other needs.

He says he would oppose government cameras that track every passing car, and he wants the state to clear a path for small nuclear reactors, including reactors that large power users could run themselves.

people.name: Erik Underwood
lines: He says he has a plan for home loans with a down payment capped at $2,500.
He says he would fund child care with 25 cents on each purchase and wants universal health care in Colorado.
He says he would offer free college and trade school and would fight for the state's water rights.

people.name: Gabe Evans
lines: He says he is fighting to secure the border, strengthen public safety, and make life more affordable.
He says he would lower the cost of living by reining in deficit spending and tax-and-regulate policy, and that the military should focus on fighting wars.
He says families should be free to pick a school, and that he will protect free expression and the Second Amendment.

people.name: Greg Lopez
lines: He says he will use zero-based budgeting and review agencies for waste, duplication, and rules that do not help people.
He says he will push for 25,000 modest starter homes in four years and for lower water and sewer connection fees.
He says he will hold the transportation department to congestion relief and road repair, and expand school choice and vocational training.

people.name: James Wiley
lines: He says elections should be held on one day, in person, with voter identification, paper ballots, and citizen hand counts.
He says he would put public records, including voter rolls and business filings, on a blockchain he calls Liberty Chain.
He says he would cut red tape and fees so it is faster and cheaper to start a business.

people.name: Jason Clark
lines: He says rent, education, and health care cost too much, and that bringing those costs down is his first priority.
He says the campaign is about good-paying jobs, and that he would back entrepreneurs, small businesses, and developers.
He says he would go after criminals and clean up Colfax Avenue, and that every Colorado child should be able to thrive.

people.name: Jason Crow
lines: He says he is fighting to make daily life more affordable and to lower health-care costs.
He says he has never taken corporate PAC money and never will, and that he wants campaign-finance reform and a ban on insider stock trading.
He says he does not trade stocks and posts his public schedule so he answers to Coloradans rather than to donors.

people.name: Jeff Crank
lines: He says he is focused on the district's military installations and its veterans.
He says he is working to make the community more resilient to wildfires.
He says he wants conservative change so Colorado stays a place to live, work, and raise a family.

people.name: Jeff Hurd
lines: He says the border should be secured now, legal immigration expanded, and law enforcement given what it needs to stop fentanyl and other drugs.
He says his first priority is higher-paying work in rural Colorado, with fewer unnecessary rules and a fairer field for small businesses.
He says he supports producing Colorado oil and gas along with competitively priced cleaner power, and that he will press the Lower Basin to live within its share of Colorado River water.

people.name: Jeff Peckman
lines: He says Colorado companies can cut air pollution without new electric-vehicle mandates, and that he would declare an air-pollution emergency on his first day.
He says he would create a chief coherence officer and a partnership to launch new technology projects.
He says he will work to end TABOR, which he calls a limit that is hurting the state.

people.name: Jena Griswold
lines: She says she will defend the rights and freedoms of Coloradans and will not be intimidated.
She says that as secretary of state she backed laws against threats to election workers, guns near voting centers, and tampering with voting equipment.
She says she expanded ballot drop boxes, in-person voting, campus and tribal voting access, and automatic voter registration.

people.name: Jessica Killin
lines: She says she would lower costs for housing, groceries, health care, and energy, strengthen VA care, and cut federal spending that does not work.
She says she would end tariffs that raise everyday prices, limit corporate landlords, and hold monopoly utilities accountable for high electric bills.
She says she would ban members of Congress from trading stocks, support term limits, and let Medicare negotiate prices on more drugs.

people.name: Joe Neguse
lines: He says public lands are central to the district, and that he moved a Colorado public-lands bill through the House that would preserve about 400,000 acres and has pushed money toward wildfire preparation.
He says climate change is an existential threat, and that he has pressed for more solar power, renewable energy, and deep cuts in carbon emissions.
He says health coverage should be available to everyone, and that he is working to lower drug prices, raise the minimum wage, and close the gender pay gap.

people.name: John Hickenlooper
lines: He says he takes no corporate PAC money and supports overturning Citizens United, tighter disclosure of political money, and protection of vote-by-mail.
He says he is working on housing costs, small-business capital, and union rights, including the PRO Act.
He says health care is a right, and that he supports a public option, Medicare negotiation of drug prices, and restoring Roe v. Wade.

people.name: Kelley Dennison
lines: She says families are squeezed by housing, gas, inflation, and property taxes, and that the district should do better by veterans and seniors.
She says parents should be partners in their children's education, and that responsible gun owners should not be punished for crimes committed by other people.
She says she has signed a pledge to cosponsor and vote for a constitutional amendment limiting how long any person can serve in Congress.

people.name: Lauren Boebert
lines: She says she believes in personal freedom, the rights of citizens, and the Constitution.
She says she has passed House bills on energy production and water rights, and has pushed back on federal land rules she says hurt ranchers and farmers.
She says a jobs bill she got signed in 2023 will create 1,000 jobs in southern Colorado.

people.name: Manny Rutinel
lines: He says he would expand tax credits for working parents, close corporate tax loopholes, and bring down the cost of drugs, insurance premiums, and energy bills.
He says he will protect Social Security and Medicare from benefit cuts and a higher retirement age, and cap insulin at $35 a month.
He says his campaign takes no corporate PAC money, and that he would ban members of Congress from trading stocks and push to undo Citizens United.

people.name: Mark Baisley
lines: He says that in the legislature he worked on jobs, education, and essential services while limiting government intrusion into private life.
He says he has defended water rights, protected the energy industry, and opposed reckless spending and government overreach.
He says he will take that approach to Washington, with an emphasis on liberty and Colorado families.

people.name: Melat Kiros
lines: She says she rejects corporate PAC money and will stand for Medicare for All, a housing-first approach to homelessness, universal child care, and an arms embargo.
She says medical bills should not bankrupt people, and that she would abolish ICE and replace it with an immigration system aimed at public safety.
She says universal child care would keep parents from having to choose between work and paying the equivalent of a second rent.

people.name: Michael Allen
lines: He says he will put victims first, use the statewide grand jury on crimes that cross county lines, and work with sheriffs and police across the state, including rural departments.
He says he will review the attorney general's spending, cut waste, and treat crime as a driver of insurance and business costs.
He says he will investigate public corruption without regard to party and will defend Colorado's water rights in disputes with other states.

people.name: Phil Weiser
lines: He says he will work with local leaders to make housing more affordable and to let more people live near their jobs.
He says he will fight to keep health coverage affordable and to protect the care Coloradans already use.
He says he will work with law enforcement, fire chiefs, and victims' advocates on safety at home, at school, and in the community.

people.name: Sean Vadney
lines: He says every voter, of any party, should feel secure, and that voting should include checks against fraud.
He says Coloradans across parties are worried about election integrity and that he wants people to feel confident when they cast a ballot.
He says starting and keeping a business should be easy and affordable, and that he has run into red tape and high costs as a business owner.

people.name: Stephen Hamilton
lines: He says he would make state spending more transparent, cut waste, and pursue property and tax relief.
He says he would rebuild mining, manufacturing, agriculture, transportation, and energy jobs while protecting land and water.
He says he would lower the burden on working Coloradans and put their interests ahead of parties and special interests.

people.name: Tim Bennett
lines: He says he will ask of every bill whether it makes life more affordable in the district, and that he wants housing within reach, careful spending, and affordable energy.
He says he will protect Colorado water rights and storage, back law enforcement against violent crime and fentanyl, and manage forests to lower wildfire risk.
He says he would protect Medicare for seniors and Medicaid for people who need it, while cutting fraud and rejecting a full federal takeover of health care.

people.name: Victor Marx
lines: He says he will back law enforcement and make public safety a first priority.
He says he will lower the cost of living, change housing policy, cut taxes, and push for good-paying jobs.
He says government should answer to taxpayers rather than to special interests.

people.name: Amy Chai
lines: She says the middle class is struggling and that she wants local economies, small businesses, and American industry strengthened so people can afford a home and a family.
Her issues page also focuses on health care, mental health and addiction, education and parents' rights, and taxes.
She says government spending and legislation should be easier for the public to see.

people.name: Chris Shea
lines: His campaign slogan is lowering costs, growing wages, and protecting America.
He says that experience, from a small business that employed six people to helping veterans start new careers, is what he would bring to Congress.

people.name: Christopher Lancia
lines: He says border security is national security and that he wants the border chaos stopped.
He says he will fight for lower taxes, a balanced budget, and an end to spending he ties to inflation.
He supports term limits, the Second Amendment, and law enforcement, and says parents should control decisions about their children's education.

people.name: George Austin
lines: He says he wants Social Security and Medicare kept solvent for people who earned them, and veterans cared for instead of left fighting the VA.
He says workers and small businesses need good jobs, less red tape, lower taxes, and a realistic chance to own a home.
He wants guardrails on artificial intelligence so the gains do not wipe out jobs for American workers.

people.name: Jahana Hayes
lines: She supports Medicare for All and says she has worked to curb surprise bills and cap prescription drug costs.
She wants housing help for first-time buyers and an economy that lowers grocery, gas, and energy costs rather than serving only the very wealthy.
She supports red-flag laws, expanded background checks, and other steps to reduce gun violence.

people.name: Jim Himes
lines: He says he is fighting for accessible, affordable health care and to protect Social Security.
He says he is taking on the gun lobby to reduce gun violence and wants more economic opportunity for working families.
As the lead Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, he says he works against foreign and domestic interference and for peaceful transfers of power.

people.name: Joe Courtney
lines: He says his first fight in Congress was to keep Electric Boat building submarines, and he still focuses on the shipyard and the region's defense work.
He says he has worked to lower college costs, expand vocational programs, support farmers and veterans, and end surprise medical bills.
His priorities page also lists infrastructure, agriculture, health care, and education.

people.name: John Bolton
lines: He says he would make utility rate cases a priority and challenge policies that raise electric costs.
He says he would investigate AI-driven pricing and pursue consumer fraud, including scams aimed at seniors.
He says he would hold neighboring states accountable when pollution harms Connecticut rivers, drinking water, or Long Island Sound.

people.name: Luke Bronin
lines: He says he will focus on bringing down costs for housing, health care, groceries, childcare, and elder care.
He wants Medicare and Medicaid protected and a push toward universal health care.
He says he would abolish ICE, build more housing, and safeguard reproductive freedom.

people.name: Michael Goldstein
lines: He says health care is expensive because regulation has reduced competition, not because medicine itself is costly.
He argues that insurers answer to shareholders and that pharmacy middlemen take profit before drugs reach patients.
He says the FDA has slowed access to treatments and that the Right to Try law has helped very few patients.

people.name: Ned Lamont
lines: He says he is running again to keep lowering costs and expanding opportunity.
He says his record includes what he calls the largest middle-class tax cut in state history, along with more funding for public schools.
He says he has expanded affordable childcare and wants to keep protecting rights he associates with the state.

people.name: Peter Lumaj
lines: He says he would reduce taxes and cut red tape to grow the state's economy.
He says he wants conditions where families can thrive.
He says he would defend constitutional rights and conservative principles.

people.name: Rosa DeLauro
lines: She says she has shifted spending toward education, health care, climate, and community safety rather than billionaires and corporations.
The campaign says she has brought more than $70 million to the district for local projects since 2021.
It says she has worked to improve schools, cut taxes for middle-class families, protect pensions, and encourage jobs in Connecticut.

people.name: Ryan Fazio
lines: He says he co-authored a 2023 bill to disclose hidden utility taxes.
He says he co-authored a 2025 bill to reduce public-benefits charges on electric bills.
He says he authored a 2024 bill supporting municipal home rule.

people.name: Stephanie Thomas
lines: She says she led the rollout of early voting and secured funding to replace aging voting tabulators.
She says the office is building a centralized voter registration system and carrying out the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Act.
She says she started a monthly newsletter of funding and training resources for business owners.

people.name: William Tong
lines: He says he has filed more than 50 lawsuits against federal cuts to police, schools, and medical research.
He says he has fought utility rate increases and taken on opioid companies and social-media companies over harm to children.
He says he is defending reproductive health care and the state's post-Sandy Hook gun laws.

people.name: Chris Coons
lines: He says he has fought cuts to Medicaid and to affordable health care for Delawareans.
He says he has secured funding for affordable housing and for protecting the state's natural areas.
He says he has backed bipartisan laws on housing access, children's online safety, and health-care research.

people.name: David Graham
lines: He says he would bring discipline, responsibility, and accountability to Delaware's Department of Justice.
He says public safety would come first.

people.name: Joseph Arminio
lines: He says private and public debt are national emergencies and calls for a one-time debt jubilee plus action on the federal debt.
He says he wants to stop endless wars, reform education, and restore what he calls constitutional government.
He describes the campaign as a populist alternative to an incumbent he says is continuing a failing economy and those wars.

people.name: Kathy Jennings
lines: She says she is running to make Delaware safer and to make justice fair and equal.
She says she prosecuted domestic violence, sexual assault, and homicide cases, and that she built the office's consumer-fraud work.
She says that as attorney general she has pursued child predators, opioid manufacturers, corruption, and elder abuse, and is pushing stronger laws on online predators.

people.name: Mike Katz
lines: He says he would halt wasteful spending, cut red tape, and lower energy and housing costs.
He says he would expand early-childhood education, line up schooling with the workforce, and close what he calls the zip-code gap.
He says each vote in Washington should be judged by whether it helps Delaware, including on health-care access and affordability.

people.name: Sarah McBride
lines: She says working people are being squeezed by grocery, gas, health, housing, and energy bills, and that policy should focus on them rather than the wealthiest.
Her priorities include a care economy, health care, making life more affordable, and workers' rights.
As a state senator she highlights the Healthy Delaware Families Act, a paid family and medical leave program, and a Medicaid bill she says brought large new funding to the state.

people.name: Brian Schwalb
lines: He says the office has prosecuted juvenile crime, pursued opioid companies, and sued landlords over dangerous housing.
He says he has opposed a federal takeover of the Metropolitan Police Department and filed cases against federal orders, including a National Guard deployment in the District.
He says the office has gone after unpaid wages and benefits, won rent refunds, and sued what he calls a housing cartel for illegally raising rents.

people.name: Janeese Lewis George
lines: She says that as mayor she would side with working people to make the District safe and affordable in all eight wards.
She says she has worked to keep tenant protections and to make housing more affordable, and has voted for raises and stronger worker protections.
She says she led bills that raised wages for early-childhood educators, ended the subminimum wage for restaurant workers, and increased SNAP food assistance.

people.name: Manuel Rivera
lines: He says the office should put public safety first, enforce the law fairly, and stand with residents rather than special interests.
He says it should protect victims, defend consumers, and fight corruption.
He says it should work with the Metropolitan Police Department, the mayor, and the D.C. Council to make neighborhoods safer.

people.name: Rhonda Hamilton
lines: She says housing is health care and that she would take on the causes of housing instability.
She says she would raise the standard of care and invest in preventive, patient-focused practices.
She says she would match the budget to community needs, cut waste, and support small businesses, youth programs, and public safety.

people.name: Robert Gross
lines: He says he would use artificial intelligence to improve city budgeting, shorten permits, and update government technology.
He says that work would speed public services, including public Wi-Fi, and publish real-time performance dashboards.
He says the platform covers affordable housing, economic opportunity, public safety, education, and transparent city government.

people.name: Aaron Bean
lines: He says his mission is to lower costs for working families, support police, and make Washington account for tax dollars.
He says he serves on Ways and Means, co-founded a caucus aimed at waste and fraud, and has pushed lower taxes and pro-business, pro-family policy.

people.name: Amanda Green
lines: She says she would lower the cost of groceries, housing, insurance, and medicine by taking on corporate price gouging and expanding affordable housing and health care.
She says she wants a seat on the House Agriculture Committee, a strong Farm Bill, and full funding for nutrition programs in the district.
She says she would ban members of Congress from trading individual stocks, support term limits, and get dark money out of politics.

people.name: Angie Nixon
lines: She says she is running to lower costs, raise wages, and put working families ahead of billionaires.
She says she supports Medicare for All and a national rent freeze with a moratorium on evictions.
She says she supports free child care and pre-K, and a Working Families Guarantee for workers.

people.name: Anna Paulina Luna
lines: She says big government is often the problem, not the solution, and that her politics come from growing up in hard circumstances and serving in the military.
She says she wants reforms aimed at problems people actually face rather than an elitist approach to Congress.

people.name: Ashley Moody
lines: She says she supports America First policies on law and order, economic prosperity, and American sovereignty.
She says that as attorney general she championed public safety, support for law enforcement, and efforts against violent crime.
She says that as a senator she is working to uphold conservative values and strengthen national security.

people.name: Austin Rogers
lines: He says he is running to secure the border, defend Florida values, back law enforcement and the military, and put American families first.
He says he is fully pro-life from conception and will defend parental rights against policies he says undermine families.
He says he will defend the First and Second Amendments and work so veterans can get care and everyday essentials stay affordable.

people.name: Bale Dalton
lines: He says his first priority is making Florida affordable again by reversing health-care premium hikes and tariffs he calls illegal.
He says he would push competition among power companies and property insurers, raise the federal minimum wage, and pass the PRO Act.
He says he would restore Medicaid funding, negotiate drug prices, and protect Social Security and Medicare.

people.name: Brent Andersen
lines: He says housing and insurance costs are pricing Broward families out, and that 16 years in insurance is what he would take to Congress.
He says he would fight the higher grocery, energy, and health-care bills hitting working families.
He says he supports legal immigration and a functioning asylum system, and opposes what he calls open borders.

people.name: Byron Donalds
lines: He says Florida should bring down costs for working families and for seniors on fixed incomes.
He says patients should know the price of care before treatment and that doctors should face less red tape.
He says the state should secure the border, keep neighborhoods safe, and stop taxpayer support he ties to illegal immigration.

people.name: Carlos Gimenez
lines: He says small businesses need lower taxes, less legal liability, and fewer regulations.
He says immigration shaped South Florida and that the border should be secured in a way that keeps that community intact.
He says China is America's most aggressive adversary, and he supports domestic energy that stays environmentally conscious.

people.name: Casey Askar
lines: He says grocery and gas prices are his top priority, and that he would cut taxes and regulations he says are driving those costs up.
He says he would keep deporting people here illegally who have committed crimes, secure the border, and keep a merit-based immigration policy.
He says he would ban members of Congress from trading stocks and defend parents' say over their children's education.

people.name: Charles Burkett
lines: He says homestead property taxes should phase out for long-time Florida homeowners, with the benefit able to pass to a spouse or children.
He says property and auto insurance laws should be rewritten to bring more competition into the market.
He says a data center should be allowed only after voters in that county and city approve it.

people.name: Curtis Gibson
lines: He says he would push a federal reinsurance backstop to bring down property-insurance premiums.
He says veterans should get timely local care, including covered local providers when the VA cannot see them nearby soon enough.
He says he would keep property taxes from pushing out homeowners, seniors, and working families, and support citrus growers against disease and unchecked development.

people.name: Dan Green
lines: He says he would safeguard constitutional rights and work with President Trump to keep the military funded.
He says he would take on overdevelopment and rising property-insurance rates.
He says he would lower grocery, gas, and housing costs.

people.name: Darren Soto
lines: He says his reelection campaign is about lower costs, protecting health care, and stopping corruption.
He says he would stop tariffs that raise grocery, fuel, and housing costs, stop Medicaid and Affordable Care Act cuts, and protect Social Security and Medicare.

people.name: David Jolly
lines: He says a state catastrophic fund that takes natural-disaster risk out of the private market would cut property and car insurance rates, and he supports no-interest state loans for condominium repairs.
He says Florida should expand Medicaid and commit to health care for residents across the state.
He says the state should pause construction of hyperscale data centers until protections for water and nearby communities are shown to be enough.

people.name: Dean Abrams
lines: He says homesteaded homes worth up to twice a county's median should pay no property tax, and that corporations should stop buying single-family homes.
He says insurer profits should be capped, rate filings written in plain language, and the right to sue restored when a claim is wrongly denied.
He says he would ban new AI data centers and end warrantless tracking by license-plate reader networks.

people.name: Debbie Wasserman Schultz
lines: She says she is fighting to protect Social Security and Medicare, defend reproductive freedom, and strengthen public schools.
She says she wants lower health-care costs and laws that reduce gun violence.

people.name: Deborah Adeimy
lines: She says immigration should be legal, and that illegal entry strains hospitals, schools, and public benefits.
She says Americans should keep more of what they earn, and that government spending is what creates inflation.
She says she would protect homeownership from overdevelopment and work on Florida's water, from Lake Okeechobee to the coast.

people.name: Eliott Rodriguez
lines: He says he would turn unused federal land into mixed-use housing, expand workforce housing, and seek a federal backstop for homeowners' insurance.
He says he would protect Medicare, Social Security, and Medicaid, oppose raising the retirement age, and let people ages 55 to 64 buy into Medicare.
He says he supports a secure border, faster immigration courts, protection for Dreamers, and removal of people who pose a genuine threat.

people.name: Eric Yonce
lines: He says families should be able to afford a home, health care, insurance, and everyday essentials, with more workforce housing and a steadier insurance market.
He says economic growth should reward work, support local businesses, and include wages and schedules that match the cost of living.
He says Medicare and Social Security must stay strong, and he would negotiate prescription prices.

people.name: Frank Russo
lines: He says an affordability plan should take on insurance, housing, property taxes, and everyday costs together and protect homeowners.
He says he wants Florida's average teacher salary raised to at least $75,000, with more skilled-trades and apprenticeship paths.

He says lawful medical decisions should be made by patients and their doctors, and that immigration enforcement should focus on violent criminals, traffickers, and gangs while supporting legal immigration.

people.name: Gay Valimont
lines: She says she would cut home and auto insurance costs, challenge shrinkflation, and stop large investors from buying up houses.
She says she would seek universal affordable care, oppose Social Security and Medicare cuts or privatization, and restore a $35 insulin cap.
She says Northwest Florida needs a full-service VA hospital, and she supports universal background checks and red-flag laws.

people.name: Greg Steube
lines: He says he is focused on rebuilding after disasters, disaster tax relief, and lowering costs.
He says he stands with veterans, privacy and public safety, and border security.

people.name: Gus Bilirakis
lines: He says he is taking on property-insurance costs, affordable housing, and the cost of living in Pasco and Hillsborough counties.
He says he backed a larger senior tax exemption, no tax on tips or overtime, and a deduction for homeowners-insurance premiums.

people.name: James Martin
lines: He says he would take on grocery prices, property insurance, and health-care costs, including a public option that leaves employer and union coverage in place.
He says he would finish Everglades restoration and stop toxic discharges into the St. Lucie Estuary and Indian River Lagoon.
He says he would not cut Social Security, Medicare, or veterans' benefits, and would ban members of Congress from trading stocks.

people.name: James Pericola
lines: He says he would oppose cuts or privatization of Social Security and Medicare and let Medicare negotiate drug prices.
He says he would protect the Affordable Care Act and seek federal funding to ease the housing crisis and lower property insurance.
He says he would eliminate income taxes for people making less than $100,000 a year and cut taxes for middle-class families.

people.name: James Uthmeier
lines: He says he is focused on prosecuting dangerous criminals, combating illegal immigration, and keeping Florida safe.
He says he has sued corporations over what he describes as sexualizing and indoctrinating children.
He says his work with the governor included education freedom, parental rights, election rules, tax relief, and public safety.

people.name: Jared Moskowitz
lines: He says he wrote legislation to cut property-insurance premiums and is fighting prescription prices, housing costs, and price gouging.
He says he would protect Social Security and Medicare and reverse Medicaid cuts.
He says that after the 2018 shooting at his high school he helped pass Florida's school-safety law, and that he supports a ban on members of Congress trading stocks.

people.name: Jeffrey Datto
lines: He says he would move toward universal, income-based health care, strengthen public hospitals and clinics, and create a Florida Institutes of Health focused on serious disease, injury, mental health, and longevity.
He says he would abolish charter schools and bring them into one state public-education system, with academic freedom and pathways from school into Florida jobs.
He says he would open a public-accountability office, require timely and accessible courts, and make renters share in property-tax relief given to landlords.

people.name: Jennifer Jenkins
lines: She says she would stabilize Florida property insurance with federal reinsurance and oppose tariffs that raise the price of everyday goods.
She says she would expand Medicaid, restore Affordable Care Act subsidies, and protect coverage for pre-existing conditions.
She says she would protect the Department of Education, fully fund special-education law, and invest in teachers and student mental health.

people.name: Jim Schwartzel
lines: He says he would stand with President Trump to secure the border, enforce immigration laws, and deport people who are here illegally.
He says families are paying too much for groceries, housing, and insurance, and he would fight to bring those costs down.
He says he would vote to make President Trump's tax cuts permanent so families and small businesses keep more of what they earn.

people.name: Jimmy Patronis
lines: He says his House priorities follow an America First agenda: cutting taxes, restraining spending, investing in the military, and reforming veterans' services.
He says that as chief financial officer he pushed benefits for firefighters diagnosed with cancer and mental-health care for first responders.
He says he fought insurance practices that let contractors take over homeowners' benefits after storms and drive premiums up.

people.name: Joe Strada
lines: He says he would investigate congressional insider trading, enact term limits, and pass a balanced-budget amendment.
He says he would finish the border wall, back law enforcement, and cut waste before asking taxpayers for more.
He says he would lower costs, restore energy independence, bring jobs back, and protect Social Security and Medicare.

people.name: John Rutherford
lines: He says he would fight inflation by blocking and cutting taxes, cutting red tape for small businesses, and lowering grocery, gas, and electric costs.
He says he has backed VA reform, higher troop pay, veterans' mental-health care, and a school-safety law he authored.

people.name: Kat Cammack
lines: She says she is focused on securing the southern border, advocating for small businesses, and defending the Second Amendment.
She describes herself as a budget hawk who wants taxes low and federal spending kept minimal.

people.name: Kathy Castor
lines: She says she works to lower family costs, create jobs, and protect Florida's environment, including wetlands and the coast.
She says she helped pass the bipartisan infrastructure law, bills expanding care for seriously ill children, and veterans' caucus work.

people.name: Kelly Kirschner
lines: He says he would lower insurance, health-care, and prescription costs, restore Medicare and Medicaid funding, and let the government negotiate drug prices.
He says he would expand affordable housing and stop Wall Street from buying single-family homes.
He says he would protect Tampa Bay, Sarasota Bay, and the coast by prohibiting offshore drilling and enforcing the Clean Water Act.

people.name: Kimberly Overman
lines: She says she would fight for affordable housing, infrastructure, and fair wages because she knows what it is like to juggle bills and worry about rent.
She says health care is a right and she would expand access, lower prescription costs, and defend reproductive care and mental-health services.
She says she would fully fund public schools, raise teacher pay, and make sure veterans get the benefits and care they earned.

people.name: LaShonda Holloway
lines: She says affordable health care should mean lower premiums and prescription costs, broader Medicare, and care that does not depend on a person's income.
She says she would cut red tape and expand capital for small businesses, and make rent lower and homeownership more reachable for working families.
She says Social Security should be protected and a full-time wage should cover food, housing, health care, and transportation.

people.name: Laurel Lee
lines: The site says that under President Trump she is focused on turning conservative priorities into results for the 15th District.
It quotes his endorsement of her on the border, innovation, the military and veterans, and the Second Amendment.

people.name: Leela Gray
lines: She says neighbors cannot keep up with the cost of housing, health care, insurance, food, and fuel, and that is why she is running.
She says she would ban stock trading by officials in Washington, bar former members of Congress from corporate lobbying, and set term limits.
She says she would protect the beaches and the coastal economy, and keep the promise of care for veterans and military families.

people.name: Lois Frankel
lines: She says she is fighting cuts to health care, Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, and working to lower costs for families.
She says she works to protect the environment and expand access to housing.
She says she is an advocate for women's reproductive freedom.

people.name: Maria Elvira Salazar
lines: She says she has voted to lower taxes, backed small businesses, and worked to recover pandemic money lost to fraud.
She says she is funding Everglades restoration, coastal flood protection, and cleaner water in Biscayne Bay.
She says she opposes socialism and communism, has pushed sanctions on the governments of Cuba, Venezuela, and Nicaragua, and supports term limits.

people.name: Mario Diaz-Balart
lines: He says he would end the tax on tips and overtime and make working-family tax cuts permanent.
He says he would detain and remove people here illegally who have committed crimes, and crack down on fentanyl trafficking.
He says he would continue Everglades restoration and fund school-violence prevention and parental rights in education.

people.name: Matthew Montavon
lines: He says he would ease housing costs with workforce housing for teachers, first responders, and families, and take on Florida's property-insurance crisis.
He says he would make health-care and prescription prices more transparent without taking away consumer choices.
He says he would modernize border security and create a background-checked path to legal status for people already working in Florida's farms and small businesses.

people.name: Maxwell Frost
lines: He says that as the first Generation Z member of Congress he is fighting to end gun violence, win Medicare for All, change the criminal justice system, and address the climate crisis.
He says he pressed to end the Hyde Amendment and organized to restore voting rights to Floridians with past felony convictions.

people.name: Mike Beltran
lines: He says he would expand clinics and telehealth so families do not have to travel an hour or take a day off work to see a doctor.
He says he would cut spending that drives prices up, after backing what he calls the largest tax cut in Florida history and tax holidays on gas and everyday purchases.
He says he would cut rules that block workers and small businesses, and require local approval before a data center is built so it does not raise energy bills.

people.name: Mike Haridopolos
lines: He says he focuses on the space industry, the Indian River Lagoon, election integrity, a ban on congressional stock trading, and affordable housing.
He says he would secure the border and fight inflation, higher taxes, and spending he calls reckless.
He says he would back law enforcement and the Second Amendment, and make sure the military and veterans get the equipment and care they need.

people.name: Moliere Dimanche
lines: He says unincorporated communities should be able to form their own cities so residents control safety, taxes, and public works.
He says he would close Alligator Alcatraz on his first day in office.
He says he would abolish homeowners associations and end property taxes on homesteaded homes.

people.name: Nicole Locklin
lines: She says she would fight price gouging on housing, insurance, health care, and groceries, and stop corporate investors from buying up neighborhoods.
She says she would protect Social Security and Medicare, oppose raising the retirement age, and treat health care as a right.
She says she refuses corporate PAC money and would ban congressional stock trading and restore abortion rights nationwide.

people.name: Oliver Gilbert III
lines: He says health care should be a right, and he would fight for a path to coverage for every American.
He says he would end funding for immigration raids that he says are separating working families, and put that money into childcare and pre-K.
He says he would expand rapid transit and job training, and back tax relief scaled to what working families earn.

people.name: Phil Ehr
lines: He says he would lower health premiums and out-of-pocket costs, and enforce anti-fraud rules to stabilize property insurance.
He says he would protect law-abiding immigrant families, open a path to permanent residency for people stuck in legal limbo, and target criminals and traffickers.
He says he would pursue a VA hospital or major VA clinic in South Dade and protect the Everglades, including a pause on large AI data centers until their effects are studied.

people.name: Pia Dandiya
lines: She says she would make housing, property insurance, prescriptions, and childcare more affordable, and end tariffs she calls illegal.
She says she would protect Social Security and Medicare, oppose raising the retirement age, and reverse Medicaid cuts.
She says she would ban members of Congress from trading stocks, support term limits, fully fund public schools, and back universal pre-K.

people.name: Rachel Grage
lines: She says she would keep health premiums and prescription costs affordable and work to stabilize home insurance.
She says she would safeguard Medicare and Social Security and their long-term solvency.
She says she would make campaign finance more transparent, reduce the influence of big money, and hold public officials to the same standards as everyone else.

people.name: Randy Fine
lines: He says he would lower insurance rates, hold insurance companies accountable, and protect Social Security and Medicare.
He says he would secure the border, boost job creation, and counter inflation.
He says he would defend the right to life and the Second Amendment, and back first responders.

people.name: Robert People
lines: He says he would protect Social Security and support Medicare for All.
He says he would protect vote by mail and the environment, and oppose a data center when the community does not want it.
He says his priorities also include housing, food, utility costs, and disaster preparedness.

people.name: Ryan Elijah
lines: He says Congress should keep taxes low, cut regulation, and pursue American energy independence so family costs come down.
He says health care should be affordable and patient-centered, with expanded health savings accounts and clear prices from hospitals and insurers.
He says he supports parental rights and school choice, and protection for Volusia County's beaches.

people.name: Scott Franklin
lines: He says he works for Florida agriculture, including help for farmers and ranchers after severe weather and a stable food supply.
He says he would secure the border, strengthen defense, and restore fiscal discipline in Washington.
He says he chairs the House Science Committee's environment subcommittee and pushes back on regulations he says threaten economic growth.

people.name: Scott Jewett
lines: He says he would take on the insurance affordability crisis, cut taxes, and shrink government so families keep more of what they earn.
He says data centers should do no harm and that the state should stop using Flock license-plate cameras.
He says parents should decide where their children go to school and that education dollars should follow the child.

people.name: Scott Singer
lines: He says he voted seven times to lower Boca Raton's tax rate and has pledged not to raise taxes.
He says he would keep the border and national defense strong, cut waste, and work with President Trump.
He says he supports a term-limits amendment and a ban on members of Congress trading stocks.

people.name: Seth Harp
lines: He says he would protect Social Security by raising the payroll tax cap to $250,000 without cutting retirees' payments.
He says every American should have affordable health care so a family is not bankrupted by getting sick.
He says he would expand child care with a sliding-scale subsidy and tax large corporate purchases of single-family homes so more families can buy a house.

people.name: Sydney Gruters
lines: She says she would cut taxes and fight rising costs so families can afford gas, groceries, and everyday essentials.
She says she would work with President Trump and ICE on the border, and stand with him to keep elections secure.
She says she would curb overdevelopment, keep homeownership in reach, strengthen veterans' benefits, and protect Social Security and Medicare.

people.name: Te Brown
lines: She says federal housing money should help low-income families buy a first home instead of staying in lifelong rental subsidies.
She says education dollars should follow the student to a public, charter, private, or home school.

She says she would secure the border and remove people who threaten public safety, and she supports an earned path to citizenship for longtime Haitian TPS holders who have worked, paid taxes, and passed a background check.

people.name: Victor Arias
lines: He says he would cut Veterans Affairs red tape and protect Medicare and Social Security for seniors.
He says he would expand economic opportunity and invest in infrastructure and education.
He says he would protect clean water and improve access to affordable health care.

people.name: Amanda Hollowell
lines: She says she will fight to fund rural hospitals, expand mental health care, and protect Medicaid, and she supports national paid family and medical leave.
She wants apprenticeship programs, the right to organize, and federal investments that reach port and other workers, plus housing and wages that let people who work in the district live there.

She says she will push flood protection and preservation of the Okefenokee, restore voting access, defend LGBTQ+ rights and reproductive freedom, and treat gun violence as a public-health problem, including a ban on assault weapons.

people.name: Andrew Clyde
lines: He says that on April 12, 2013, the IRS confiscated $940,000 from his business through civil asset forfeiture, and that the agency later offered to return part of it if he forfeited the rest.
He says most small-business owners hit by that process lacked the money to fight, and he presents the case as a fight against overreaching government.
On guns, he argues that taxes on firearms and ammunition, from the National Firearms Act to local per-gun taxes, treat a constitutional right as a privilege and could tax it out of reach.

people.name: Austin Scott
lines: He says he represents Georgia values and free-market principles, and that the goal is to protect personal freedoms, individual liberties, and economic opportunity for the next generation.
He says his agenda is to strengthen local businesses and benefit Georgia families.
He supports limited government, small-business job growth, a strong national defense, and a healthy agricultural economy.

people.name: Brian Jack
lines: He calls the border the country's most pressing issue and says he will push to finish the border wall, fund ICE and the Border Patrol, deport people he calls criminal immigrants, and rewrite immigration law around working-class prosperity.
He says he will return to tax cuts and energy production he credits with an earlier economic boom, arguing that spending and energy policy have driven up gas and grocery prices.
His issues list also names stopping crime, ending what he calls the weaponization of justice, and leading on digital innovation.

people.name: Brian Strickland
lines: He says that as judiciary chairman he handles the state's laws on courts, crime, and criminal procedure.
He says he wrote the law that fixed long delays in competency hearings and has been a leading voice for mental-health reform.
He says he worked to stop foster children from being housed in state offices and supported stronger laws on gangs, counterfeit drugs, and human trafficking.

people.name: Caitlyn Gegen
lines: She says she would fight for a livable minimum wage, more affordable housing, and Medicare for All so people in the 9th District can save and buy a home.
She says the wealthiest people, whom she calls the Epstein Class, are not paying their fair share of taxes, and that the revenue should fund social programs.
She says she would fund the Forest Service and protect the Roadless Rule, replace lead water pipes in rural North Georgia, and have Congress reclaim its war and taxation powers.

people.name: Ceretta Smith
lines: She says her vision for the 12th District is good jobs, strong schools, and healthy communities, with investment in new industries and infrastructure.
She says she will seek fair wages and health care now, and longer-term resources that keep the district thriving.
She says government should work for people rather than special interests, and that dignity, fair pay, and opportunity should not depend on ZIP code.

people.name: Chris Harden
lines: He says he would make health care more affordable, expand Affordable Care Act premium tax credits, lower prescription costs, and improve access in rural communities.
He says he takes no corporate PAC money, would ban members of Congress and their immediate families from trading individual stocks, and would cut taxes for working and middle-class families.
He says data centers should not shift water and power costs onto ordinary customers, and he would invest in affordable energy and modernize the grid, roads, and bridges.

people.name: Clay Fuller
lines: He says he is fighting for President Trump's agenda to bring manufacturing jobs back to northwest Georgia.
He says he supports removing people who are in the country without permission, and that border security is national security.

people.name: Greg Dolezal
lines: He says he wrote the Riley Gaines Act to keep men out of women's sports and out of girls' locker rooms.

He says he led an effort to hold Fani Willis accountable and is running because he believes public safety, livelihoods, and children's futures are at risk.

people.name: Hank Johnson Jr.
lines: He says he supports DACA, temporary protected status, refugees, and immigrants who come to build a better life for their children.

He says he will oppose efforts to take away affordable health insurance and will stand with consumers seeking coverage.

people.name: Houston Gaines
lines: He says immigration enforcement should keep cooperating with ICE, deportations should continue, and the border should stay secured.
He says he led opposition to defunding the police in Georgia, backed hundreds of millions of dollars for law enforcement, and took on district attorneys he says endangered public safety.

He wants spending cuts and tax cuts to match what he calls Georgia's balanced budgets, more American manufacturing, a military rebuilt around strength, and a block on Chinese purchases of U.S. farmland.

people.name: Jasmine Clark
lines: Her agenda lists lowering the cost of living, protecting education at every stage, and building an economy that works for people.

She says she is running because funding has been stripped from the CDC and the NIH and health care has been cut, and she says a policy that hits one group affects the whole community.

people.name: Jim Duffie
lines: He says he supports the FairTax Act, H.R. 25, which would end the federal income, payroll, estate, and gift taxes, abolish the IRS, and replace them with a national sales tax plus a monthly rebate so households at or below the poverty level pay no net federal tax.
He says families should be able to go to school, church, and the store without fear, and he would back law enforcement and first responders.
He says he would cut regulations that make it harder for small businesses to hire and grow, and defend the Second Amendment, religious liberty, and free speech.

people.name: Jim Kingston
lines: He says he will fight to lower taxes so families and small businesses keep more of what they earn, and he wants regular appropriations, balanced budgets, and agency accountability for spending.

He says he is running to defend President Trump, make the district more affordable, and back border enforcement.

people.name: John Cowan
lines: On health care, he says he would fix problems he attributes to the Affordable Care Act by lowering premiums, expanding choices, and putting patients in charge of their care.

people.name: John Salvesen
lines: He says that if elected he will own no stock, take contributions only from individuals, and report to constituents once a week on a podcast.

He says he wants attention on what he calls poison in food, and he describes FedNow as a tracking program that would eliminate cash.

people.name: Jon Ossoff
lines: He says he has worked to cap insulin costs for seniors at $35 a month and to lower housing costs.

people.name: Jonathan Chavez
lines: He says he would lower taxes on working families, help small businesses add jobs, and cut regulations while still protecting consumers.
He says he would expand Medicaid, widen rural and telehealth access, and defend patient choice so care is closer and cheaper.
He says he would fund classrooms, work with parents, and strengthen career and technical education, and he supports term limits.

people.name: Josh McLaurin
lines: He says he passed a bipartisan law that for the first time set statewide rules on the car-booting industry.
He says he secured the first $1 million in the state budget for research into therapies for veterans' post-traumatic stress.
He says he has fought efforts at the Capitol to advantage corporations and to target vulnerable people for political gain.

people.name: Keisha Lance Bottoms
lines: She says that as mayor she secured major investments in affordable housing and a historic pay raise for Atlanta's first responders.
She says she supported small businesses and became a national voice on civil-rights reforms.

people.name: Kelly Esti
lines: He says education is a public good and he would fund affordable learning beyond K-12, including job skills for the district's health-care, retail, and manufacturing workers.

He says he would seek federal money for roads, broadband, and utility upgrades, including solar and wind where communities want them, and back labor standards for workers.

people.name: Kevin Martin
lines: On schools, he wants federal education money returned to Georgia without federal strings, and he wants student aid and career programs to cover shorter technical training.

people.name: Lucy McBath
lines: She highlights House passage of universal background checks and red-flag laws, and she says her work in Congress is aimed at laws that help children and families.

She supports the Equality Act to bar LGBTQ discrimination in work, housing, and credit, and she points to federal infrastructure spending for safe water, high-speed internet, and a cleaner environment.

people.name: Matt Day
lines: His local list includes fathers who show up, ending generational poverty, farmers, teachers, manufacturing, white-collar jobs, rural health care, timber, ports, and pharmacists.
He also says he is working to save the Okefenokee Swamp and lists national priorities that include Social Security, Medicare, and the cost of living.
He says he is going to Washington to fight what he calls a woke liberal agenda and to defend Christianity and conservative freedoms.

people.name: Maura Keller
lines: She supports a higher minimum wage, labor rights, affordable housing, Social Security that keeps up with inflation, and student-loan relief, and she says she would vote against funding a war with Iran.
She backs the Agricultural Right to Repair Act, farm safety nets, prescription-drug caps, restored Medicare subsidies, and easier VA care, including telehealth for rural veterans.
She also calls for stronger border enforcement alongside faster legal immigration, legal protections for LGBTQIA+ and BIPOC Americans, and infrastructure to handle storms, floods, and heat.

people.name: Mike Collins
lines: He says Georgia needs a senator who has met tight schedules in the trucking industry, where he says you do not get paid if you do not deliver.
He says working-class Americans are the backbone of the campaign and of the country, and he asks voters to join that fight.

people.name: Nikema Williams
lines: She says she is working to stop corporate and hedge-fund purchases of single-family homes, fund whole-home repairs for low- and middle-income owners, and help families pass a home down without a formal deed.

She also says she will keep fighting for affordable health care, equitable public-school funding, voting rights, and reproductive health care, which she calls a human right.

people.name: Pamela Delancy
lines: She says she would protect and expand health coverage for families, seniors, and veterans, including mental health care, and oppose cuts to benefits veterans have earned.
She says she would seek relief from housing and food costs, and that data-center growth should not come at the expense of the water supply.
She says she wants a secure border, an asylum process that works, a legal path to work that keeps families together, and oversight so enforcement follows the law.

people.name: Penny Reynolds
lines: She says the office should protect the right to vote and run elections that are fair, secure, and accessible regardless of zip code, race, or income.
She says she would empower small business, modernize professional licenses, and safeguard seniors.
She says she would press government accountability and build systems that serve the public.

people.name: Rich McCormick
lines: He says Congress should be judged by whether costs come down, communities are more secure, and Washington works for the people it serves.
He says he is fighting inflationary spending, deficits, and debt, and he introduced the Incentivize Savings Act so federal agencies have a reason to save taxpayer money.
He says he has helped bring more than $319 million back to the district and introduced the Litigation Reimbursement Act to push accountability in the legal system.

people.name: Rick Allen
lines: He says growing the economy is the way to create jobs, and that small businesses are being taxed and regulated while families face rising prices.
He says seniors paid into Medicare and Social Security and Congress should protect both, including Medicare Advantage, and lower seniors' health and prescription costs.
He says a four-year college is not the right path for every student, and he points to career and technical education, local control by parents and teachers, and school safety.

people.name: Rick Jackson
lines: He says he is running to cut the income tax, freeze property taxes, and lower costs so Georgia is the most affordable state.

people.name: Sanford Bishop
lines: He says the district's farms, including its peanut crop, need disaster aid, market access, rural broadband, and a farm bill that supports food security and local food networks.

He describes his goal as jobs, education, safe communities, a clean environment, energy independence, and a strong defense, pursued alongside a balanced budget.

people.name: Shawn Harris
lines: He says he would protect and expand Medicaid and Medicare, reject vouchers that shift the cost onto seniors, and bring specialists to northwest Georgia so people do not have to drive for hours.
He says small and medium farms should get the same help as corporate farms, that SNAP should keep paying during a shutdown, and that rural water systems need upgrades.
He says Social Security should not be privatized, and that Wall Street firms should lose federal tax breaks for buying up houses.

people.name: Tanya Miller
lines: She says she will go after consumer fraud, including predatory lenders, scammers, and price gouging.
She says she will take on corporate negligence and monopolistic practices that hurt small businesses.
She says she will use her prosecution experience on public safety and will defend voting and privacy rights.

people.name: Tim Fleming
lines: He says elections should be secure, accessible, fair, and trusted, and he says he will protect voter ID and election transparency.
He says he reformed professional licensing so a new license could be issued in five days and renewals became automatic.
He says he will cut red tape for small businesses, improve customer service, and use technology so state government works for Georgians.

people.name: Tony Kozycki
lines: He says members of Congress should not trade individual stocks or hide behind omnibus bills nobody reads, and he lists a ban on congressional stock trading as a way to rebuild trust.
He points to child-care costs, families priced out of homeownership, and full-time work that no longer covers a household, and he says he has a plan to lower those costs.

people.name: Adriel Lam
lines: He says Hawaii needs a representative who will speak for shared values and use the federal government's resources for the islands.

people.name: Brenton Awa
lines: He wants to limit corporate purchases of single-family homes and open suitable federal land for local workforce housing.
He says federal infrastructure money should be tied to housing for people who live and work in Hawaii, and he wants down-payment help for first-time local buyers.
He says he refuses gifts and has founded roadside food forests and other land-restoration projects.

people.name: Ed Case
lines: He says the country needs experienced leadership to defend democracy and deliver practical solutions.
He says he will keep speaking honestly, listening, and representing all of Hawaii, pointing to his work through COVID-19, Red Hill, and the Maui wildfires.

people.name: Gary Cordery
lines: He says he would eliminate the general excise tax on food and medicine, freeze property taxes for kupuna on a primary home at retirement, and seek tax exemptions for Native Hawaiian homeowners.

He says a housing plan would produce 15,000 fee-simple homes priced between $400,000 and $600,000 for working families, teachers, nurses, and kupuna, with faster permitting and an end to no-bid contracts.
He says he would open a government transparency office, require annual audits of public-private partnerships and departments, and send corruption cases to the attorney general.

people.name: Jill Tokuda
lines: She says zip code and income should not decide the quality of care, and she wants rural hospitals, mobile clinics, telehealth, and Medicare for All.
She says she is fighting tariffs, wants the federal gas tax suspended, and wants childcare and the child tax credit expanded so families can stay in Hawaii.
She says getting sick should not push people into debt.

people.name: Josh Green
lines: He says that since 2022 he has worked to lower the cost of living.
He says he is working to build affordable housing.
He says he is working to reduce homelessness statewide.

people.name: Brad Little
lines: His campaign says he cut or simplified 95 percent of Idaho regulations and calls Idaho the least regulated state.

His campaign says teacher pay rose, literacy funding increased five-fold, and school-facility spending also worked as property-tax relief, along with new school-choice options and the Idaho LAUNCH program.

His campaign says he and the Legislature delivered tax relief with a balanced budget and a AAA credit rating, and that Idaho sent more missions to the border than any other state through an effort he calls Operation No Return.

people.name: Ellie Gilbreath
lines: She says she would ban corporate purchases of single-family homes, expand the ROAD to Housing Act, and give counties the last word on data centers so they do not drain local water and power.
She says she would keep public lands public, protect the Roadless Rule, and pass farm bills that give Idaho farmers and ranchers a stable plan.
She says Congress should check executive power, ban stock trading by members and their immediate families, and ban dark money.

people.name: Eric Myricks
lines: He says taxes should stay low, but that roads, schools, and senior care cannot be met by cuts alone.
He says he will fight House Bill 328, which he says adds Medicaid work rules, shifts care to profit-driven companies, and lets officials cut benefits overnight.
He says he will fully fund public schools, repeal the voucher program, and connect career training to jobs that keep young people in Idaho.

people.name: Jim Risch
lines: He says he led the Senate fight against selling some of Idaho's public lands and will keep defending multiple use, including hunting, logging, and grazing.
He says he will keep cutting taxes and red tape for small businesses and farms, and he cites a 100 percent approval rating from the American Farm Bureau.
He says he supports border enforcement, Second Amendment rights, and returning natural-resource decisions to state and local leaders.

people.name: Kaylee Peterson
lines: She says she takes no corporate PAC money, would ban stock trades by members of Congress and their families, and supports term limits of six House terms and two Senate terms.
She says she would cut taxes on middle-class families and local businesses, raise the federal minimum wage, repeal right-to-work laws, and direct USDA help to family farms.
She says Idaho's public lands are not for sale, and she would fund the Forest Service, local timber, and wildfire work, and move health coverage to a universal single-payer system.

people.name: Lori Hickman
lines: She says she will give state agencies and the Land Board legal advice based on the law, and hire for ethics and skill rather than ideology.
She says she will issue prompt opinions for legislators and state officials and follow the statute even when that is politically inconvenient.
She says she will oppose selling federal public lands in Idaho or closing them to the public.

people.name: Matt Loesby
lines: He says the border should be closed except to people invited by citizen landowners who take financial responsibility for them, that uninvited immigrants should be deported, and that he would end birthright citizenship.
He says he would repeal minimum-wage laws and the Affordable Care Act, end the Federal Reserve, and cut federal budgets rather than only slow their growth.

He says no U.S. troops should be sent outside the country unless Congress declares war, that the government should send no money or weapons abroad, and that he would abolish the VA and pay veterans directly for care.

people.name: Mike Simpson
lines: He says securing the border is the country's top issue and that he is fighting to build a wall and add Border Patrol agents.
He says promoting Idaho agriculture, including potatoes, sugar, and dairy, has been one of his top priorities.
He says he wants the country to meet its obligations to veterans and to fully fund the VA.

people.name: Natalie Fleming
lines: She says she will curb corporate landlords and reopen paths to homeownership and homesteading.
She says personal data should be treated as private property, with a ban on exploitative surveillance by companies and government.

She says the economy should favor small businesses, cooperatives, and local supply chains, and she wants the food supply shifted from global toward local, with regenerative farming and rural infrastructure.

people.name: Paul Sand
lines: He says he would invert Idaho government so counties set their own rules, fund their own social programs, and collect taxes, with state revenue sharing running from the county upward.
He says he opposes abortion, open borders, and legalizing narcotic drugs, and he supports large cuts to state agencies and state taxes.
He says he opposes public benefits for any immigrant, whether here legally or not.

people.name: Phil McGrane
lines: He says he strengthened safeguards that keep Idaho elections secure, transparent, and accessible.
He says he trained as a wildland firefighter and works with timber, mining, agriculture, and recreation on public-land challenges.
He says he will protect faith, family, personal responsibility, and limited government.

people.name: Pro-Life
lines: He says legal personhood begins when sperm meets egg, that abortion is murder, and that as governor he would keep abortion facilities closed and block abortifacient drugs from being sold or shipped into Idaho.
He says he would also bar transgender medical treatment at any age and would veto bills that expand government.
He says education, welfare, health, and recreation should be phased out of government and returned to faith communities.

people.name: Raul Labrador
lines: The site's headline says he is protecting Idaho families.
It highlights his defense of women's sports at the U.S. Supreme Court.

people.name: Russ Fulcher
lines: He supports full enforcement of immigration law and an orderly legal process, and he opposes illegal immigration.
He opposes breaching the lower four Snake River dams, which he says supply hydropower, irrigation, and a path for Idaho wheat to market.
He says he is pro-life, will defend the Second Amendment, and wants local communities to have more say over Idaho's forests, minerals, and energy.

people.name: Scott Bedke
lines: He says he has an A+ rating from the NRA and a 100 percent pro-life record with Idaho Chooses Life.
He says he led a fight to keep critical race theory out of Idaho schools.
He says he was named legislator of the year by the Fraternal Order of Police and will oppose defunding the police, work to secure the border, and keep families safe.

people.name: Terri Pickens
lines: She says growth should rest on small business, a stable tax structure, a living wage, and health care that is affordable.
She says she would repeal the school-voucher program, raise teacher pay, and fund rural districts, pre-K, and full-day kindergarten.
She says public lands must stay public and open for recreation, hunting, and fishing, and that women, not the state, should make family-planning decisions.

people.name: Todd Achilles
lines: He says he will seek a constitutional amendment limiting senators to two terms and House members to three, ban members of Congress from trading individual stocks, and close tax loopholes he says the wealthy and corporations use.
He says he will protect health-insurance tax credits, require upfront medical prices, and build on a housing bill that limits large investors from buying single-family homes.
He says he will oppose selling Idaho public lands, vote against new federal bans on firearms or magazines, and staff Customs and Border Protection while updating legal visas for farm work.

people.name: Alexi Giannoulias
lines: He says the office should expand voter registration, including automatic registration that does not require an extra step at the counter and pre-registration for 16- and 17-year-olds.
He says he would tighten ethics rules, including a ban on officials lobbying, a two-year wait before lawmakers become lobbyists, and a public database of lobbyist activity.

He points to office modernization such as appointment scheduling to cut lines, and to a library law he says he championed so public and school libraries are not pressured to remove books for partisan reasons.

people.name: Collin Corbett
lines: He says he would start by lowering property taxes, freeze discretionary state spending in the first year, and end or fix programs that do not show results.
He says he would cut outdated business rules, stop further tax and fee increases, and back small businesses, manufacturers, farmers, and a skilled workforce.
He says data centers should pay their own energy and grid costs, protect water, be negotiated in public, and be tied to property-tax relief.

people.name: Darren Bailey
lines: He says that as governor he would push for fully funded schools, more choices for parents, and more support for teachers.
He says he would stand with law enforcement, hold violent offenders accountable, and oppose policies he argues put politics ahead of public safety.
He says he would lower taxes, cut state spending, and seek property-tax relief so families are not taxed out of their homes.

people.name: Delia Ramirez
lines: In just a few months she has introduced legislation with bipartisan support to help student veterans, is co-leading the Dream and Promise Act, and introduced the Tenants Right to Organize Act.
Her campaign is people-funded, people-centered, and refuses to accept corporate contributions.

people.name: Diane Harris
lines: She says she would add self-service kiosks beyond the current mostly urban sites, study drive-up service, and send mobile units from Cairo to Rockford.
She says she would review the office budget, seek lower fees for seniors and veterans, and strengthen cybersecurity around personal data.
She says she would clean voter rolls during registration and share records with other agencies as part of what she calls an election-integrity agenda.

people.name: Don Tracy
lines: He says his first priority is lowering the cost of living, including taxes, energy, health care, and inflation.
He says he would support law enforcement, enforce immigration law, and oppose taxpayer-funded benefits for people in the country illegally.
He says he would speak for the whole state, including communities outside Chicago, and ease rules on small businesses, manufacturers, and farmers.

people.name: Eric Sorensen
lines: I support codifying Roe v. Wade and permanently restoring a woman's right to choose into law.
Year-Round E-15. Affordable Generic Drugs in Months, Not Years. Affordable Housing Now. Helping Farmers Feed Us. Clean Water for All.

people.name: JB Pritzker
lines: He says Illinois has recorded credit upgrades, balanced budgets, more jobs, and higher wages, and that he would keep working on the cost of living.
He points to a higher minimum wage, abortion protections written into state law, and expanded preschool.
He says he has opposed federal actions he argues would raise costs for working families or send troops into Chicago.

people.name: Juliana Stratton
lines: She says she would raise the federal minimum wage, seek Medicare for All, and cut taxes for the middle class while raising them on income above a million dollars a year.
She says she would restore the Department of Education, expand support for trades and technical schools, and fund grants for small-business owners.
She says she would abolish ICE, pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Act, restore the abortion protections of Roe v. Wade, and pass gun laws, and that she is rejecting corporate PAC money.

people.name: Kwame Raoul
lines: He highlights gun-trafficking prosecutions, a state gun-tracing database, and work with police on violent crime and organized retail theft.
He says he has defended abortion access, challenged junk fees and high drug prices, and recovered wages owed to workers.
He says he has filed dozens of cases against the Trump administration over funding, voting rights, and the use of federal forces in Illinois.

people.name: Lauren Underwood
lines: The Health Care Affordability Act limits the cost of health care coverage for people who choose Marketplace plans to eight and a half percent or less of their income.
Lauren responded to skyrocketing insulin prices with the bipartisan Lower Insulin Costs Now Act.

people.name: Mike Bost
lines: He's always fighting for the federal government to live within its means and to prioritize your tax dollars. He knows what it means to live within a budget- just as your family does and just as Mike and Tracy Bost do managing their business and household.

people.name: Robert Fioretti
lines: He says he would protect consumers from fraud and scams and hold government accountable for corruption.
He says he would support local law enforcement, fight gun violence, and defend equal protection under the law.
On his donation page he says he would put crime victims, taxpayers, and constitutional rights, including the Second Amendment, ahead of the priorities he attributes to the current attorney general.

people.name: Sean Casten
lines: Sean is the lead author of the Cheap Energy Act, a consumer-focused approach to US energy policy. He believes that, for far too long, we have prioritized energy companies and their profits. We must shift this approach, and put American consumers first.

people.name: André Carson
lines: He says he would invest in early childhood and K-12 schools, raise teacher pay, and expand Pell Grants and workforce training as alternatives to a four-year degree.
He says tariffs are raising household costs, and he wants tax cuts for working families, small businesses, and entrepreneurs rather than policy aimed at the ultra-wealthy.
He says he opposes cuts to SNAP, introduced a Food Deserts Act to finance grocery stores in underserved areas, and supports military and humanitarian aid to Ukraine.

people.name: Barb Regnitz
lines: She says safe cities, secure borders, and smarter spending are her vision, including arresting and prosecuting criminals and ending catch-and-release.
She says she would curb inflation and waste so families keep more purchasing power, and reduce the national debt by putting American families and businesses ahead of foreign interests.
She says schools should teach students how to think, that girls' sports and facilities should be reserved for biological females, and that law-abiding people should keep the right to bear arms.

people.name: Beau Bayh
lines: He says his first priority is to stop waste and insider dealing in the secretary of state's office, including unnecessary travel, luxury vehicles, no-bid contracts, and high-paying jobs for family and friends.
He says illegal votes should not count and that every eligible Hoosier should be able to vote.
He supports statewide ballot referendums, including on redistricting, and says he will advocate for new small businesses and for working families.

people.name: Brad Meyer
lines: He says he supports Medicare for All so no one goes broke trying to stay alive, and he wants higher wages, fair taxes, and restored collective bargaining.
He says he is focused on making a first home possible again, lowering the cost of education, and an immigration system that respects the dignity of work.
He says policy has shifted wealth upward, and he is running so working people are not left behind from their first jobs through retirement.

people.name: Cynthia Wirth
lines: She says working-class Hoosiers should have good-paying jobs, affordable housing and child care, and access to sick time and paid family leave.
