She says she would support professional teachers and neighborhood pre-K through 12 schools that are safe and welcoming for students of all backgrounds and abilities.

She says health care should be affordable enough that no one skips treatment because of cost, job loss, or discrimination, and she would invest in cleaner energy and oppose data centers that consume large amounts of fuel, water, and electricity.

people.name: Drew Cox
lines: He says he supports a single-payer Medicare for All system and would overturn Citizens United to get big money out of politics.
He says he would raise the minimum wage, support unions, and fight poverty, and he wants affordable-housing legislation.
He says that as a Marine veteran he would vote against further wars he calls needless, rein in unilateral military action, and fund the VA.

people.name: Erin Houchin
lines: She says she supports finishing a border wall, backing law enforcement, and deporting people she calls criminal illegal aliens.
She says the federal government spends too much, and she backs a balanced-budget amendment and opposes late-term abortion.
She says parents should direct their children's education, that she would not defund the police, and that cutting red tape and taxes is how small businesses create jobs.

people.name: Frank Mrvan
lines: He says he supported the bipartisan infrastructure law and has delivered community-project funding for local infrastructure, the environment, first responders, and colleges, including work on the South Shore rail expansion.
He says the Inflation Reduction Act let Medicare negotiate drug prices, capped insulin at $35 a month for Medicare, and capped Medicare Part D out-of-pocket drug costs at $2,000.
He says he would ban stock trading by members of Congress, backs the Protecting the Right to Organize Act, and supports codifying Roe v. Wade.

people.name: Greg Ballard
lines: He says the secretary of state should run elections and should not endorse, raise money for, or donate to candidates who appear on those ballots.
He says he will not take sides in other state or local races.
He says the campaign is meant to give voters more choices at the ballot box.

people.name: J.D. Ford
lines: He says he would cap health-care and prescription costs and push corporations to account for prices on groceries, housing, and energy.
He says Washington needs a Democratic check so federal agencies are not above the law.
He says he grew up in a union family, with a father who drove trucks and a mother who was a school secretary, and that he is running because that middle-class promise is no longer guaranteed.

people.name: Jamee Decio
lines: She says gas, groceries, housing, utilities, and health care should be affordable, and that tax dollars should go to Indiana families rather than Wall Street or endless foreign conflicts.
She says universal health care alongside private payers would help small businesses compete and improve life for Hoosiers.
She says data-center growth should not raise utility bills or silence local voices, and that the president and members of Congress must be held to the Constitution.

people.name: Jefferson Shreve
lines: His office says he wants policy that encourages economic development, and that he is focused on reining in federal spending and the national debt.
His office says he is working to advance border security and to safeguard conservative Hoosier values.
His campaign lists making life more affordable, supporting farmers and small businesses, backing law enforcement and the military, protecting the unborn, and defending the Second Amendment.

people.name: Jim Baird
lines: He says his priorities are protecting family farms, cutting federal spending, and expanding rural health care through more competition and telehealth.
He says he would secure the southern border and give immigration enforcement the resources to remove people here illegally who have committed crimes.
He says he would protect Second Amendment rights and support veterans.

people.name: Kelly Thompson
lines: She says she would lower costs for housing, health care, education, utilities, and energy, and fight for Medicare for All.
She says she would fully fund education from child care to college by taxing Wall Street, and put Hoosiers ahead of corporations and foreign governments.
She says she would end U.S. wars in the Middle East and bring troops home, ban stock trading by Congress and the president, and release the Epstein files.

people.name: Lauri Shillings
lines: She says she is running to restore trust in elections and to keep the office from being used as a party tool.
She wants simpler, reliable online services for business filings and records.
She says government systems should be efficient and that voters should have clear guides for registration and voting.

people.name: Mark Messmer
lines: He says voters should know he is a Hoosier businessman and a Christian who will stand up to what he calls the woke mob in Washington.
He says he is a pro-Trump conservative and will keep fighting for the values he learned growing up in Jasper.
He says faith, family, and hard work are what make communities strong, and that he wants those communities more prosperous.

people.name: Marlin Stutzman
lines: He says Washington's debt and spending, which he puts at $37 trillion, are the biggest threat to the American dream, and that waste should be cut without raising taxes.
He says a repaired tax system should let workers keep more of what they earn, and that Social Security and Medicare can be preserved alongside entitlement reforms that reduce the debt.
He says he wants to finish a border wall and strengthen national security.

people.name: Mary Allen
lines: She says health care is a human right and that she would protect and expand Medicaid and Medicare and keep rural hospitals open.
She says universal coverage, not tied to a job, would lower costs by focusing on prevention and let people change jobs or start businesses without losing doctors.
She says every Hoosier deserves a decent place to live, food on the table, and a home they can keep livable.

people.name: Max Engling
lines: He says he will work so that only eligible citizens vote in Indiana and will advocate closed primaries.
He wants business filings screened for fraud, including shell companies, and he wants regulations on small businesses cut back.
He proposes a public portal where people can report possible election problems.

people.name: Patrick McAuley
lines: He says he would push for closer community-police ties, more officers living in the precincts they patrol, and resources aimed at reducing crime.
He says he would expand housing supply, put vacant properties to use, and support practical paths off the street.
He says not every young person needs a four-year degree, and he would expand trades, apprenticeships, and skilled jobs.

people.name: Rudy Yakym
lines: He says Washington is stuck in gridlock and bureaucracy, and that he wants limited government, individual liberty, and fiscal responsibility.
He says power should sit with the people rather than an expanding federal bureaucracy, and that he would cut red tape and restore a balance between federal and state power.
He says his priorities in Congress are shrinking the federal bureaucracy, restoring fiscal responsibility, and making sure veterans get the care and benefits they earned.

people.name: Victoria Spartz
lines: She says the national debt should be cut by reducing spending and balancing the budget, not by raising taxes on citizens.
She says the legal immigration process is too long, expensive, and bureaucratic, and that a stronger work-visa program should serve the national interest.
She says health-care costs need more transparency, competition, and consumer choice, and that politics should be a duty rather than a career.

people.name: Ashley Hinson
lines: She says she is working with President Trump to secure the border, cut wasteful spending, and pursue pro-growth policies.
She says she has introduced bipartisan bills to improve child care for working families and to ban federal lobbying as a check on corruption.
She says that on Appropriations she works to account for every taxpayer dollar, and that on the China committee she works to hold the Chinese Communist Party accountable.

people.name: Brenna Bird
lines: She says she has worked to get criminals off the street, advocate for crime victims, and stand with law enforcement.
She says that as counsel to Governor Branstad she fought federal health-care policy and rules from other states that she says tried to dictate Iowa farm practices.
She says she led a fight against EPA regulations that were hurting Iowa farmers and will use the office to defend what she calls the rule of law.

people.name: Chris McGowan
lines: He says he will work with the Trump administration to secure the border, stop fentanyl, and support immigration enforcement.
He says standing up for agriculture means protecting markets, defending landowner rights, and backing trade agreements for what farmers produce.
He says he will put America first, stand up to China, bring jobs back, restore energy independence, and defend life from conception to natural death.

people.name: Christina Bohannan
lines: She says her top priority is lowering the cost of living: end tariffs she says raise family costs, stop hedge funds from buying family homes, build more housing, let Medicare negotiate more drug prices, and cap insulin at $35 a month.

She says she takes no corporate PAC money and would ban stock trading by members of Congress and other high officials, seek a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United, and set term limits.
She says her father's insurer canceled coverage after he became ill, and she wants a health system that does not drop people when they get sick.

people.name: Dave Dawson
lines: He says he would let Medicare negotiate drug prices, cap insulin and other lifesaving drugs, protect the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid, and offer a voluntary public option while letting people keep private coverage.
He says he would push a long-delayed farm bill, rural broadband, help for beginning farmers, and tougher anti-monopoly enforcement against corporate processors.
He says he would seek to overturn Citizens United, ban members of Congress from trading individual stocks, and limit House service to six terms and Senate service to two.

people.name: Joe Mitchell
lines: He says he takes no corporate PAC money and supports term limits of 12 years in the House and 12 in the Senate, plus a ban on members of Congress trading stocks.
He says immigration policy should put Americans first, including a secure border, removal of people he describes as criminal illegal immigrants, and a temporary ban on H-1B visas.
He says deregulating homebuilding would lower home prices, and he wants lower taxes for middle-class families and small businesses and fewer rules on farmers.

people.name: Josh Turek
lines: He says economic policy should benefit the middle class and workers rather than Wall Street and billionaire donors.
He says he supports public education and opposes school vouchers.
He says Iowa's health care system needs major reform, and he supports protection of air, food, and water.

people.name: Lindsay James
lines: She says no one should go bankrupt or ration medicine because of a medical emergency, and that rural health care needs urgent changes as cancer rates rise.
She says money in politics has fueled partisanship, and that getting money out of politics is necessary for a healthier system.
She says Iowa farmers cannot wait another decade for a farm bill, and she opposes private-school vouchers she says benefit the most fortunate.

people.name: Mariannette Miller-Meeks
lines: She says she is running for re-election because Iowans deserve someone who will keep fighting for them and for Iowa values.
On her 2026 tour she says she is fighting for lower health-care costs, lower taxes, and common sense.

people.name: Nate Willems
lines: He says he will go after wage theft, worker misclassification, and unpaid overtime.
He says he will hold corporations accountable for cheating families, work with prosecutors on violent crime, and protect seniors from scams and nursing-home safety failures.
He says the office is the one that can fine corporate polluters who contaminate air and water, and that it should focus on Iowa rather than national political fights.

people.name: Paul Pate
lines: He says he made it easier for service members overseas to vote, started online voter registration, and brought voter ID to Iowa.
He says he started the Safe at Home program for survivors of violence and has pushed election cybersecurity and ballot access for Iowans with disabilities.
He says business-filing changes have cut bureaucracy and sped processing for Iowa companies, under a slogan of easy to vote and hard to cheat.

people.name: Rob Sand
lines: He says he would ban stock trading by the governor, legislators, and other covered officials, require personal financial disclosures and blind trusts, and make violations carry mandatory prison time.
He says anyone who steals more than $10,000 in taxpayer dollars should face mandatory prison, a ban on doing business with the state, and loss of taxpayer-funded retirement and health benefits.

He says he would restore powers taken from the auditor in 2023, extend whistleblower protections beyond state employees, and require annual audits, tuition limits, and income limits for the private-school voucher program.

people.name: Ryan Peterman
lines: He says the job is to make sure every eligible Iowan can vote and that elections are fair and secure.
He says he has met county auditors across the state and wants to be a partner they can trust.
He says trust in the office depends on keeping politics out of the work.

people.name: Sarah Trone Garriott
lines: She says she has met parents who ration medicine so their children can eat and seniors who skip meals to pay heating bills, and she wants to crack down on price gouging and end tariff policy she says raises family costs.
She says she would expand the Child Tax Credit and Earned Income Tax Credit, provide paid family and medical leave, and eliminate junk fees and surprise medical bills.
She says she would stand up for hardworking Iowans and protect their freedom, paycheck, and future rather than chase partisan wins.

people.name: Thomas Laehn
lines: He says the two major parties have taken political power from the people and that he would work to give that power back.
As county attorney he says he prosecuted child rape, attempted murder, and other violent crime, and also built a community-service program for nonviolent offenders.
He says that program, and his leadership, drove recidivism down.

people.name: Zach Lahn
lines: He says he will free Iowa's farmers from a system that leaves the farmer last, and break up monopolies that treat farmers and families as numbers.
He says more than 25 percent of Iowa land is owned by out-of-state investors and foreign governments, and he will fight to keep that land in Iowa hands.
He says a classroom should be for learning rather than political doctrine, and that anyone who uses a teaching job to push political doctrine will not teach in the state.

people.name: Zach Nunn
lines: He says out-of-control federal spending drove inflation, and he has worked to rein in bureaucracy and stop what he calls tax-and-spend policies.
He says he backs law enforcement and a border-security law aimed at drugs, trafficking, and exploitation.
He says he fights for a farm bill and for renewable fuels that support Iowa farmers and energy independence.

people.name: Adam Hamilton
lines: He says tariffs, foreign wars, and erratic leadership have raised the cost of food, medicine, and gas, and that farmers, ranchers, and small businesses are facing higher fuel, input, and health-care costs.
His listed focus is listening to Kansans, the cost of food, energy, and health care, and working with Democrats, Republicans, and independents.
He says Washington should not be a bully or a place of gridlock, and that he went on a listening tour before deciding to run.

people.name: Chris Mann
lines: He says the attorney general should answer when local departments ask for help investigating and prosecuting major crimes, including drug distribution and child sexual abuse.
He wants officer training held around the state, mental-health care for first responders, and workers' compensation coverage for PTSD.
He says he will prosecute scams, push treatment access outside the northeast corner of the state, and fund shelters for people leaving domestic violence.

people.name: Cindy Holscher
lines: She says she will lower the cost of living, including health care, housing, child care, and groceries, and fully fund public schools.
She says she will expand Medicaid, protect rural hospitals, and protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid.
She calls for a pause on new data centers until guardrails are set, and she supports legalizing recreational and medical marijuana.

people.name: David Graham
lines: He says he will vote against bailouts, pork, and agencies he cannot explain, and that he wants every Epstein-related file released.
He wants license-plate cameras he says track where people drive taken down unless the government gets a warrant.

He also says he will vote to ban congressional stock trading, legalize marijuana, oppose new gun restrictions, defend the unborn, scrap climate mandates, and require Congress to vote before the country goes to war.

people.name: Derek Schmidt
lines: He says his Armed Services work advocates for Fort Riley, Fort Leavenworth, and Forbes Field, and for service members and their families.
On Judiciary, he says he works to secure the southern border, reform the federal bureaucracy, fight taxpayer fraud and abuse, and support law enforcement.
On Small Business, he says he works so Kansas small businesses have the resources to grow.

people.name: Don Coover
lines: He says rising grocery and housing costs and closing local hospitals are leaving people in despair, and that Washington keeps making it worse.
He says the district needs people who will work together, spend within their means, and reward hard work.
He says he is running so people who know a hard day's work are the ones making decisions again.

people.name: Eric Jenkins
lines: He says he will fight wasteful spending, push a balanced-budget framework, oppose new broad-based tax increases, and make Trump-era tax cuts permanent.
He says he will fully fund and modernize the military, support veterans' health care, and strengthen Kansas installations including Fort Leavenworth.
He says secure borders are a national-security need, and he lists the Second Amendment, free speech, and religious liberty as rights he will defend.

people.name: Jennifer Day
lines: She says voting systems should stay accurate and free of disinformation, and that she will coordinate with county election officials.
She says she will look at states with higher turnout and consider similar ways to bring eligible Kansans into voting.
She says she will keep modernizing business registration so it is easier to start and run a company.

people.name: Katy Tyndell
lines: She says she will work for affordable health care, including mental health care, after her family navigated a sister's schizophrenia and she watched insurance premiums rise at her business.
She says she will look for common ground to lower taxes on working Kansans and bring costs down, instead of tax breaks aimed at corporations and the wealthy.
She says tariffs and the war with Iran have hurt Kansas farm markets and raised fertilizer and diesel costs, and that she will fight to reverse those tariff policies and end the war.

people.name: Kris Kobach
lines: The site points to prosecutions involving fentanyl trafficking and to a partnership with federal immigration enforcement that detained people with serious criminal records.
It describes a multistate settlement with Meta that requires new safety features for children on Instagram and Facebook.
It also describes a push to cut off phone numbers used for scam robocalls.

people.name: Lauren Reinhold
lines: She says rural hospitals are the lifeblood of their communities and pledges to rebuild rural health care.
She says farm policy should put producers, family operations, and main-street businesses ahead of corporate monopolies.
She calls Social Security a hard-earned promise and says she will fight underfunding and political interference that delay benefits.

people.name: Pat Proctor
lines: He says he has backed laws so that only U.S. citizens vote, so Election Day is the deadline for casting ballots, and so paper audits of elections are stronger.
He says he will watch foreign and domestic threats to elections and work with law enforcement and other states.
He says the office should help people start and run businesses and should recruit jobs to Kansas.

people.name: Roger Marshall
lines: He highlights farm bills on fertilizer costs, whole milk in schools, and interstate sale of state-inspected beef.
He points to hospital and Medicare bills on prior authorization, price transparency, Medicare Advantage, and lasting telehealth.
He also lists border legislation, energy production including ethanol and natural gas, aerospace work in Wichita, and water conservation over the aquifer.

people.name: Ron Estes
lines: He highlights tax reform, free and fair trade, retirement security, lower health-care prices, Wichita's aviation industry, and the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement.
He says he will defend the Second Amendment, stand for the sanctity of life, secure the border, and support the military and veterans.
He says he is working to rein in federal spending, balance the budget, and ease regulations on Kansas farmers, workers, and small businesses.

people.name: Scott Morgan
lines: He says the secretary of state should be a referee, not a partisan player, and that elections should be fair, secure, accessible, and professionally run.
He supports voter participation, local election officials, public transparency, secure systems, and reliable audits.
He says he will keep modernizing the office and favor practical reforms that reduce polarization.

people.name: Sharice Davids
lines: She says she is focused on lowering the cost of living for Kansas families.
She says she wants good jobs in the community.
She says government should work for people rather than special interests.

people.name: Tracey Mann
lines: He says life begins at conception and that he will protect unborn life.
He says he will be a voice for farmers and ranchers and wants rural communities to thrive, not just survive.
He supports the Second Amendment and says the southern border should be secured with a wall.

people.name: Ty Masterson
lines: He says that as Senate president he led a tax-cut package he calls the largest in Kansas history, and that he wants lower taxes, safer streets, and a government that answers to the people who pay for it.
He proposes a Homeowners Bill of Rights aimed at property taxes and a stronger voice for taxpayers.
He offers a Kansas Ratepayer Protection Pledge against higher costs he says outside interests would push onto families, farms, schools, hospitals, and small businesses.

people.name: Andy Barr
lines: He says he would deport people he calls criminal illegal immigrants, restart border-wall construction, hire more border agents, restore Remain in Mexico, and end catch-and-release.

He says he voted for tax cuts that end taxes on Social Security for seniors, on overtime, and on tips, and he wants to expand Kentucky coal and block climate rules he says were imposed through financial regulators.

He says he will defend girls' sports and private spaces, veterans' disability and health benefits, the Second Amendment, police funding, sanctions on fentanyl tied to China, and Kentucky farmers, including a federal framework for hemp products.

people.name: Brett Guthrie
lines: He says he is focused on lower health-care and prescription costs, energy independence, and cutting taxes and regulations.
He says he wants to protect seniors, strengthen domestic manufacturing, and keep government out of the doctor-patient relationship.
The campaign says he is pro-life, has an A rating from the NRA, and has been called a friend of the Farm Bureau.

people.name: Charles Booker
lines: He says Kentucky needs a senator who treats poverty as an emergency, because families can be one medical bill, layoff, or storm from losing everything.
He says health care is a human right and that he wants union jobs in every county.
He also calls for clean water, clean air, and a politics grounded in the dignity of the people it serves.

people.name: Christopher Campbell
lines: He supports Medicare for All and says the federal government should provide basic medical care.
He says workers need safe conditions, strong benefits, good pay, and a way to raise grievances without retaliation.
He wants a constitutional environmental amendment and a ban on carbon credits that he says let facilities keep polluting.

people.name: Ed Gallrein
lines: He says he would cut taxes and regulations, stop spending he blames for inflation, and bring jobs back to Kentucky.
He says he would finish a border wall, fund Border Patrol and ICE, and rebuild the military.
He says he would defend gun rights without compromise, that he is pro-life, and that he would eliminate DEI programs in schools, the military, and government.

people.name: Hal Rogers
lines: He says that as Appropriations chair from 2011 to 2016 he cut discretionary spending by $126 billion and pushed oversight of federal agencies.
He says he led the first Homeland Security appropriations subcommittee and pressed for immigration enforcement and border security.
After winning the 2026 primary he said he would keep fighting for conservative values, jobs at home, and energy independence.

people.name: James Comer
lines: He says that as Oversight chair he is leading major investigations and pushing to reduce government waste, fraud, and abuse.
He says he wants a balanced federal budget, rebuilt infrastructure, and business-friendly policies that create opportunity for families.
He says his record includes work on the 2018 farm bill and legislation to lift regulations and increase government accountability.

people.name: John Williams
lines: The campaign says it is grassroots and does not take corporate money.
His site says he stands for farm resilience, congressional accountability, workplace dignity, fairer drug prices, and veterans' services.
He also lists infrastructure, data-center rules, child care, tax policy for everyday Americans, and health-insurance reform among the issues he is running on.

people.name: Maria Rodriguez
lines: She says she believes in free enterprise, safe communities, legal immigration, and constitutional rights.
Her campaign lists defending capitalism, a safer Louisville, lower taxes, and protecting the unborn among her priorities.
She also lists protecting women's sports.

people.name: Megan Wingfield
lines: She says one job should support a family, workers need a living wage, and health care should be universal so illness does not cause bankruptcy.
She says she would protect reproductive freedom, support universal pre-K and affordable child care, and expand VA care, mental-health services, and housing for veterans.
She says she signed a term-limits pledge and wants independent mechanics to have access to vehicle diagnostics that manufacturers now lock behind paywalls.

people.name: Melissa Strange
lines: She says she would protect and expand Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security, lower drug costs, and make treatment easier to find than a dealer.
She says she takes no corporate or foreign PAC money and supports term limits, a ban on congressional stock trading, and an end to Citizens United.
She says data centers should need community approval, and she wants the government out of reproductive health care and a right to repair farm and consumer equipment.

people.name: Morgan McGarvey
lines: He says health care is a human right and that he supports Medicare for All, Medicare drug-price negotiation, and coverage for vision, dental, and hearing.
He says he has brought home federal funding, including money for Simmons College, and that his office has returned Social Security, veterans' benefits, and tax refunds to families.
He says he passed a House bill to protect veterans' benefits and is pushing a nationwide ban on no-knock search warrants in Breonna Taylor's name.

people.name: Ned Pillersdorf
lines: He says he opposes cuts to Medicaid, Medicare, food stamps, utility aid, public media, Job Corps, and cancer research that he says fund tax breaks for billionaires.
He says the incumbent's vote for the tax-and-spending bill betrayed a district that depends on rural hospitals and the Affordable Care Act.
He says he will campaign on health-care access, better internet, education, and clean drinking water, and that he supports uncapping the House and term limits.

people.name: Ralph Alvarado
lines: He says he will work with both parties on affordable health care, lower costs, more transparency, and more patient control.
He says he wants groceries, gas, and health care to cost less, good-paying jobs to grow, and wasteful spending that feeds inflation to end.
His campaign says he would toughen punishments for Medicare and Medicaid fraud and make big insurers disclose profits, denial rates, and wait times.

people.name: Zach Dembo
lines: He says tariffs are taxes crushing small businesses and that full-time work should cover a family's bills, including a living wage of at least $15 an hour.
He says Medicaid cuts hurt families and hospitals, that one in three Kentuckians relies on Medicaid, and that women should make their own health-care decisions.
He says data centers are driving up energy bills and taking farmland without enough local say, and that he left the Justice Department to fight corruption.

people.name: Blake Miguez
lines: He says he passed a law so Louisiana can prosecute corrupt politicians after they leave office, and in Congress he would push term limits and a permanent ban on members trading individual stocks.
He says he wrote the state law forcing New Orleans to follow immigration law, and he would finish a border wall, mandate E-Verify, and treat cartels as foreign terrorist organizations.
He says he authored constitutional carry, banned Big Tech money in Louisiana elections, and banned ultra-processed food in school cafeterias.

people.name: Clay Higgins
lines: He says a sworn officer's oath is to the Constitution, not to a sheriff, chief, or marshal.
The site says that, as a Christian, he focuses on the power of an individual to be redeemed.

people.name: Conrad Cable
lines: He says he would raise wages, protect the right to organize, and shift power from corporations to the people who do the work.
He says more than a third of the district relies on Medicaid, that he supports Medicare for All, and that health care should depend on need rather than income.
He says he would open public grocery stores stocked with local food that SNAP and WIC can buy, and he supports overturning Citizens United and banning congressional stock trading.

people.name: Jamie Davis
lines: He says Louisiana has become unaffordable and that he wants lower grocery, insurance, and utility bills.
He says he will work to expand access to affordable care and will not vote for hospital closings.
He says he opposes secret nondisclosure agreements in development deals and land takings for industry, and that his campaign is funded by Louisiana donors rather than corporate PACs.

people.name: John Day
lines: He says he wants lower everyday costs, better pay, safer communities, and storm protection, with an all-of-the-above energy strategy that keeps oil and gas jobs and invests in renewables.
He says insurance should have fair rates and faster claims, and that homeowners should get the coverage they pay for after storms.
He says government should not control a person's body, health care, or personal life, and that patients rather than politicians should be in charge of care.

people.name: Julia Letlow
lines: She says her work in Congress has been for parents, students, farmers, law enforcement, and Louisiana families.
She says she is guided by faith, family, service, and love of the state.
She says she is running for the Senate to give Louisiana conservative leadership, and she notes President Trump's endorsement.

people.name: Lauren Jewett
lines: She says Louisiana families are squeezed by unaffordable insurance, health-care costs, underfunded schools, and an economy that leaves too many people behind.
Her campaign says the district needs lower costs, strong schools and hospitals, safe communities, and a representative who fights for working people.
She says she wants to advocate for environmental, constitutional, economic, and health protections in a region she calls overlooked.

people.name: Lindsay Garcia
lines: She says she would make daily life more affordable, protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, lower prescription costs, and raise wages.
She says she would bring federal money home for I-10 and I-12, bridges, drainage, flood protection, and affordable flood insurance.
She says she would fight violent crime, trafficking, and fentanyl while supporting voting rights, civil rights, and due process.

people.name: Michael Echols
lines: He says insurance premiums should fall if Washington lowers inflation, expands domestic energy, and drops federal rules that raise the cost of rebuilding after storms.
He says grocery prices rose because of federal spending, and that cheaper fuel and fewer rules on farmers, truckers, and stores would bring checkout prices down.
He says he would expand oil and gas production, support LNG exports, protect Louisiana refineries, and speed permits for energy projects.

people.name: Mike Johnson
lines: He says that with President Trump he has worked on lower costs, American energy dominance, peace through strength, and tax cuts he says will save district families nearly $1,300.
He says he will keep fighting for the principles that make Louisiana a place to live, work, and raise a family.
His campaign quotes a Trump endorsement that highlights border security, law and order, farmers, and the Second Amendment as parts of the agenda Johnson is carrying.

people.name: Misti Cordell
lines: She says she would cut taxes and red tape, defend agriculture and energy jobs, and stand up to federal overreach.
She says she would secure the border, finish a wall, back law enforcement, and protect Second Amendment rights.
She says she would vote pro-life, defend girls' sports, support school choice, and return control of education to parents and local communities.

people.name: Peter Williams
lines: He says the new district map covers both urban and rural communities and that a representative should plan around agriculture, health, housing, education, transportation, recreation, and incarceration.
He says voters should have a choice based on policies and people rather than a party-chosen status quo.
He says he has spent more than 30 years as a community advocate trying to improve quality of life in the district.

people.name: Steve Scalise
lines: He says he is working to promote fiscal discipline, create good-paying jobs, protect freedoms, and get the economy back on track.
His site lists creating jobs, building a border wall, fixing health care, cutting spending, and making America safe among the priorities supporters can choose.
He says that as majority leader he sets the floor schedule and works with colleagues on conservative solutions to the country's hardest problems.

people.name: Troy Carter Sr.
lines: He says he will keep fighting for fair housing, people with disabilities, criminal and environmental justice, equal pay, and a living wage.
He says government should let women make their own health and reproductive decisions, and he wants quality, affordable health care and less student-loan debt.
He says he championed the Social Security Fairness Act so teachers, police, and firefighters are not docked by the windfall and pension offsets.

people.name: Bobby Charles
lines: He says he would cut crime and treat the drug trade as a central threat to Maine communities.
He says he would cut taxes and regulation that he argues weigh on businesses and working families.
He says schools should improve and that too much state policy has been driven by ideological agendas he opposes.

people.name: Chellie Pingree
lines: She says her Appropriations work has focused on opportunities for working families, support for farmers, veterans, and wider access to health care.
The campaign says she knows meeting payroll and offering benefits is hard because she has run an organic farm and island businesses.

people.name: Hannah Pingree
lines: She says her record includes expanding access to health care and affordable housing and helping lead the state's climate work.
She says that in the Legislature she worked on rural broadband, clean energy, lower health costs, reproductive rights, and Maine's working waterfronts.
She says that work included the Kid-Safe Products Act, aimed at keeping toxic chemicals out of products children use.

people.name: Matthew Dunlap
lines: He says he will fight blanket tariffs and the war in Iran, which he says have raised gas and grocery prices, and he supports universal child care, good-paying jobs, and more affordable housing.
He says he will protect Medicare, Social Security, and Medicaid, reverse Medicaid cuts he says are hurting rural hospitals, and support Medicare for All.
He says he is fully pro-labor, supports the PRO Act, and will defend a woman's right to make her own reproductive decisions.

people.name: Paul LePage
lines: He says he will cut wasteful spending that he argues drove inflation, and he pledges to protect Social Security and Medicare.
He says he will finish a border wall, end illegal immigration, and lower taxes and red tape so Maine gets more jobs.
He says he will defend the Second Amendment and veterans' health care and benefits.

people.name: Rick Bennett
lines: He says families are paying more for housing, groceries, and energy, and that many young people are unsure they can afford to stay.
He says his record includes fights against dark-money interests, work to expand broadband, and challenges to the utilities.
He says a governor should make daily life more affordable and answer to residents rather than to either major party.

people.name: Ronald Russell
lines: He says Maine cannot afford more federal taxes on top of a high state and local burden, and he wants tax relief he ties to the law he calls the Big Beautiful Bill made permanent, with inflation adjustments and a larger work-linked earned-income credit.
He says energy independence is the main way to strengthen the economy and lower fuel, grocery, and heating-oil costs, and that renewable energy should be a choice rather than a mandate.
He says he supports vetted legal immigration and assimilation, and that securing the border against unlawful crossings should come first.

people.name: Susan Collins
lines: She says her legislative work has focused on health care, the economy, and jobs in Maine.
She says she has worked to help small businesses and on education, national security, and veterans.
She says help for older Americans has been a major part of that record, and that she chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee.

people.name: Troy Jackson
lines: He says that in the Legislature he worked to lower prescription-drug prices, pass universal school meals, and expand rural health care.
He says he protected union jobs, delivered property-tax relief, and backed strong reproductive-health laws.
He says he is running because working families are being squeezed while the wealthiest keep gaining more.

people.name: Adrian Boafo
lines: He says he would raise the federal minimum wage to $15 and tie it to inflation, cut taxes for working and middle-class families, and expand the child tax credit and earned income tax credit.
He supports universal child care and says he would defend Social Security.
He says he is fighting what he calls unlawful attacks on democratic institutions and civil rights and wants voting rights and equal protection strengthened.

people.name: Andy Ellis
lines: He says the state should stop data-center projects that he argues threaten communities, water, and public health.
He says unaffiliated and third-party voters are shut out of meaningful elections and that he has a plan aimed at two-party political corruption.
He says the state should spread wealth, power, and opportunity so more residents have a say in incentives, public funds, and budgets.

people.name: Andy Harris
lines: He says he is fighting to restore fiscal responsibility in Washington and protect taxpayer dollars.
The campaign describes him as a common-sense conservative with the courage to change Washington.
He says he is unafraid to speak for the priorities of Maryland's 1st District.

people.name: Anthony Brown
lines: He says he created a civil-rights division and widened the Independent Investigations Division so it can prosecute police-involved deaths.
He says he has defended gun-safety laws in court and pursued wage theft and corporate conduct that harms workers and consumers.
He says he has sued when federal policy threatened environmental rules, voting rights, and protections for women and immigrants.

people.name: April McClain Delaney
lines: She says she will work on rising costs, health care, and equal access to a good education, and that she wants more job training, small-business support, and better-paying work in the district.
She points to her work expanding broadband and says technology should drive development across the 6th District.
She says she will put progress ahead of partisanship and defend democratic institutions.

people.name: Berney Flowers
lines: He says he advocates term limits, fiscal responsibility, and working across party lines.
He says he supports taking politics out of public schools, parental involvement, and local control of education.
He says he supports strong immigration enforcement, national defense, and public safety.

people.name: Cathy White
lines: She says workers need their own political organization because neither major party represents them on jobs, low wages, and rising prices.
She says child care and elder care cost more than most workers can pay, and that many older workers cannot afford to retire.
She says workers have no reason to support the current war in the Middle East, which she argues enriches defense and energy companies while raising the price of gas.

people.name: Cheryl Riley
lines: She says safety comes first and that she will push to keep people who commit crimes off the street, especially to protect older people, women, and children.
She says she will back pro-growth policies that put American businesses and workers first, and she argues for limited government rather than what she calls democratic socialism.
She also says she will defend the Constitution, the Second Amendment, veterans, and law enforcement, and she calls for sealed borders, more energy production, and parents' rights in schools.

people.name: Chris Chaffee
lines: He says high costs have pushed taxpayers out of Maryland and that he would work to bring resources back to the 5th District.
He points to the delay rebuilding the Baltimore bridge and says the state should also look at a new crossing from Calvert County toward St. Mary's County and the Patuxent River Naval Base.

people.name: Dan Cox
lines: He says he would cut taxes and fees and limit property taxes so retirees are not taxed out of their homes.
He proposes down-payment help and tax credits for first-time and younger buyers, and says building and permitting costs should come down.
He says Maryland should reopen closed power plants, study small modular reactors, and give households more energy choices so electric bills stop climbing.

people.name: Dan Schwartz
lines: He says he would hold monthly town halls and support a ban on members of Congress trading stocks, options, and crypto.
He says he would fight spending freezes and tariffs that hurt farmers and raise prices, and protect consumers from what he calls corporate grift.
He says he would restore safety programs for food, water, bridges, and air travel, protect the environment, and defend affordable care and public-health research.

people.name: Dave Wallace
lines: He says he will vote to equip police and other first responders, and that he would sponsor a gold-standard bill to stop the dollar from losing value.
His mission statement calls for restoring constitutional freedoms, a free-market economy, public safety, and national sovereignty.
He says that work includes opposing socialism and what he describes as strict Sharia law and movements that weaken faith, family, and the Bill of Rights.

people.name: George McDermott
lines: He says he will not vote blindly with a party and that legislation should serve citizens rather than corporate insiders and lobbyists.
He says he opposes corruption in local, state, and federal government and argues that courts and private prisons have a financial stake in incarceration.

people.name: Glenn Ivey
lines: He says the Trump administration is attacking federal workers, diversity programs, and constitutional rights, and that he is fighting those actions in Congress and in court.
He says he is working with unions, advocacy groups, and attorneys and will not give ground to the administration.

people.name: James Rutledge III
lines: He says he would fight crime at every level without turning the office into a partisan fight.
He says the office should go after hackers, online predators, and scams that target older and vulnerable people.
He says he would protect clean water and the Chesapeake Bay.

people.name: Jamie Raskin
lines: He says Democracy Summer teaches the history of democratic freedom and lessons for political leadership today.
The campaign is organizing volunteers to defend what it calls strong democracy and freedom.
He is asking voters to send him back to the House for another term representing the 8th District.

people.name: Johnny Olszewski Jr.
lines: He says he wants higher wages, affordable health care, and fully funded public schools, and he opposed a budget he says gave tax breaks to the wealthy while threatening programs families use.
He says he would extend health-insurance tax credits, end tariffs that raise prices, cut drug costs, expand housing, and protect Medicare, Medicaid, SNAP, and the Child Tax Credit.
He says he supports expanding voting rights, protecting court independence, and banning stock trading by members of Congress.

people.name: Kweisi Mfume
lines: The campaign says he still argues for bipartisan work on economic, education, and health-care issues.
It highlights his role on the Americans with Disabilities Act, a ban on assault weapons, and the Henrietta Lacks law on diversity in cancer research.
It also points to legislation that codified and increased funding for the Minority Business Development Agency.

people.name: Robin Ficker
lines: He says he would cut wasteful spending and the deficit, support police, and hold people who commit crimes accountable.
He says he would lower taxes and regulation so jobs stay in the United States and in Maryland.
He opposes making the District of Columbia part of Maryland and says only American citizens should vote in American elections.

people.name: Sarah Elfreth
lines: She says she is working to revoke tariffs that raise prices, expand affordable child care, ease student loans, build more housing, and roll back utility rate increases.
She says affordability is personal as a first-time homeowner and young professional with student loans.
She says she is also standing up for federal workers, supporting veterans, and protecting the Chesapeake Bay.

people.name: Scott Collier
lines: He says he wants to work with District 7 residents on crime, gangs, schools, drugs, and the juvenile and criminal justice systems.
He lists ending food deserts and addressing illegal immigration among his priorities, and says communities are safer when he keeps working with law enforcement.
He says he will not rubber-stamp legislation and wants constituent service aimed at quality of life in the district.

people.name: Wes Moore
lines: He says he has cut taxes for veterans and middle-class families and wants more Marylanders to be able to afford to live in the state.
He points to record spending on public schools and says he wants those schools to be the best in the country.
He says public safety is a priority and that homicides in Baltimore are at their lowest level in 50 years.

people.name: Andrea Campbell
lines: She says she is trying to make life more affordable by putting money back into people's pockets.
She says she is defending freedoms against rollbacks from the Trump era.
She says she is fighting for the next generation and for wider opportunity for every child, including reproductive rights, civil rights, and cases against powerful corporations.

people.name: Andrea James
lines: She says a governor's priorities should be housing, health care, child care, education, and quality of life, and she calls housing a human right.
She says people should be able to see a doctor without going into debt and that families should have child care they trust.
She says Massachusetts should not have contracts with ICE, and she wants data centers banned in favor of lower utility costs and green energy.

people.name: Anne Brensley
lines: She says she wants to encourage business growth.
She says she will engage directly with disenfranchised voters.
She says she will protect the integrity of the ballot and campaign on transparency and local control.

people.name: Ayanna Pressley
lines: She says the campaign has worked on abortion access, student-loan cancellation, and housing justice.
She says more than $35 million has come home for community health centers, transit, workforce training, and climate justice.
Her site lists a just economy, the climate crisis, housing as a human right, and changes to the criminal legal system among the issues she is organizing around.

people.name: Bill Keating
lines: He says he is challenging tariffs that raise prices and hurt small businesses, and that he wants health care that is more affordable and accessible.
He says he has fought to protect Social Security, Medicare, reproductive rights, and veterans and military families.
He says he serves on Foreign Affairs and Armed Services and has brought home federal money for coastal resiliency, public safety, clean energy, and jobs.

people.name: Dan Koh
lines: He says he is running to defend democracy, protect rights, and reduce the cost of living against what he calls a dismantling of the country.
He says that in the Biden administration he worked on infrastructure, clean-energy jobs, education, and lower prescription costs for seniors.
He says that at the Labor Department he helped recover wages, improve workplace safety, and increase union participation, and that he takes no corporate PAC money.

people.name: Ed Markey
lines: He says he is fighting to lower costs, protect workers, and expand opportunity in education and jobs.
He says health care is too expensive and that he wants lower costs, wider access, stronger public health, and corporations held accountable.
He also lists clean energy and transit, civil rights for LGBTQ people and immigrants, stronger gun laws, and a fairer justice system.

people.name: Gary Grossi
lines: He says energy costs are crushing families and that he will push affordable energy, fewer housing rules that limit supply, and a health system that puts patients ahead of bureaucracy and malpractice costs.
He says safe communities depend on law-enforcement partnerships, small-business growth, intact families, and community mental-health and addiction services.
He says he will defend freedom of speech and the right to bear arms, and he supports term limits with end-of-term audits.

people.name: Jake Auchincloss
lines: He says he works in Washington to defend democracy and lower prices against corruption that makes the American dream too expensive.
He describes a New American Dream as an excellent education by 18, a home by 30, and a dignified retirement by 65.

He says housing, health care, and utility costs should be treated by cutting rules that block starter homes, using technology to lower hospital prices, and fixing Social Security so the wealthiest pay more in.

people.name: James McGovern
lines: He says hunger, housing insecurity, and unaffordable health care are political choices, and that he is running against tax breaks for billionaires.
He says his work in Congress is to defend human rights, reform campaign finance, end hunger, and build an economy where everyone can thrive.
He says he walks 43 miles each year through the Pioneer Valley to raise money and attention for the Food Bank of Western Massachusetts.

people.name: Joe Tache
lines: He says the largest corporations should be taken into public control and the economy reorganized around housing, health care, food, education, child care, retirement, and a living wage.
He says climate policy and meaningful jobs require working people in power, and he wants spending shifted from war to domestic needs.
He says immigrants, Black Americans, women, and LGBTQ people should not be blamed for the crisis, and he wants rent capped as a share of income, free health care, and millions of union jobs.

people.name: John Deaton
lines: He says affordable health care is a right and that he will work to break up large insurers and pharmacy benefit managers, lower drug prices, and expand telehealth.
He wants faster permitting for housing and an energy mix that includes nuclear power, and he says he will not support what he calls blank checks for foreign aid.
He says he will secure the border, expand legal immigration, and support an earned path to citizenship for Dreamers who meet strict standards.

people.name: Katherine Clark
lines: She says she is fighting to cancel cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act, end a war she says raised gas prices, and lift tariffs that made goods more expensive.
She says that if Democrats control Congress she would lead efforts to crack down on ICE, stop unauthorized wars, and hold the president accountable for using the office to enrich himself.
She says every worker should have a living wage, paid family leave, and the right to join a union, and she highlights the expanded child tax credit in the American Rescue Plan.

people.name: Lori Trahan
lines: She says health care is a right, that she would strengthen the Affordable Care Act, and that Medicare should be able to negotiate drug prices.
She says she would invest in education from early childhood through apprenticeships and fight student debt.
She says she supports a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United and a pathway to citizenship alongside updated border security.

people.name: Maura Healey
lines: Her campaign says the first term ended renter's fees, capped health-care deductibles and co-pays, opposed utility rate increases, cut taxes, and protected SNAP from federal cuts.
It also points to work on the MBTA, free school meals, free community college, and veterans' homes.
For a second term she says she will defend health care and abortion rights, access to vaccines, research, jobs, and lower costs, and stand up to Donald Trump.

people.name: Micah Jones
lines: He says accountability means officials are answerable to the people, and he backs conflict-of-interest rules, congressional term limits, and Congress reclaiming its constitutional duties.

He says energy, grocery, housing, and child-care costs are shrinking opportunity, and he pledges work on energy reliability, faster permitting, and tax relief tied to child care and the state and local tax deduction.
He says security should include support for service members, veterans, and first responders, a lawful and humane immigration system, and a technological edge in artificial intelligence.

people.name: Michael Minogue
lines: He says a voter-backed audit of the Legislature is not being enforced and that the political establishment is wasting tax dollars and growing debt.
He says taxes and regulation are pushing young people out and making it hard for seniors to stay, and he asks supporters to join a call to suspend the gas tax.
He says the state needs entrepreneurs and manufacturing to stay and expand, and that the governor's basic job is public safety, including enforcement against fentanyl dealers.

people.name: Michael Walsh
lines: He says he will enforce laws already on the books, including the legislative audit, with no selective enforcement.
He opposes state zoning mandates that he says override local home rule and threaten funding.
He says he will fight utility rate hikes, vet ballot questions for clarity and legality, and investigate fraud, waste, and abuse.

people.name: Nadia Milleron
lines: She says she would eliminate federal income tax on earnings under $100,000, stop price gouging, and vote against sending tax dollars to foreign wars.
She says she would bar corporations from buying elections, cap rents, and ban corporate speculators from buying local homes.
She says she supports health care for all that removes corporate insurers, more local doctors, and a personal term limit of three House terms.

people.name: Richard Neal
lines: He says grocery and prescription costs are too high, and he is fighting for middle-class tax cuts, community investment, and an end to tariffs that raise prices.
He says he opposes wars he calls reckless because they threaten security and the economy.
He says he has fought to protect Social Security and Medicare and to make sure the region gets its fair share.

people.name: Robert Burke
lines: He says his Boxer Works plan would make Brockton a manufacturing hub for aerospace, defense, medical devices, and other goods, with a stated goal of 21,000 jobs and Junior ROTC training.
He says voting should require citizenship and voter identification, and he calls for a pause on immigration programs from H-1B visas to temporary protected status.
He says he would cut taxes, bring manufacturing back, support law enforcement, and shift health coverage toward catastrophic insurance people buy themselves.

people.name: Shiva Ayyadurai
lines: He says he wants to solve hard problems by finding root causes and bringing people together, outside the major parties.
He campaigns on a platform he calls Truth, Freedom, and Health, tying systems science, education, technology, and local action.
He says Massachusetts is deleting digital ballot images and that he is fighting to preserve them.

people.name: Stephen Lynch
lines: He says families are working more and receiving less, with stagnant wages and rising costs.
He says he has worked for fair wages, economic security, higher-education funding, housing assistance, and Social Security.
He says health care should be affordable and accessible, and that he will keep being a voice for the district.

people.name: Thomas Stalcup
lines: He says he will push immediate, broad drug-price negotiation without limits on which drugs are included.
He says prices stay high because markets limit competition, and he wants lower-cost alternatives, antitrust enforcement, and fair pricing when the public helps fund innovation.
He says he will work to unify people around shared concerns, including health-care and housing costs, and reject language that divides them.

people.name: Tyler Macallister
lines: He says he will defend the fishing fleet with practical, science-based rules and oppose industrial wind farms in fishing grounds and data centers that drain the grid and water.
He says he will take on mandates and federal spending that raise grocery, fuel, and housing costs, and he backs an all-of-the-above energy policy aimed at lower bills.
He says he will back local police and child-safety standards, and protect the benefits veterans and seniors have earned.

people.name: William Galvin
lines: He says he is in federal court resisting efforts to limit registration and voting by mail and to obtain detailed personal information about Massachusetts voters.
He says he intends to expose and resist federal interference with the 2028 presidential election and the Electoral College.

He says he wants a complete Census count in 2030, including group quarters and residents who were not born in the United States, and he lists election integrity, early voting, vote-by-mail, consumer protection, and historical preservation.

people.name: Abdul El-Sayed
lines: He says he is running so the Senate works for residents rather than for billionaires.
He says his local health work included free glasses for children, removing lead from Detroit elementary schools, and making naloxone widely available.
He says he led a program to cancel medical debt and wrote a citizen's guide to Medicare for All.

people.name: Anthony Forlini
lines: He says he would protect election integrity by removing ineligible and deceased voters from the rolls and by requiring watermarked ballots statewide.
He says he would stop sending voter information to outside groups and audit county clerks so election practices match across the state.
He says he would cut secretary of state wait times and make routine services easier to finish online or in person.

people.name: Anthony Hudson
lines: He says he would eliminate property taxes and the state income tax.
He says he would stop data-center and solar-panel development and protect farmland.
He says he wants lower taxes, smaller government, and decisions returned to local communities.

people.name: Ben Ambrose
lines: He says he would bring down grocery and gas prices, back small businesses, strengthen collective bargaining, and bring manufacturing jobs back with Buy American policies.
He supports more funding for public schools, larger Pell Grants, and vocational training, and he says he backs Medicare for All.
He also lists veterans, the natural environment, and community safety among his priorities.

people.name: Bill Huizenga
lines: He says he has pushed to rein in federal spending to fight inflation and lower the cost of energy, groceries, and housing.
He supports more American energy production and fewer regulations so small businesses can hire.
He says he backs limited government, secure borders, and safe communities, and that he has worked on Great Lakes and PFAS issues.

people.name: Callie Barr
lines: She says health care should be a right, wants Medicare available from birth, and wants Medicaid cuts restored and drug prices lowered.
She wants homes people can afford, less red tape for local builders, and a balance between short-term rentals and year-round residents.
She says work should pay enough to live in the district, and she supports unions, Social Security, childcare, farms, and broadband.

people.name: Christian Vukasovich
lines: He says he would fight for living wages, union jobs, and an economy that rewards hard work.
He says quality, affordable health care is a right, and he wants housing working families can afford.
He also calls for education and job training, and says he would put people ahead of corporate and billionaire interests.

people.name: Christina Hines
lines: She says she would lower the cost of groceries, gas, and health care and fight for good-paying Michigan jobs.
She says she would support safer communities, schools, and law-enforcement resources to prevent violent crime and protect children and seniors online.
She says she refuses corporate PAC money, would ban members of Congress from trading stocks, and would work with either party against corruption.

people.name: Christine Sloan
lines: She says she would keep voter rolls accurate, let people verify how elections are run, and treat independent and minor-party candidates fairly.
She wants government limited to protecting rights, maintaining essential services, and enforcing laws consistently.
She says she would restrict mass surveillance, including vehicle-tracking cameras and unchecked data collection, and push open records and plain-language budget reports.

people.name: Debbie Dingell
lines: She says she is working to protect the Great Lakes, lower health-care and prescription costs, and support seniors and veterans.
She says she backs U.S. auto manufacturing and fuel-economy standards that also keep cars affordable.
She says quality health care is a right and that climate change requires action from the federal government.

people.name: Donavan McKinney
lines: He says he would defend the right to form a union, fight for a living wage, tax billionaires, and support a universal basic income.
He calls for a Green New Deal, clean air and water, and more public transit, and he says Detroit's lead pipes and pollution are personal.
He supports Medicare for All, a national housing guarantee, an end to cash bail, and federal protection of abortion access, including repeal of the Hyde Amendment.

people.name: Doug Lloyd
lines: He says he would prosecute crimes fairly, without political favor or bias.
He says he would advise lawmakers as they write what he calls strong, commonsense laws.
He says he would protect constitutional rights, oppose politically motivated prosecutions, and root out corruption.

people.name: Douglas Marsh
lines: He says he would advocate a universal basic income of $1,000 a month for every adult citizen and $1,500 a month for descendants of chattel slavery.
He supports single-payer health care, and he says private-equity firms should not own homes, with rents tied to local wages and leases based on need.
He calls for an end to U.S. hostilities with Iran and for ceasefires in Gaza and Ukraine, and he wants accountability for Flint's water and a stop to Line 5.

people.name: Eli Savit
lines: He says his office built units for sexual assault and domestic violence and pursued cold-case rape prosecutions.
He says that after Roe v. Wade was overturned he went to court to challenge Michigan's abortion ban and has kept arguing for reproductive freedom.
He says he created a unit aimed at wage theft and consumer harm and has sued large companies over pollution of air and water.

people.name: Eric Borregard
lines: He wants ranked-choice voting so people can rank the candidates they support and so third-party votes are not dismissed as wasted.
He says he would lower the voting age to 16, arguing that youth political power matters more than claims of voter fraud.
He says the stations that sell candidate ads should not control debate questions, and he points to Green Party pickets of those studios.

people.name: Ethan Baker
lines: He says he is running because constant political division is unhealthy, and that people can hold their principles while still listening to one another.
He says most people want stability for their families, opportunity for their children, and safe communities, and that he would bring that approach to Congress.

people.name: Garlin Gilchrist II
lines: He says he would defend the right to vote and push for laws that disclose more dark money in politics.
He says he would modernize licensing and registration and oppose misuse of voter-registration or license-plate data.
He says he would hold car-repair companies accountable when they overcharge customers, and that his campaign takes no corporate PAC money.

people.name: Heather Smiley
lines: She says she would cut wasteful spending, balance the budget, and limit spending bills that bundle unrelated items.
She wants schools focused on academics, elections limited to citizens, and energy independence through the free market.
She says she would close the border, protect the right to self-defense, and restrict foreign ownership of land.

people.name: Hillary Scholten
lines: She says she is working to lower health-care and drug costs, defend the Affordable Care Act, and stop insurers from dropping people who get sick.
She says decisions about pregnancy belong with women, and that she will protect the right to choose.
She wants well-paying jobs, semiconductor manufacturing in Michigan, and protection of drinking water from PFAS.

people.name: Jack Bergman
lines: He says he has worked to expand rural broadband, including a bill that would account for short construction seasons in northern Michigan.
He says his veterans work includes suicide-prevention grants, more home and community care, and a burial-benefit fix he calls Gerald's Law.
He says he backs Michigan farms, including cherry growers, opposes taxpayer funding of abortion, and wants a military strong enough to deter adversaries.

people.name: James Hooper
lines: He says he is pro-life from conception to natural death and that the Second Amendment should not be infringed.
He says representative government exists to secure the rights of the governed, and he calls himself an America First conservative.
He says he is a conservative Christian and that he will be a voice for those positions in the House.

people.name: Jason Dye
lines: He says he would build a public-corruption unit aimed at government abuse, retaliation, fraud, and misuse of office, and investigate patterns of courtroom misconduct.
He wants to end qualified immunity and stop civil asset forfeiture without real due process, and he says hidden contracts and pay-to-play lobbying should be exposed.
He says he would defend homeowners from property-tax foreclosure abuse and treat secret corporate-welfare deals as corruption.

people.name: Jeremy Moss
lines: He says he would lower everyday costs, push back on tariffs he says raise prices, and defend Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid.
He says he reduced barriers to voting as elections committee chair, strengthened the state civil-rights law, and acted to protect abortion access after Roe was overturned.
He says he passed gun-safety laws, restored labor rights, and returned tax relief to seniors and working families.

people.name: Jocelyn Benson
lines: She says she would expand rural health-care options and build more housing.
She says she would take on utility companies over the rates they charge.
She says she would make child care free so more people can afford to live in the state.

people.name: John James
lines: He says he would bring down the cost of housing, energy, groceries, and car insurance.
He says schools should put reading, math, and skilled trades first, with parents in charge of their children's education.
He says he would back police and prosecute violent crime from Detroit to the Upper Peninsula.

people.name: John Moolenaar
lines: He says he opposed a Chinese-linked battery plant in Michigan and wants to stop adversaries from buying American farmland.
He says he will defend the Second Amendment, protect the unborn, and preserve Social Security and Medicare, including tax relief on those benefits for seniors.
He says he has worked to support farmers, protect Line 5, and improve patient safety and rural health care.

people.name: Kristen McDonald Rivet
lines: She says she has introduced bipartisan bills to lower grocery, housing, and medicine costs and to invest in child care, and that she led an effort to let families on SNAP buy hot prepared chicken.
She says she worked to keep Saginaw's Social Security office open and opposes cuts to Social Security benefits.
She says she wants to ban members of Congress from trading stock on insider information and to reverse Citizens United.

people.name: Lisa McClain
lines: She says she would cut taxes and regulations on small business and support trade deals that help Michigan farmers and workers.
She says she would build a border wall, enforce immigration law, and defend the Second Amendment for law-abiding owners.
She says health coverage should be sold across state lines with wider use of health savings accounts, and she opposes taxpayer funding of abortion.

people.name: Lydia Christensen
lines: She says she would protect the Great Lakes and push affordable health care, including Medicaid for all.
She calls for fair wages, green jobs, and support for small businesses, and for social, racial, and LGBTQIA+ equity.
She says she would defend voting rights and constitutional freedoms, and that she is not beholden to party bosses or corporate donors.

people.name: Michael Bouchard
lines: He says he would bring manufacturing jobs back to Michigan and cut red tape on small businesses.
He says he would finish the border wall, restore Remain in Mexico, end catch-and-release, and stop fentanyl smuggling.
He says schools should return to reading, writing, math, and science, and he backs a Parents' Bill of Rights.

people.name: Mike Rogers
lines: He says that as a state senator he wrote the law creating Michigan's 529 college-savings program and worked with police on tools to pursue child predators.
He says that in Congress he worked to end federal taxes on education savings and to expand American energy production by easing regulation.
He says that as Intelligence Committee chair he warned about China and worked to stop theft of intellectual property affecting Michigan's auto industry.

people.name: Rashida Tlaib
lines: She says her priorities are economic and housing justice, racial and immigration justice, environmental justice, and health care for all.
She says she is demanding ICE leave communities, an end to forced family separation, and spending at home instead of blank checks for war.
She says she does not take corporate PAC money and has directed federal funding to community spaces, water projects, and housing in the district.

people.name: Ray Pooley
lines: He lists manufacturing and jobs, affordable health care, and family farms and clean land as his top priorities.
He says jobs should provide a dignified living, health care should not bankrupt families, and corporations should be held accountable.

people.name: Sean McCann
lines: He says his first priority is lowering everyday costs, from utilities and drugs to housing, while protecting jobs in southwest Michigan.
He says he would extend Affordable Care Act tax credits, lower prescription prices, and strengthen care in rural and urban communities.
He supports solar, wind, and nuclear power, including the Palisades plant, and says he would protect the Great Lakes and drinking water.

people.name: T.P. Nykoriak
lines: He says he would defend the Constitution, oversee federal agencies, and fight waste, fraud, and corruption.
He says he would support law enforcement, secure the border, and enforce immigration laws, including against trafficking and fentanyl.
He says he would cut unnecessary regulation, expand manufacturing, lower the cost of living, and reduce the national debt.

people.name: Terri DeBoer
lines: She wants more health-care choice, including direct primary care and health savings accounts, plus price transparency.
She says she would cut taxes and spending to fight inflation, ease rules on small businesses, and support educational freedom.
She backs an all-of-the-above energy policy, including nuclear power, and says she would secure the border and enforce immigration law.

people.name: Thomas Smith
lines: He says he would protect First and Second Amendment rights and resist federal overreach.
He says he would support finishing a border wall, restoring deportations, and ending catch-and-release.
He says he would cut wasteful spending and regulations and lower taxes, and that as the father of three veterans he would defend veterans' care and benefits.

people.name: Tim Walberg
lines: He says his focus is job creation, higher incomes, and a federal government that lives within its means.
He says lowering drug costs, protecting people with pre-existing conditions, and fighting addiction are health-care priorities.
He says he has voted to support veterans, religious freedom, the Second Amendment, and a right to life.

people.name: Tom Barrett
lines: He says taxpayer subsidies for large corporations are the wrong use of public money, and that infrastructure, tax and regulatory reform, and a lower cost of living matter more.
He says he opposes defunding police, wants schools focused on teaching and safety, and has signed a taxpayer-protection pledge to lower the tax burden.
He says he would finish the border wall and give border agencies the tools to stop illegal crossings, and he describes himself as pro-life.

people.name: William Lawrence
lines: He says he would lower the cost of living by taxing the wealthy to protect Social Security, building affordable housing, and guaranteeing health care.
He wants a 12-month federal pause on new data centers, restored wetlands and rivers, and polluters held accountable.
He says he would end what he calls an illegal war on Iran, stop arms sales to Israel and other human-rights violators, and ban stock trading by members of Congress.

people.name: Amy Klobuchar
lines: She says she would work to lower health care, housing, child care, and utility bills, and to build more homes.
She says she would root out fraud and make it easier to start a business and get a permit.
She says she would take on organized crime and gang violence and help local police hire and keep officers.

people.name: Betty McCollum
lines: Her office says she champions education, environmental protection, health-care access and affordability, fiscal responsibility, and international engagement that pairs diplomacy and development with a strong national defense.
She says she wants higher education kept affordable and public schools accountable to parents and local officials, and she supports universal health coverage and the Affordable Care Act.
On defense, she says funding should keep the armed forces trained and equipped, with priority for military health care and ending military sexual assault.

people.name: Brad Finstad
lines: His office says his work as Minnesota's USDA Rural Development director supported rural infrastructure, business development, homeownership, schools, public safety, health care, and high-speed internet.
He previously served three terms in the Minnesota Legislature and held executive roles with the Minnesota Turkey Growers Association and the Center for Rural Policy and Development.

people.name: Doug Chapin
lines: He says he will fight for single-payer health care so people can get care without going broke, and to reverse Medicare and Medicaid cuts.
He says he will eliminate the income cap on Social Security taxes and repeal tax cuts for billionaires in the White House budget bill.
He says he will defend Congress's power over spending, taxes, tariffs, and war, and support immigration laws with a clearer, less costly path to citizenship.

people.name: Eric Pratt
lines: He says he will focus on lowering costs, supporting small businesses, and restoring an economy that working families can afford.
He says he supports law enforcement and first responders, and that laws should be enforced consistently from neighborhoods to the U.S. border.
He says he will crack down on fraud and abuse, pointing to his banking work against financial scams and his Senate work on taxpayer accountability.

people.name: Erik Osberg
