lines: He says he will defend constitutional rights and fair elections, and he supports a constitutional amendment to end Citizens United and a ban on members of Congress trading individual stocks.
He says health care should be more affordable and accessible for rural families, seniors, and towns that depend on local clinics and hospitals.
He says he will back federal funding for public schools and support for farms, small businesses, housing, child care, and public safety.

people.name: George Tangen
lines: He says the chief elections officer should be unbound from the two major parties so voters in either party can count on impartiality.
He says he would push to remove barriers that keep independent and minor-party candidates off the ballot.
He says same-day registration should stay, and that ballots from voters whose eligibility is not clear on Election Day should be counted only after eligibility is confirmed.

people.name: Ilhan Omar
lines: She says she has fought to codify Roe v. Wade, pass climate legislation, address opioids, and ban assault weapons.
She says she negotiated a public-safety bill with local investment and accountability, and funding that fed more than 30 million children during the pandemic.
She says community projects she brought home include veteran housing in Robbinsdale and help for entrepreneurs in north Minneapolis.

people.name: Jake Johnson
lines: He says he will vote to end tariffs and the Iran war that he says are raising grocery, gas, and fertilizer prices, cut taxes for working families, and raise taxes on big corporations and the very wealthy.
He says he supports a balanced-budget amendment, term limits, a ban on members of Congress trading stocks or becoming lobbyists, and recovering money lost to fraud in Minnesota.

He says he will push a bipartisan farm bill, a right to repair for farm equipment, protection of Social Security, Medicare, and veterans' benefits, and a moratorium on data centers until protections are guaranteed.

people.name: John Nagel
lines: He says he will cut taxes, fight inflation, and eliminate fraud and waste that he says are driving up prices.
He says he will work with the attorney general so violent criminals are kept off the streets, schools are protected, and law enforcement is funded and supported.
He says he will keep the border secured, support legal immigration and faster processing for people who follow the rules, and treat border security as national security.

people.name: Keith Ellison
lines: He says the office has lowered costs, including cutting the price of insulin, and has taken on price-gouging, medical debt, and opioid companies.
He says he is protecting tenants, going after scammers, and standing up for student borrowers.
He says he is challenging the Trump administration because no one is above the law, and that he is defending reproductive rights and access to gender-affirming care.

people.name: Kelly Morrison
lines: She says she is fighting health-care cuts she says would push Minnesotans off insurance and force hospitals to close, and that no one should go bankrupt to get care.
She says she is working to exempt small businesses from tariffs and get them refunds, and to lower the costs of housing and child care.

She says she takes no corporate PAC, federal-lobbyist, or dark-money money, supports a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United, and backs a ban on stock ownership by presidents, vice presidents, and members of Congress.

people.name: Lisa Demuth
lines: She says her first priority as governor would be helping families afford their lives, including lower income-tax brackets, lower car-tab fees, and an end to the state tax on Social Security benefits.
She says she would create a nonpartisan inspector general to look for fraud in state programs before money leaves the door.
She says she would back police, firefighters, and other first responders.

people.name: Matt Little
lines: He says he is fighting for Medicare for All, affordable child care, tax breaks for everyday Americans, and a tax on the ultrawealthy.
He says he wants a moratorium on data centers, an end to Citizens United, and corporate PAC money out of politics.
He says he will champion women's reproductive freedom and keep Minnesota a refuge for LGBTQ people.

people.name: Michele Tafoya
lines: She says she would cosponsor a bill to deport an immigrant convicted of fraud and would seek mandatory federal prison terms for fraud.
She says she would push to withhold federal money from a state that will not put anti-fraud controls in place.
She says Minnesota's criminal-justice experiment has failed and that she would stand with victims and law enforcement.

people.name: Michelle Fischbach
lines: She says she stands up for agriculture, Second Amendment rights, respect for law and order, and defending the unborn.

people.name: Paul Wikstrom
lines: He calls for mandatory audits of major federal spending and for fraud-prevention controls as a condition of funding.

He says he would protect and expand tax cuts, including no tax on tips or overtime, a larger child tax credit, and an end to the estate tax, and increase energy, food, and housing supply by cutting regulation.
He says he would secure the border to stop fentanyl, back local police with federal grants, and fund investigators aimed at large-scale taxpayer fraud.

people.name: Peggy Flanagan
lines: She says she wants a fair economy so people can afford the lives they want for their families.
She says she will not take corporate PAC money and wants to reverse Citizens United and limit dark money in elections.
She says Washington works for special interests and that she would make the government answer to Minnesotans instead.

people.name: Pete Stauber
lines: He says he is focused on the economy of northern Minnesota, American energy independence, and ending reliance on foreign minerals as chair of the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee.
He says being shot while off duty as a police officer convinced him that more must be done to support law enforcement and safer communities.

people.name: Rebecca Whiting
lines: She says the country should stop funding wars that Congress has not declared.
She says overspending and printing money are driving up the cost of groceries and gas.
She says the two major parties, the military industry, banks, and corporations are not being held accountable.

people.name: Ronald Schutz
lines: He says fighting fraud and protecting tax dollars would be a top priority, and that he would try to stop fraud before it starts.
He says seniors, families, and small businesses need a consumer-protection lawyer who will take on scammers and powerful companies.
He says he would enforce the law and put public safety ahead of political headlines.

people.name: Seth Kuhl-Stennes
lines: He says he would keep paper ballots, early and absentee voting, and same-day registration, and he wants Election Day to be a paid state holiday.
He says he would expand voting rights to Minnesota residents regardless of U.S. citizenship or a criminal conviction.
He says he would end the legal split between major and minor parties and support ranked-choice voting for state executive offices.

people.name: Steve Simon
lines: He says his top priority is protecting the freedom to vote for every eligible Minnesotan.
He says he has worked for an election system that is fair, accurate, honest, and secure, including for seniors and students.
He says he has opposed federal efforts to add voting restrictions and to collect sensitive information on Minnesota voters.

people.name: Tad Jude
lines: He says he would require a photo ID to vote and work to limit voting to U.S. citizens.
He says he would work with local, state, and federal partners to clean up voter rolls.
He says he would try to prevent fraud in public programs and make business filings and other office services more reliable.

people.name: Tom Emmer
lines: He says he is fighting high grocery, gas, and electricity costs and backed a tax law that keeps cuts in place and ends taxes on tips, overtime, and adds relief for seniors.
He says he led the border bill H.R. 2 and supported the Laken Riley Act so people in the country illegally who commit crimes are deported.
He says he supports the SAVE Act's proof-of-citizenship requirement, school choice, and ending the U.S. Department of Education.

people.name: Trina Swanson
lines: She says work should buy a life with dignity and that people should not go bankrupt if they get sick, and she is fighting for affordable health care in rural communities where hospitals can be hours away.
She says mining built the region and union jobs built the middle class, and that economic development and environmental stewardship can coexist.
She says every young person deserves an affordable path through college, trade school, or an apprenticeship so talent stays in northern and central Minnesota.

people.name: Tyler Bass
lines: He says he will secure the border, support ICE, and remove people who are here illegally no matter how long they have been here, and cut H-1B loopholes so jobs go to Minnesotans.
He says he will fight Washington's hand in local property taxes and will not vote to ban AR-15s, restrict magazine capacity, or add new hurdles for law-abiding gun owners.
He says fraud that robbed children with autism and Minnesota taxpayers has to be confronted, and that his opponent has not spoken up about it.

people.name: Bennie Thompson
lines: The campaign says that funding covered health care, infrastructure, agriculture, and education.
It also says the money covered broadband, public safety, clean water, and disaster recovery.
He presents that record as results on the issues that matter most in the district.

people.name: Cindy Hyde-Smith
lines: Her campaign issues page highlights Second Amendment rights and balancing the budget.
It also highlights health care and defending unborn life.
It lists stopping illegal immigration and supporting the military and veterans.

people.name: Cliff Johnson
lines: He says he wants to combat inflation and the policies driving up costs for Mississippians.
He says he will protect and expand affordable health care.
He says north Mississippi should get its fair share of federal dollars for economic development, infrastructure, and struggling schools, and he wants the right to have a vote counted preserved.

people.name: Jeffrey Hulum III
lines: He says South Mississippi needs an economy in which families can earn a living wage, support their children, and build a secure life at home.
He says every child deserves a quality education no matter their ZIP code, and that taxpayer money spent on children is an investment in the future.
He says no family should go broke to see a doctor or buy medicine, and he points to closing rural hospitals and reduced health-care funding in Mississippi.

people.name: Michael Chiaradio
lines: He says simply raising taxes or cutting spending is not enough, and he wants federal investment in factories, farms, infrastructure, and a broader safety net so more people can take part in the economy.
On health care he wants lower out-of-pocket costs and premiums, more trained medical workers, and modern facilities so people can age with access to care.
He wants to expand USDA homebuilding, help small farms with loans, equipment, and new markets, and put federal money into a more resilient electric grid.

people.name: Michael Guest
lines: He says he believes in limited government, lower taxes, fewer regulations, the right to life of the unborn, a strong national defense, and Second Amendment rights.
He says he works to secure the border and has opposed efforts to defund the police.

people.name: Mike Ezell
lines: His office lists agriculture, conservative values, crime and public safety, immigration and border security, jobs and the economy, national security, transportation and infrastructure, and veterans among the issues he works on.

people.name: Ron Eller
lines: He says he stands for free enterprise, limited government, individual liberties, national defense, and traditional values, and he lists himself as pro-life and pro-Second Amendment.
He says Mississippi needs more business opportunity and less government interference and red tape.
He supports congressional term limits and says the general-election campaign is about economic growth, secure borders, voter integrity, and constitutional rights.

people.name: Scott Colom
lines: He says he would vote to take back Congress's power over tariffs and to require a vote of Congress before the country goes to war.
He says a full day's work should pay enough to build a life in the community where the job is.
He says he would seek a seat on the Agriculture Committee so farmers have a senator answering to them.

people.name: Trent Kelly
lines: On his issues page he says the primary role of the federal government is to keep the country safe at home and abroad, and he points to his National Guard service.
He says the Second Amendment means the right to keep and bear arms shall not be infringed, and that law-abiding gun owners should be protected.
He supports an all-of-the-above energy strategy and says Washington should not pick winners and losers. He also says he will keep pushing agriculture policies that encourage rural development.

people.name: Ty Pinkins
lines: He says health care is a right and that he supports the Medicare for All Act.
He says he is not tied to either party or to lobbyists who profit from the current insurance system.
He says his own father's untreated diabetes, and the loss of work and a vehicle that followed, is why the issue is personal.

people.name: Ann Wagner
lines: She says she has worked to cut taxes and regulation so local businesses can hire, and she voted for a tax bill that removes taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security.
She highlights the Fight Online Sex Trafficking Act and funding for rape-kit testing through the Debbie Smith Act.
She says she will keep defending a right to life, and she introduced a bill to require medical care for infants born alive after an abortion.

people.name: Ann Wagner
lines: She says she has worked to cut taxes and regulation so local businesses can hire, and she voted for a tax bill that removes taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security.
She highlights the Fight Online Sex Trafficking Act and funding for rape-kit testing through the Debbie Smith Act.
She says she will keep defending a right to life, and she introduced a bill to require medical care for infants born alive after an abortion.

people.name: Bethany Mann
lines: She supports full, equal funding for public schools from pre-K through college and union apprenticeships.
She wants affordable physical and mental health care, and federal infrastructure money for rural roads, bridges, broadband, and water.
She ties her environmental work to clean air and water, and she supports the Women's Health Protection Act, the Equal Rights Amendment, and Medicare for All.

people.name: Bethany Mann
lines: She supports full, equal funding for public schools from pre-K through college and union apprenticeships.
She wants affordable physical and mental health care, and federal infrastructure money for rural roads, bridges, broadband, and water.
She ties her environmental work to clean air and water, and she supports the Women's Health Protection Act, the Equal Rights Amendment, and Medicare for All.

people.name: Bob Onder
lines: He highlights a bill aimed at visa overstays and earlier Missouri legislation against sanctuary cities and employment of people without legal status.
He says he co-chairs the Pro-Life Caucus and has backed federal abortion limits, after authoring Missouri clinic rules and helping write the 2019 heartbeat bill.
He points to work on constitutional carry and the Second Amendment Preservation Act, and to the tax bill he says he passed with House Republicans.

people.name: Bob Onder
lines: He highlights a bill aimed at visa overstays and earlier Missouri legislation against sanctuary cities and employment of people without legal status.
He says he co-chairs the Pro-Life Caucus and has backed federal abortion limits, after authoring Missouri clinic rules and helping write the 2019 heartbeat bill.
He points to work on constitutional carry and the Second Amendment Preservation Act, and to the tax bill he says he passed with House Republicans.

people.name: Chris Reichard
lines: He supports the PRO Act to protect organizing and the Major Richard Star Act so combat-injured veterans receive full benefits.
He wants the United States kept out of another long war and supports a bill to count the full human and financial cost of war up front.

She also lists equal rights and expanded liberty under the Constitution.

people.name: Jeff Van Drew
lines: He says he is working to lower health-care costs and everyday expenses, including energy bills and delivery fees.
He says he will protect veterans' benefits, back law enforcement, and keep investing in South Jersey beaches, aviation, and infrastructure.

He says he supports border enforcement and proof of citizenship plus photo identification for federal voting, and that he will not back cuts to Social Security, Medicare, or Medicaid for people who qualify.

people.name: Joe Hathaway
lines: He says he would cut taxes for first-time homebuyers, including a tax freeze and a refundable credit for closing costs.
He says he would cap federal student-loan interest rather than cancel debt outright, and invest in vocational and technical training.
He says he would expand the child tax credit and childcare tax relief, require upfront health-care prices, and finish the Gateway Tunnel.

people.name: Josh Gottheimer
lines: He says voters sent him to Congress to fight for lower taxes and what he calls Jersey values.
He says he works across party lines to find common ground rather than follow a national political agenda.

people.name: Justin Murphy
lines: He says he wants the Pinelands kept intact and the Jersey Shore kept free of pollution and offshore wind turbines.
He lists parental rights, medical freedom, and Medicare for seniors among his national priorities.
He says he would argue conservative positions and calls the race a break from a long stretch without a Republican senator from New Jersey.

people.name: LaMonica McIver
lines: She says she will not back down from attacks on women's rights or from a Justice Department prosecution she ties to her opposition to immigration enforcement.
She says these are hard times and that she will keep protecting her community.

people.name: Michael McGuire
lines: He says his first priority is affordability: cutting wasteful spending and lowering taxes so working families can keep more of what they earn.
He says he wants people to feel safe at home and wants government held accountable.
He says he fully supports a ban on stock trading by members of Congress and term limits.

people.name: Nellie Pou
lines: She says she is fighting to lower housing, grocery, and child-care costs and to extend Affordable Care Act tax credits.
She says she wants to expand health coverage, lower drug prices, and protect Medicaid for mothers and working families.
She says she supports police and first responders, and she wants to protect VA benefits for veterans.

people.name: Rachel Peace
lines: She says people belong in power so families can go from surviving to thriving.
She says she does not accept money from corporate PACs, foreign lobbies, or billionaires.

people.name: Rebecca Bennett
lines: She says she would bring down costs for New Jersey families and use private-sector experience to support good-paying jobs.
She says she would expand access to health care and stand up to anyone trying to strip coverage away.
She says national security should be a priority and that the campaign is powered by people rather than billionaires, lobbyists, or corporate interests.

people.name: Rob Menendez
lines: He says he is running again to defend freedoms and not back down, including over immigration enforcement.
He says the district shares values of respect, hard work, and a chance for everyone to succeed.
He says he serves as a regional whip and as northeast vice chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

people.name: Rosie Pino
lines: She says she would lower the cost of living, create good-paying jobs, and keep neighborhoods safe.
She says she will oppose large spending bills that fuel inflation and support tax cuts for working families.
She says affordable American energy brings down the cost of groceries, transportation, housing, and utilities.

people.name: Sean Kirrane
lines: He says he would restore the full state-and-local tax deduction, end taxes on retirement income, and cap administrative waste in federal programs.
He says he would reduce taxes for working families and secure the border.
He says he wants to preserve what he calls immigrant-American values and protect elderly and disabled people.

people.name: Thomas Kean Jr.
lines: He says he is working to lower the cost of living and protect health care.
He says he wants stronger communities, reliable infrastructure, more innovation at home, and help for students.
He says he brings both parties together on common-sense solutions and wants America strong at home and abroad.

people.name: Veronica Fernandez
lines: She says Congress has to be cleaned up so big money and special interests stop controlling it, and that the people who created the problem will not be the ones to fix it.
She says she has lived with the same costs for health care and groceries, help for a child with special needs, and trying to save for retirement.
She says she is not a lawyer and is not connected to people in power, and that new leadership has to come from outside the circle that created the problem.

people.name: Zack Mullock
lines: He says he would create good-paying jobs and support small businesses.
He says he is fighting for affordable health care and lower prescription costs.
He says he wants to address housing costs so working families can stay in their communities.

people.name: Amanda López Askin
lines: She says she is running to protect the right to vote and to keep elections safe, secure, and fair.
She says the office should make campaign finance more transparent.
She says she would give small businesses clearer, more stable dealings with the state.

people.name: Ben Ray Lujan
lines: He says he has worked to lower prescription prices and to protect Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security.
He says he has defended nutrition assistance for working families, seniors, veterans, and rural communities.
He says he has worked to connect families to the internet and to deliver results in all 33 counties.

people.name: Deb Haaland
lines: She says that as governor she would concentrate on crime, schools, and prices from health care to groceries.
She says she would protect communities from Donald Trump and immigration enforcement so the state can focus on those problems.

people.name: Gabriel Vasquez
lines: He says he would raise wages, support the right to join a union, and cut taxes on working families while lowering the cost of health care, child care, and utilities.
He says he would keep public lands open for hunting, fishing, and hiking, and keep working on wildfire risk.
He says he would fund border security, deport people convicted of violent crimes, and provide a path to legal status for Dreamers and other working families.

people.name: Greggory Hull
lines: His Four Steps to Zero plan would phase out state tax on eligible personal income, starting with the first $25,000 for single filers and $50,000 for married couples filing jointly, while still taxing net business profits.
He says he would strengthen rural health care, recruit doctors and nurses, and change medical-malpractice law.
He says he would add police, treat fentanyl as a border problem, and use a zero-tolerance approach to violent crime and crimes against children.

people.name: Gregory Cunningham
lines: He says he would listen to people who live and work in New Mexico rather than take direction from Washington.
He says he would be a steady voice that puts people ahead of party politics.
He says his campaign is about restoring trust and strengthening communities for the next generation.

people.name: Larry Marker
lines: He says he would defend oil and gas, including hydrogen and nuclear development, and oppose federal permitting delays that he says threaten school funding.
He says the border is still a path for fentanyl and that he would back Border Patrol and local police.
He says farmers and ranchers should not lose grazing, water, or working land to agency enforcement.

people.name: Martin Zamora
lines: He says he would defend private property and water rights and cut federal rules he says burden farmers and ranchers.
He says he would lower taxes, cut red tape, and support small businesses as the source of jobs.
He says he would stand with law enforcement against fentanyl and other drug trafficking, and would secure the southern border.

people.name: Melanie Stansbury
lines: She says she would expand the economy, support local businesses, and raise the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour.
She says health care is a human right and that she supports Medicare for All, lower out-of-pocket costs, and protection for pre-existing conditions.
She says she would keep working on climate, renewable energy, water security, and public lands.

people.name: Ndidiamaka Okpareke
lines: She says she would use her work as a pharmacist to make care more affordable, protect quality, and expand access.
She says she would bring federal investment to New Mexico to create jobs and grow paychecks.
She says she answers to New Mexico families rather than party leaders in Washington.

people.name: Ramona Goolsby
lines: She says every eligible voter should be able to register and vote under clear rules.
She says public money should be managed in the open, and that trust depends on professional oversight.
She says her campaign is built on access, responsibility, and trust in elections.

people.name: Raul Torrez
lines: He says protecting children is his priority, including lawsuits against Meta and Snap over online abuse and investigations of the child-welfare system.
He says the office has pursued online predators and school harms such as cyberbullying.
He says he is also working on consumer rules for online markets, oversight of higher education, and protection of natural resources.

people.name: Samuel Kane Sr.
lines: He says he would challenge license-plate reader surveillance that tracks people without a warrant.
He says methamphetamine and fentanyl are driving a crime crisis and that he would back officers on those cases.
He says he would scrutinize data-center projects and utility rate increases, and that environmental laws should be enforced so the land stays intact.

people.name: Teresa Leger Fernandez
lines: She says every person should have affordable health care in their own community.
She says the country should invest in broadband, transportation, housing, and clean energy.
She says she would protect land, air, and water, and keep working on education and the right to vote.

people.name: Aaron Gies
lines: He says medical debt is a leading cause of bankruptcy and he supports universal health care while opposing cuts to Medicare, Medicaid, VA benefits, and rural hospitals.
He says housing in western New York and the Southern Tier is scarce and increasingly unaffordable, and he treats housing as a basic need.
He supports higher wages and stronger bargaining power for workers, and he says he would remove the cap on earnings subject to Social Security tax so benefits last.

people.name: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
lines: She calls for Medicare for All so health care is not tied to a job and so the government can bargain down drug and medical prices.
She says housing should be treated as a right, with more affordable and public housing and protections for current tenants.
She supports a Green New Deal built around clean-energy jobs, and she says undocumented immigrants should have a path to full membership in the country and that ICE should be abolished.

people.name: Alissa Ellman
lines: She says she would protect and expand Medicaid, arguing a Republican budget bill would cut coverage in the district and close rural hospitals.
She says she would expand child care, home-repair help, and the low-income housing tax credit, and seek funding for rural buses and water systems.
She says she would pass the PRO Act, defend abortion access and LGBTQ rights, and not be funded by large corporations.

people.name: Andrew Garbarino
lines: He says he led the push for permanent funding of the World Trade Center Health Program.
He says a tax law he supported raised the state-and-local tax deduction cap from $10,000 to $40,000 and ended federal tax on tips.
He also points to an expanded child tax credit, a new deduction for seniors, and a policing bill he says passed the House.

people.name: Anthony Constantino
lines: He says he would cut waste, bring reliable internet and cell service to the North Country, and oppose regulations he argues are driving up food and utility prices.
He says he would work to secure the northern border, treat farmers more fairly, and restore First and Second Amendment rights he says have been restricted in New York.

people.name: Blake Gendebien
lines: He says he would repeal costly regulations, support fair trade, and bring manufacturing back so prices fall for families and for seniors on fixed incomes.
He says this border district needs more Border Patrol staffing, a harder path for illegal entry and an easier legal one, and fixes to the guest-worker programs farms rely on.
He says farms and Main Street businesses also need fewer burdensome rules and investment in rural roads and bridges.

people.name: Brad Lander
lines: He says he would be a check on Donald Trump and fight attacks on immigrants, trans kids, the rule of law, health care, Social Security, and working- and middle-class families.
He says Congress should help cities end street homelessness, fix public housing, protect tenants, and build more affordable homes.
He says he would take on billionaires and corporate power and get money out of politics rather than take Wall Street, crypto, and AIPAC contributions.

people.name: Bruce Blakeman
lines: He says public safety is the center of the campaign, including opposition to sanctuary policies and work with federal immigration officers to remove people he calls criminals.
He says he blocked scheduled property-tax increases in Nassau County and would seek relief for homeowners and renters as governor.
His site names Madison County Sheriff Todd Hood as his lieutenant governor running mate and describes Hood as a career law-enforcement officer.

people.name: Cait Conley
lines: She says she would lower drug and premium costs by holding pharmaceutical and insurance companies accountable and creating a public insurance option.
She says she would ban members of Congress and the White House from trading stocks, and stop utility monopolies from passing private-jet, lobbying, and campaign costs on to ratepayers.

people.name: Caroline Shinkle
lines: She says she would protect paychecks and push schools to treat every student like an honors student while using innovation to improve results.
She says she would back law enforcement and first responders, fight antisemitism, and stand with Israel and the city's Jewish community.
She says she would restore competition and price transparency in health care and pass the Access to Breast Cancer Diagnosis Act.

people.name: Christopher Gallant
lines: He says he would seek federal investments that reduce the cost of housing, energy, and basic goods for Long Island families.
He says he would protect Medicare and Medicaid and push changes that expand access and lower out-of-pocket costs for older adults.
He also says he would press for long-term investment in the shoreline and for the tools first responders need to keep neighborhoods safe.

people.name: Claire Valdez
lines: She says she would strengthen the PRO Act, give active federal support to union organizing, and end at-will employment.
She says everyone should be able to count on a living-wage job, paid parental and sick leave, health care, and a dignified retirement.
She says the campaign will not take corporate PAC or dark money.

people.name: Claudia Tenney
lines: She says she has led efforts against Chinese theft of American intellectual property and against China's grip on the financial system.
She says the border has to be secured now, that Social Security and Medicare are personal because her parents relied on them, and that the Second Amendment is a way of life in Upstate New York.
She also says the health-care system is not working and that Congress has to deliver solutions, and she highlights veterans' issues as what she calls a Marine mom.

people.name: Darializa Avila Chevalier
lines: She says she would abolish ICE, expand paths to citizenship, and secure free legal help for immigrants.
She says she would fund child tax credits and baby bonds instead of spending billions on wars, and treat housing and Medicare for All as rights.
She says she will not take corporate PAC money and would fight monopolies, price gouging, and super PACs.

people.name: Dennis Hannon
lines: He says he would disrupt fentanyl trafficking, focus immigration enforcement on serious public-safety threats, and support cooperation between local and federal agencies.
He says he would seek tax relief for working families, lower drug costs by reforming pharmacy benefit managers, and stop governments from banning particular energy sources.

He says he would limit online targeting of children, bar commercial artificial intelligence from generating content involving minors, and criminally target people who he says profit from medical procedures on children.

people.name: Diamant Hysenaj
lines: He says he would focus on affordable rent and quality homes, lower health-care costs by cutting waste and fraud, and lower taxes.
He says immigration policy should secure the border, speed citizenship for people who follow the law, and support neighborhoods where he says nearly half of residents are immigrants.
He says he would cut red tape and taxes for small businesses so they can grow and hire.

people.name: George Latimer
lines: He says that as county executive he funded job training and grants for minority- and women-owned businesses, and free summer and holiday bus rides, without raising county taxes for five years.
He says affordable housing is a human right and that he pushed to create more than 2,500 affordable units since 2018, with thousands more in the pipeline.
His priorities page also lists defending democracy, reproductive freedom, infrastructure, public safety, and protecting Medicare and Social Security.

people.name: George Marsh
lines: He says he would reintroduce the infrastructure law to modernize roads, bridges, and water systems, and invest in transit and safer streets.
He says he would cut red tape and expand access to capital so neighborhood businesses can start, hire, and stay open.
He also says he would protect veterans' earned benefits and expand apprenticeships in skilled trades such as plumbing, electrical work, and construction.

people.name: Grace Meng
lines: She says she defends access to abortion, contraception, and IVF, and that she has led legislation on menstrual products.
She says she uses her seat on the Appropriations Committee to steer federal money toward women, families, and communities.
Her issues page also groups her work under health care, gun laws, housing, education, and immigration.

people.name: Gregory Meeks
lines: He points to his vote for the bipartisan infrastructure law and says it included nearly $28 billion for New York roads, bridges, transit, ports, and airports.
He says diversity of race, religion, gender, and national origin helps both the private and public sectors, and he opposes efforts to demonize equity and inclusion in schools and workplaces.

people.name: Hakeem Jeffries
lines: He says he is working to lower child care, health care, education, and prescription costs, including a $35 monthly insulin cap for people on Medicare.
He supports universal background checks and a ban on assault weapons, and he highlights a law that made gun trafficking a federal crime.
He says he wants more affordable and public housing, better-paying jobs through infrastructure and manufacturing investment, and protection of abortion access.

people.name: Jackie Auringer
lines: She says she would work on taxes, energy, everyday bills, and health care so more income stays with families and small businesses.
She says she would focus on good-paying jobs, skilled trades, and education connected to careers in the region.
She also calls for congressional ethics, government transparency, and protection of local rights and public safety.

people.name: Jeanine Driscoll
lines: She says she would restore the full state-and-local tax deduction and seek more relief for families and seniors.
She says she would support law enforcement and keep the southern border from being opened again.

people.name: Jennifer Moore
lines: She says she will support the NYPD and first responders and reject policies she says have made streets less safe.
She says New Yorkers are being priced out of their neighborhoods and wants practical answers to the cost of living.
She says she will stand for working families, parents, and small-business owners.

people.name: Joel Azumah
lines: He says the country should bring manufacturing home and stay out of a major war so it can reinvest in infrastructure, pointing to tensions over Taiwan and Greenland.
He warns that artificial intelligence could outrun human guardrails and asks how government stays accountable if machines run more of the market and the state.

people.name: John Mannion
lines: He says he joined a caucus on utility bills, voted to extend Affordable Care Act tax credits, and cosponsors a bill to make the child tax credit permanent.
He says he would restore cuts to Medicare and Medicaid, bring back a public health-care option, and negotiate lower drug prices, including a broader cap on insulin.
He says he cosponsors a bill to restore Roe v. Wade and would expand access to reproductive care and mental-health treatment.

people.name: Jomo Williams
lines: He says his case is for what he calls universal capitalism rather than socialism, and against a sanctuary city.
He highlights the SAVE Act and election-integrity litigation, and says extreme politics are dividing neighbors in Harlem.

people.name: Joseph Chou
lines: He says he wants a balanced tax policy that eases the burden on working families and new small businesses, plus fairer interest rates on student loans.
He says he would back public, private, and vocational education and improve access to health care and affordable child care.
He says he wants a fair immigration system with secure borders and closer cooperation against criminal threats, and he wants to reform cashless bail.

people.name: Joseph Cinquemani
lines: He says he wants tax relief, lower energy costs, high-paying union jobs, a smaller budget, and lower interest rates so housing is more affordable in Westchester and the Bronx.
He says that work will take a generation of cutting federal spending, lowering taxes, producing affordable American energy, and shrinking the administrative state.

people.name: Joseph Morelle
lines: He says he is fighting to expand child care and affordable housing, strengthen job training, and support local businesses.
He says he has worked to end surprise medical bills, lower prescription prices, and protect people with preexisting conditions, and he opposes efforts to dismantle the Affordable Care Act.
He also highlights climate action, gun laws, abortion rights, and equal rights for people who live in the country.

people.name: Josh Riley
lines: He says utility bills are out of control and that he is taking utility monopolies to court, backing home energy upgrades, and trying to ban foreign ownership of American utilities.
He says data centers should pay for the grid upgrades they require instead of passing those costs to Upstate families.
He says he backs the Equality Act and mental-health services for LGBTQ young people.

people.name: Kailee Buller
lines: She says she would grow good-paying jobs and lower everyday costs so families do not have to leave New York to get ahead.
She says her work in government has focused on cutting red tape, strengthening American agriculture, and protecting jobs in the food and energy supply chain.

people.name: Kathy Hochul
lines: She points to inflation refund checks, a larger child tax credit, middle-class tax cuts, and work toward universal child care and lower auto insurance costs.
She highlights free school meals, a ban on cell phones during the school day, and gun laws she says are meant to make streets and subways safer.
She says the ticket would keep lowering costs, invest in community safety, and protect New York from what she calls MAGA extremism.

people.name: Laura Gillen
lines: She says she is committed to keeping families safe, growing the economy, and making Nassau County a place where people can afford a home or a business.
She says her first term has focused on working across the aisle to lower the cost of living and bring federal investment back to the county.

people.name: Letitia James
lines: The site lists public safety, jobs and affordability, consumer protection, and health care as her priorities.
She says the office should keep challenging powerful interests that she argues are trying to control government.
She ties that work to protecting funding for health care, public education, and jobs.

people.name: Melvin Rivera
lines: He says public assistance should build independence, with apprenticeships aimed at higher-paying work and room for families to keep benefits while they advance.
He says tenants should get the first chance to buy when a landlord decides to sell, so more renters can become homeowners.
He also names free enterprise, breaking monopolies, and holding government accountable among his top priorities.

people.name: Micah Lasher
lines: He says Democrats should use every available lever against what he calls Trumpism and also spell out a positive agenda on affordability, health care, corruption, and climate.
His platform also covers protecting immigrants and civil rights, reproductive freedom, public schools, and safeguards on big technology companies and artificial intelligence.

people.name: Michael LiPetri Jr.
lines: He says that in the Assembly he opposed policies he argues raised the cost of living and threatened Long Island's quality of life.
He says he wants to help House Republicans secure the border, keep a higher state-and-local tax deduction, and cut what he calls waste, fraud, and abuse.

people.name: Mike DeCillis
lines: He says Congress should act as a co-equal branch and put guardrails around civil and constitutional rights instead of leaving government to executive action alone.
He says he would lower the tax burden on the working class, have billionaires pay a larger share, and stop what he calls the dismantling of the Education Department.
He says he would also protect Social Security and Medicare and make groceries, gas, health care, and housing more affordable.

people.name: Mike Lawler
lines: He says he crossed his party to raise the state-and-local tax deduction cap to $40,000 and backed tax cuts on tips, overtime, and Social Security benefits.
He says he forced a House vote to extend Affordable Care Act subsidies and supports a tax credit for IVF.
He says he would reopen the Indian Point nuclear plant, back an all-of-the-above energy mix, and pair border enforcement with a bipartisan legal-immigration bill.

people.name: Nicholas LaLota
lines: He says he is focused on border security, support for law enforcement, and a stronger military.
He says he has pushed for a larger state-and-local tax deduction and for tax relief on tips, overtime, and for seniors.
He also highlights Long Island water quality and bringing federal money back for local infrastructure and public safety.

people.name: Nick Langworthy
lines: He says he would curb spending that is raising the price of groceries, gas, cars, and housing, and use tax and deregulatory policy to raise take-home pay.
He says he would speed energy permits, move supply chains away from China, and fully fund border enforcement while ending catch-and-release.
He says he would support hiring more police officers and oppose efforts to defund them.

people.name: Nicole Malliotakis
lines: She says a 2025 tax law she worked on raised the state-and-local tax deduction so most households in the district can deduct local taxes, and ended federal tax on most tips and overtime.
She says the same law expanded the child tax credit and effectively ended federal income tax on Social Security for most seniors.
She says she was the lead plaintiff in a case that stopped noncitizens from voting in New York City elections and that she pushed to fund Staten Island's East Shore sea wall.

people.name: Pat Ryan
lines: He says he is trying to lower utility and health-care bills by challenging companies such as Central Hudson and UnitedHealth.
He says his housing agenda would build more homes, cut red tape, and lower costs for owners and renters in the Hudson Valley.
He says middle-class families should get tax relief instead of permanent tax cuts for billionaires and corporations, and he supports paid family leave.

people.name: Patrick Halpin
lines: He says he would expand housing for working families, take on corporate price gouging, and put those families ahead of billionaires and special interests.
He supports building toward universal Medicare coverage while protecting plans people already have, lowering drug prices, and reversing health-care cuts he says threaten Long Island hospitals.
He says he is refusing corporate PAC money, supports a ban on congressional stock trading, and wants immigration enforcement that is both secure and orderly.

people.name: Paul Tonko
lines: He says he is protecting abortion access after Roe v. Wade was overturned, and he cites a Planned Parenthood endorsement for that work.
He says fighting climate change is also a way to bring stable, well-paying jobs to the Capital Region.
He says people struggling with mental illness and opioid addiction face both the illness and public stigma, and that those communities have to be included as the country rebuilds.

people.name: Peter Oberacker
lines: He says that in every office he has focused on results and low taxes, and that he has never written a budget that raised taxes.
He says he believes in common sense, accountability, and putting people over politics.

people.name: Ralph Ambrosio
lines: He says he would cut taxes and regulation to lower the cost of living and pursue an all-of-the-above energy strategy.
He says government should support law enforcement, secure the border, and defend the right to self-defense.
He also supports term limits, voter identification, parental rights in education, and rooting out corruption.

people.name: Ritchie Torres
lines: He says he will fight for health care, housing, schools, and jobs, and stand up for immigrants, seniors, and young people.
He says he will work to protect neighborhoods from gun violence and make the Bronx safer, more decent, and more affordable.

people.name: Saritha Komatireddy
lines: She says the attorney general should enforce the law by prosecuting crime, and that safety is the office's first job.
She says she would get people who are homeless or sick off the street in a humane way.
She says she would go after corruption and fraud, and that she would work with police and district attorneys on repeat offenders, hate crimes, and fentanyl cases.

people.name: Thomas Suozzi
lines: His affordability plan says he would roll back tariffs he argues are raising prices on groceries, cars, and building materials, and seek trade deals that bring manufacturing jobs back.
He says he would rein in federal spending to ease pressure on interest rates and speed permits for energy projects, including clean energy, gas, and nuclear.
He says he would extend health-insurance tax credits, make long-term care more affordable, and offer a payment to new parents.

people.name: Timothy Kennedy
lines: He says he is fighting cuts to veterans' services and to health care for families, seniors, and people with disabilities, and working to lower the cost of living in Western New York.
He says that as a state senator he pushed a multiyear transportation building plan, protections for organized labor, record school funding, abortion rights, LGBTQ students, and stronger gun laws.

people.name: Virginia McIntyre
lines: She says she would support community policing and prevention programs, and expand vocational and technical education tied to good careers.
She says she would grow good-paying jobs, ease the burden on working families, fix roads and bridges, and expand broadband.
She says health-care billing should be transparent so families are not surprised by the cost of care.

people.name: Yvette Clarke
lines: She says she has worked to keep Brooklyn affordable for low-income residents, including a 2019 bill to cut rent in subsidized areas and a change to the income formula used for affordable housing.
She says she is a cosponsor of a public-housing bill that would fund outstanding capital repairs so residents have a decent home.
Her issues page also groups her work under immigration, health care, women and children, LGBTQ rights, and climate.

people.name: Addison McDowell
lines: He says securing the border and stopping illegal drugs is personal because his younger brother died of a fentanyl overdose.
He supports an America First trade agenda to protect U.S. jobs, says he will vote against federalizing elections, and wants federal grants tied to voter ID plus tighter absentee-ballot rules.

He says every life, born or unborn, is a gift, that he will vote entirely for what he calls pro-life bills, and that he opposes taxpayer funding of abortion. He also says he will oppose gun rules that punish law-abiding owners.

people.name: Alma Adams
lines: She says abortion is a private medical decision and that she is still fighting for equal pay and paid family leave.
She says she champions public schools, teachers, and historically Black colleges, and she sponsored permanent federal funding for minority-serving institutions.
She says Congress should restore the Voting Rights Act and stop what she calls an assault on the working class and the poor.

people.name: Ashley Bell
lines: Her campaign lists universal health care, rules for artificial intelligence and data centers, anti-corruption, and affordability as its top issues.

people.name: Brad Knott
lines: He says he would finish the border wall and send an immigrant who commits a felony to prison for at least five years before deportation.
He says he supports school choice, a balanced-budget amendment, and police, and he opposes new gun laws aimed at law-abiding owners.
He says he is pro-life, supports state laws protecting the unborn, and would defend faith-based pregnancy centers.

people.name: Chuck Hubbard
lines: He says he would raise the minimum wage, shift taxes toward the wealthy, and support public schools, small businesses, and farms.
He says he would protect Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security, and veterans' benefits, and add a public option so rural towns have a hospital nearby.
He says abortion belongs between a patient and a doctor, and he wants to overturn Citizens United and ban members of Congress from trading stocks.

people.name: Colby Watson
lines: He says he will not take money from lobbyists for corporate or foreign interests and will not trade stocks in office.
He says homeownership should be back in reach and that health care should heal people rather than maximize profit.
He says markets should reward work and entrepreneurship, and that corporate monopolies are squeezing small businesses and family farms.

people.name: Cyril Jefferson
lines: He says his priorities are affordability, health care and hunger, democracy and accountability, education and the workforce, economic development, and immigration.
He says that as mayor he focused on violent crime, workforce funding, housing, and small businesses.
He says Washington should make paychecks, schools, neighborhoods, and businesses better, not score political points.

people.name: David Rouzer
lines: He says he would fund dredging, beach nourishment, and flood insurance so coastal homeowners are not priced out.
He says he supports a strong military, intervention only when the national interest is threatened, and a strong alliance with Israel.
He says taxes and rules are crushing small businesses and farms, and he backs an all-of-the-above energy policy aimed at exporting oil and gas.

people.name: Deborah Ross
lines: She says she is working for affordable health care, public education, smaller classes, higher teacher pay, and relief from student-loan debt.
She says housing should be more affordable, retirement benefits should be protected, and workers and unions should have a champion.
She says she supports clean energy, a woman's decisions about her own health care, accessible transit, and an immigration overhaul that keeps families together while securing the border.

people.name: Don Davis
lines: He says he is working to make life more affordable and to expand opportunity in coastal and rural communities.
His campaign lists lowering the cost of living, jobs and economic growth, education, rural infrastructure, and support for the military and veterans.

people.name: Eugene Douglass
lines: He proposes a flat tax with minimal deductions for people and businesses, and less federal regulation so states handle more local affairs.

He says human life should be protected from conception to natural death, and he calls for a ban on partial-birth abortion and for states to limit what he describes as gender surgeries on children and euthanasia.
He wants elementary and secondary education controlled by states and localities, with the focus on reading, writing, science, and math.

people.name: Greg Murphy
lines: He says he helped write the Working Families Tax Cut, including no tax on tips or overtime, relief for seniors, and a larger child tax credit and standard deduction.
He says he supports the president's border enforcement and opposes returning to earlier policies he says let millions of people enter illegally.
He says he is focused on Camp Lejeune water contamination, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and faster VA care.

people.name: Jack Codiga
lines: He pledges not to accept PAC money and not to trade individual stocks.
He says he would hold more than 10 town halls a year.

people.name: Jamie Ager
lines: He says he is running because of Hurricane Helene recovery, affordability for working families, and the need to preserve the region's environment and culture.
He says people in western North Carolina work hard and still struggle to pay bills, and he distinguishes a hand up from a handout.
His platform also covers health-care costs, government waste, immigration, veterans, small business, local farms, public lands, and community safety.

people.name: Jennifer Balkcom
lines: She says working families should be able to own a home and keep more of what they earn.
She says she supports local credit unions and helped change state law so more rural towns can be served by them.
She says she supports ending the state income tax on tips, overtime, and bonuses.

people.name: Kimberly Hardy
lines: She says she would raise the federal minimum wage, close the overtime salary loophole, and end taxes on tips.
She says she would protect Medicare and Medicaid, lower drug costs, and restore cancer-research funding.
She says she would fund Head Start, Title I, and career education, and protect drinking water and coastal towns from flooding.

people.name: Lakesha Womack
lines: She says health care is a necessity and that she would protect the Affordable Care Act, cap drug costs, and fund rural hospitals.
She says she would raise the federal minimum wage, help small businesses get capital, and invest in affordable housing.
She says she would put more federal money into public schools, apprenticeships, and student-debt relief, and demand oversight of federal spending.

people.name: Laurie Buckhout
lines: She says she will fight to cut taxes and lower health-care and living costs so families can get ahead.
She says border security is national security and that Border Patrol agents need the resources to keep dangerous drugs out of the country.
She says she grew up on a farm and will cut regulations on farmers, fishermen, and the seafood industry, defend the Second Amendment, and invest in a ready military.

people.name: Mark Harris
lines: He says he believes in the sanctity of life from conception to natural death and in what he calls traditional family values.
He says he would fortify the border, enforce immigration law, and keep a strong military that honors veterans.
He says parents, not Washington, should choose public, private, charter, or home schools, and he wants to cut spending that he says drove inflation.

people.name: Max Ganorkar
lines: He says his policies are meant to expand opportunity, strengthen families, and increase prosperity for every American.
He says he is running to represent all of the people, not some of them.

people.name: Michael Dublin
lines: He says he would try to overturn Citizens United, end gerrymandering, and stop what he calls voter suppression.
He says he wants a Green New Deal for the state, with renewable energy, union jobs, and accountability for corporate polluters.
He says he prefers diplomacy to war and would reduce military spending in favor of schools, hospitals, and communities.

people.name: Michael Whatley
lines: He says he is running to fight for secure borders.
He says he wants strong leadership and what he calls North Carolina values.
He asks voters to stand with him and with President Trump.

people.name: Pat Harrigan
lines: His campaign organizes its platform around the economy, energy, national security, immigration, the Second Amendment, election integrity, and crime.

people.name: Paul Barringer
lines: He says he would put the district ahead of corporations, a partisan agenda, or the Washington establishment.
He says he believes in fiscal responsibility, local control, and practical health and justice reforms.
He says Congress should independently make laws, control spending, and oversee the other branches.

people.name: Raymond Smith
lines: He says that in the legislature he worked to expand rural health care, fund public education, and improve infrastructure, and that he would keep doing that in Washington.
He says Congress is controlled by billionaires and lobbyists, and he wants campaign-finance reform, an end to Citizens United, and a ban on stock trading by members.

people.name: Richard Hudson
lines: He says he would finish a border wall, restore Remain in Mexico, and keep working on the opioid epidemic.
He says he backs police and wants bipartisan work that keeps communities safe.

people.name: Richard Ojeda II
lines: He says he would improve VA care, pensions, and mental-health support, and raise teacher pay while cutting student debt.
He says he would strengthen Medicare and Medicaid, fund rural hospitals, cap drug prices, and codify a national right to abortion.
He says he would raise wages, repeal right-to-work laws, back farmers and skilled trades, and block a higher Social Security retirement age.

people.name: Roy Cooper
lines: He says he is running to lower the cost of food, health care, energy, child care, and housing.
He says the middle class feels out of reach while the largest corporations and the richest Americans have gained wealth.
He says that as attorney general he prosecuted crimes and went after scammers, predatory lenders, drug companies, and big banks.

people.name: Shannon Bray
lines: He calls for lower costs, simpler taxes, and an end to wasteful spending, and he says inflation should not quietly drain people's savings.
He argues people should own their data, with consent that is specific and revocable, and he says he will defend privacy, free speech, and due process.
He also wants secure borders with a workable legal process, and elections that are secure and auditable.

people.name: Tim Moore
lines: He says he serves on Financial Services and the Budget and is standing up for fiscal responsibility and smarter regulation.
He says he wants stronger support for working families and local economies, and a government that is accountable.

people.name: Valerie Foushee
lines: She says Donald Trump is the biggest threat to democracy the country has faced, and she points to court briefs, impeachment support, and a boycott of his joint address.

She wants to limit ICE, ban agents from wearing masks, require body cameras, and she says she introduced articles of impeachment against Secretary Kristi Noem and voted against a Homeland Security bill that funded ICE.
She calls health care a universal right, supports Medicare for All and extended Affordable Care Act subsidies, and says she will protect abortion access and focus on schools, jobs, and a fair shot.

people.name: Virginia Foxx
lines: She says she would ban elective abortion later in pregnancy, end federal funding of abortion, and protect people punished for living out their faith.
She says immigration changes should secure the border and uphold the law, and that Americans need the Second Amendment to defend themselves.
She says patients, including people with preexisting conditions, should have lower costs and more choices, and she opposes Medicare for All.

people.name: Julie Fedorchak
lines: She says that on the Public Service Commission she pushed to finish the Dakota Access Pipeline and to keep coal and oil energy reliable and affordable.
Her issues list includes securing the border, reducing the federal debt, backing law enforcement, and defending the Second Amendment.
She says she will work with President Trump to secure North Dakota's energy and agricultural future and to support farmers and ranchers.

people.name: Michael Howe
lines: He says he wants elections that stay secure and open to every eligible voter, including a citizenship check and a valid North Dakota ID for every form of voting.
He says the state uses paper ballots, keeps ballot equipment off the internet, audits elections after the vote, and counts only ballots in by the close of polls.
He says he will keep cutting red tape so North Dakota stays an easy place to start and grow a business.

people.name: Trygve Hammer
lines: He says Americans pay the world's highest health-care prices and that people should not have to choose between care and rent or food.
He says he will protect Social Security and put North Dakota seniors first, and he opposes raising the retirement age.
He says profitable corporations and the ultra-wealthy should pay a fair share, and that rural towns need support for public schools and farm markets, with Congress asserting its power over tariffs.

people.name: Allison Russo
lines: She says the secretary of state should protect each voter's voice and keep elections fair, secure, and accessible.
She says voters should choose their politicians, and that she has fought officials who rig the system to protect their own power.
She says she would restore trust in elections, protect personal data, and make government answerable on costs and the other problems families face.

people.name: Amy Acton
lines: The site lists lower household costs, health-care costs, education, jobs, worker protections, safer communities, and corruption as her priorities.
A campaign update says medical debt should be eliminated and health care made more affordable.
She also lists reproductive freedom and the ability to age in place among the issues on the site.

people.name: Bob Latta
lines: He lists rural broadband, less government spending, a strong national defense, the substance-use crisis, energy independence, and commonsense government reform as top priorities.
He points to the INFO Act on opioid data, the Advanced Nuclear Technology Development Act, and the Critical Electric Infrastructure Act to protect the power grid.
He highlights the Drinking Water Protection Act on algal toxins, faster processing of VA appeals, and laws on propane supply and precision-agriculture connectivity.

people.name: Brian Poindexter
lines: He says companies that benefit from America should invest in American workers instead of sending jobs overseas for cheaper labor.
On the council he says he has opposed right-to-work laws and school vouchers and supported the postal service and public schools.

people.name: Brian Shaver
lines: He supports campaign-finance limits, term limits, stronger checks and balances, and transparency in legislation.
He also wants guardrails so elected officials cannot profit from their positions, and he says they should stay present and accountable to their communities.

people.name: Carey Coleman
lines: He says he will rein in federal spending, expand American energy to lower fuel and utility costs, and protect middle-class families from new taxes.
He also says he will defend the First and Second Amendments and religious freedom, back law enforcement, secure the border, and give parents a stronger say in education.

people.name: Cleophus Dulaney
lines: He says he will push Medicare to negotiate drug prices, take on pharmacy middlemen, and support tax relief for working and middle-class families.
He also wants infrastructure, manufacturing, and clean-energy jobs, apprenticeships, and fewer rules that do not make small businesses safer, plus voting-rights protections and fair maps.

people.name: David Taylor
lines: He says he will secure the border, cut taxes, and put working families first.
He says his years as a prosecutor shape his push to give law enforcement resources against fentanyl, violent crime, and corruption.

people.name: Derek Merrin
lines: He says he led efforts to cut the state income tax, reduce regulations, and expand school choice.
He also says he played key roles in requiring photo identification to vote and in recognizing a constitutional right to carry a firearm.

people.name: Don Kissick
lines: The site says too many institutions have become corrupt, self-serving, and comfortable expanding power without representing Ohioans.
It says liberty, kindness, justice, common sense, and integrity should be the test for every bill and political leader.
It says the campaign will not support a policy that asks voters to give those principles up.

people.name: Don Leonard
lines: He says every American deserves quality insurance they can afford to use, and that every working American should be able to own a home.
He also says good child care should not cost as much as a second mortgage, and that seniors should be able to retire with dignity.

people.name: Elizabeth Kirtley
lines: She says ICE should be abolished because she believes an agency that blocks constitutional rights should not exist.
She wants abortion rights written into federal law so they do not change at state lines, and she says each person should have one vote that cannot be bought.

people.name: Emilia Sykes
lines: She says clean water, clean air, and a healthy environment are basic rights, and that environmental policy can also create jobs and hold down utility costs.
She says every northeast Ohioan deserves to have their voice heard and their vote counted.

people.name: Eric Conroy
lines: He says he will lower inflation, cut red tape, and back pro-growth policies for Ohio workers and small businesses.
He also says he will stand with law enforcement, secure the border, protect Social Security and Medicare from benefit cuts, and support parents and local control of education.

people.name: Greg Landsman
lines: He says he is running again to protect freedoms and human rights and to make it easier to raise a family.
His campaign says he is focused on lowering costs for families in southwest Ohio.

people.name: Jen Mazzuckelli
lines: She says the representative should work for the people rather than campaign donors, and that neighbors who disagree are not enemies.
She says public servants should keep promises and that the way to earn reelection is to do the job well.

people.name: Jerrad Christian
lines: He wants to overturn the Citizens United ruling, cap campaign spending, and stop foreign-linked money in elections.
He also supports universal health care, a higher minimum wage, and more housing by changing exclusionary zoning and limiting large corporate buyers.

people.name: Jim Jordan
lines: He says he is using the Judiciary Committee to investigate federal agencies, including the IRS, and to defend constitutional freedoms.
He points to a Cut, Cap and Balance plan and says he has offered deep spending cuts and a balanced federal budget.
The campaign says that as a state legislator he opposed higher taxes and spending and received awards from Ohio anti-abortion groups.

people.name: John Kulewicz
lines: He says the attorney general should be independent of Columbus politics and should work for the people who pay the office.
He says he would take on corrupt politicians and restore transparency and accountability.
He says he would pursue price-fixing, scams, robocalls, and fraud by Medicaid providers and nursing homes.

people.name: Joshua Kolasinski
lines: He says federal taxes should be used in local communities rather than on more wars or corporate welfare, and that housing, gas, health care, education, and food should be affordable.
He proposes a registered-voter lobby and a district think tank, and he says Medicare should negotiate drug prices and patients should see prices before care.

people.name: Joyce Beatty
lines: She says she supports a livable wage, equal pay, workforce training, and lower college costs, and she calls health care a right she would strengthen through the Affordable Care Act.
She says she will protect and expand Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, defend abortion access and civil rights, and support a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants and DREAMers.

people.name: Keith Faber
lines: He says he would defend constitutional rights, including religious liberty, and challenge federal actions he argues exceed federal authority.
He says he would fight the drug epidemic with treatment, prosecutions, and efforts to cut supply chains, and that he would work with police on human trafficking and survivor services.

He says he would enforce consumer-protection laws against fraud, scams, and deceptive businesses, especially cases that target seniors, and he proposes a program to help patients challenge health-insurance denials.

people.name: Kristina Knickerbocker
lines: She says she would ban congressional stock trading, end corporate PAC influence, pass term limits, protect voting rights, and close the lobbying revolving door.
She also says she would cut taxes for working families, repeal tariffs that raise prices, build more housing, cap child-care costs, and make data-center companies pay for their own infrastructure.

people.name: Marcy Kaptur
lines: She says she would oppose foreign bailouts and wars she argues put Wall Street ahead of northwest Ohio, and make data-center companies pay for the power and water they use.
She says she would take on corporate buyers of houses and expand the supply of affordable homes.
She says she would fully fund Medicare and Medicaid, restore Affordable Care Act tax credits, and lower prescription prices and the cost of child care and long-term care.

people.name: Maria Jukic
lines: She says she will defend the Constitution and the rule of law, and that she is looking for practical answers to a health system in which many people lack insurance or carry medical debt.
She says she will stand up for workers and regular people and look for common ground instead of sorting the country into two extremes.

people.name: Max Miller
lines: He says he has voted to make tax cuts permanent and to end taxes on tips and overtime, and that workforce training should not require a four-year degree.
He also says he will fund law enforcement, keep the southern border secure, expand American energy, and invest in roads, bridges, rail, and broadband.

people.name: Michael Rulli
lines: He says that as school board president he led the district out of a financial crisis without raising taxes.
He says that in the state Senate he brought funding back to communities and stood up for local values.

people.name: Mike Carey
lines: He says he is running to keep fighting for lower taxes, a stronger economy, secure borders, affordable energy, and safer communities.
His campaign also lists protecting Social Security, supporting veterans and first responders, and reducing government spending.

people.name: Mike Turner
lines: He says he has worked to add jobs at the base, grow regional manufacturing and defense work, and restore pensions for Delphi retirees.
He also says he has pushed for veterans' health care and housing, supported law enforcement, and worked to secure the border and slow illicit drugs.

people.name: Robert Sprague
lines: He says he is running to defend the vote, the voter's voice, and the family.
He says he wants the office to run the most secure elections in the state's history.

people.name: Sherrod Brown
lines: He says he led the effort to restore pensions after Wall Street losses, including retirement payments for more than 100,000 Ohioans.
He says he fought drug-company prices, including a cap on insulin and lower prices on other prescriptions for seniors.
He says he worked to get care for veterans exposed to burn pits and to restore full Social Security payments for former public workers.

people.name: Shontel Brown
lines: She says she helped pass the Social Security Fairness Act, which restored benefits for public workers and retirees who had been penalized.
She says she co-led a bipartisan bill requiring stronger cybersecurity protections from federal contractors.
She says she introduced the Hunger Free Future Act to protect SNAP from cuts that would hurt families, seniors, and children, and that she has helped secure millions for local projects.

people.name: Tom Pruss
lines: He says the office has been used as a gatekeeper for the two major parties and should treat every candidate equally, including on ballot access.
He says election security and access can go together, with accurate voter rolls, secure systems, and procedures that do not change at the last minute.
He says the office should publish election and campaign-finance information more clearly, and should make business filings faster and less burdened by red tape.

people.name: Troy Balderson
lines: He says the border should be closed to people who do not enter lawfully, and he wants more agents and technology aimed at cartels, drugs, and illegal crossings.
He says government is too big and that the answer is usually to get it out of the way, and he wants shop classes back in schools.

people.name: Vanessa Enoch
lines: She says affordability means updating the rules that drive up health care and housing costs and expanding places to rent or buy near jobs.
She says data-center companies, not working families, should pay for the power lines and grid upgrades they need, and that those facilities should not pollute neighborhoods or replace farmland.

people.name: Vivek Ramaswamy
lines: He says the state should be more affordable, with lower taxes, lower energy bills, and more money in household budgets.
He says children should get a world-class education.
He says the state should protect neighborhoods, revive cities, and put unity ahead of division.

people.name: Warren Davidson
lines: He opposes the income tax, argues deficits are driving up prices, and says regulation should be cut back to the minimum needed for fair competition.
He says the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms, and he wants people to choose their own mix of health care, coverage, and cost.

people.name: Brandon Wade
lines: He says health care should be affordable for everyone and not tied to a job, and that he would protect women's health care choices and strengthen Social Security and Medicare.
He says the economy should grow from the working class up, with fair wages, safe workplaces, and corporations and the wealthy paying their fair share.
He says he would fully fund public schools, modernize immigration, and defend the rights of women, LGBTQ+ people, immigrants, and minorities.

people.name: Frank Lucas
lines: He describes himself as a crusader for the American farmer and says he has fought to protect Oklahoma values.
In the state House, his biography says, he fought to defend private-property rights and focused on agriculture.
In Congress he has helped write every farm bill since 1996 and serves on Agriculture and as a senior Republican on Financial Services.

people.name: Jena Nelson
lines: She says Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid should be protected and strengthened, and that Medicare should negotiate lower drug prices.
She says a secure border and a fair immigration system both matter, with more agents and sensors against drug trafficking, faster asylum decisions, and more work visas.
She says she would expose backroom deals and opposes adding trillions to the deficit to pay for tax breaks for the wealthiest.

people.name: John Croisant
lines: He says he would lower costs so families are not choosing between bills and care, and that hard work should be enough to own a home, send children to college, and retire with dignity.
On schools, he says public money should stay in public schools with accountability, and he supports a program to help people earn education degrees and teach for five years debt-free.

He says he would keep illegal guns off the streets, expand affordable care so people are not skipping treatment, and back term limits, an end to congressional stock trading, and tighter lobbying rules.

people.name: Jon Echols
lines: He says everyone, including political elites, should be treated equally under the law, and that the office should back police and defend liberties.
He says he would watch taxpayer dollars and support border and fentanyl enforcement.
He says he would defend private property against foreign adversaries and out-of-state interests, work with tribal nations, and back the state's energy industry.

people.name: Josh Brecheen
lines: He says he is focused on reining in unsustainable debt and deficit spending, which he believes is undermining national security.
His House site lists his legislative priorities as deficit spending, border security, traditional values, constitutional adherence, and energy dominance.

people.name: Kelly Forbes
lines: He says he would invest in small business, CareerTech, workforce training, and partnerships with Native nations, and would work on affordable housing and food insecurity.
He says he would put more funding into public schools, respect teachers, and keep public dollars in public schools.
He says he would expand health-care access in underserved places, promote tourism, and lead the office with public integrity rather than as a career politician.
