people.name: Kevin Hern
lines: He says he has backed bills to recognize groups of veterans and a constitutional amendment aimed at a balanced budget.
He says he has voted to fund a border wall and to cut off federal money for sanctuary campuses, and that he wants small businesses to get capital.
He says he would protect religious liberty, restrict abortion funding, and protect gun rights, including concealed-carry reciprocity.

people.name: Mark Tedford
lines: He says he would lower costs for working families by cutting inflationary spending, red tape, and energy and regulatory costs, and by restoring fiscal discipline.
He says every nation has a right to secure its borders, enforce its laws, and put its citizens first.
He says he is running to help build an economy that works for the people who fund it and to bring good jobs back.

people.name: Mike Mazzei
lines: He says he would phase out the property tax for seniors and veterans while keeping essential services and the budget stable.
The site also lists protecting Oklahoma land, schools that teach students to read, and more high-paying jobs.
He says government should be accountable, respect taxpayers, and make daily life less expensive.

people.name: Mitchell Jacob
lines: He says public schools should be funded, serve free meals, and be the top priority, and that education is the greatest equalizer.
He says the national debt is the biggest threat to democracy and that Congress should stop raising the debt limit, cut spending, and eliminate the debt.
He says health care is a human right, that work visas and asylum claims should be processed fairly and quickly, and that he does not accept PAC money.

people.name: N'Kiyla Jasmine Thomas
lines: She says the campaign is funded by individual Oklahomans and will not take corporate PAC money or money from AIPAC.
She lists honest education reform, health-care access for rural and underserved communities, and support for military families.
She also lists protections for Native sovereignty, equity in autism care, and transparency in government.

people.name: Nick Coffey
lines: He says those cases covered money laundering, immigration, illegal firearms, and drug conspiracies.
He also lists counterfeiting and fraud among the crimes he has prosecuted, and says the work was about protecting communities and holding criminal organizations accountable.

people.name: Robert Brooks Sr.
lines: He proposes an app in which registered voters would weigh in on bills, pardons, and policy before he acts, and says he would follow the majority.
He says schools should put parents, teachers, and students first and show measurable gains.
He says he would respect property rights and working families, and that he has no tolerance for pay-to-play politics.

people.name: Stephanie Bice
lines: Her biography says that in the state legislature she focused on fiscal responsibility, economic development, and job growth.

In Congress she serves on Appropriations, including as vice chair of the Transportation, Housing, and Urban Development Subcommittee, and chairs a House Administration subcommittee on modernization and innovation.

people.name: T. Shannon
lines: He says Oklahoma can lead in economic opportunity, energy, agriculture, education, and innovation while protecting the state's values.
The site lists growing the economy, cutting taxes and red tape, and supporting farmers and ranchers.
It also says he would back law enforcement and defend freedoms.

people.name: Tom Cole
lines: Announcing his 2026 reelection bid, Cole says a Republican Congress and White House have secured the border, brought inflation down, and cut taxes, including on tips, overtime, and Social Security.
He says Republicans passed energy legislation to create jobs in Oklahoma and raised military pay, expanded VA services, and increased law enforcement funding.
He says he is running to support America First policies, national security, and continued work at Fort Sill and Tinker Air Force Base.

people.name: Andrea Salinas
lines: She says she will fight rising costs for working families, seek more living-wage jobs, and keep backing worker protections and investments in rural health care, education, and infrastructure.
She says she led efforts to cap prescription prices in Oregon and is pushing Congress to let Medicare negotiate drug prices and to strengthen hospital and insurance price transparency.
She also treats mental health and substance use as part of health care that is too often overlooked.

people.name: Barbara Kahl
lines: She says economic growth comes first, through small-business relief, infrastructure, and jobs, and she wants housing built faster by cutting permitting delays.
On schools, she supports public schools, school choice, vocational pathways, and funding that follows the student, and she says parents rather than federal officials should control curriculum.

She also calls for lower health-care costs and stronger veterans' care, more accountable federal spending, forest stewardship that keeps timber communities working, and support for ports and local police.

people.name: Brett Smith
lines: He proposes a surcharge on large employers whose wages leave workers needing public assistance, with small employers exempt and the money directed to health coverage, food aid, and wage support.
He proposes expanding the Oregon Health Plan into a public option open to every resident, with private insurance still available.
He also says he is the only candidate against data centers, and he backs a state limit on sending the National Guard into combat without a congressional declaration of war.

people.name: Chris Beck
lines: He says Congress should repeal the bill he calls the Big Beautiful Bill and restore Medicaid and SNAP funding, and he wants wildfire-prevention funding and staffing restored at the Forest Service.
He says ending the war with Iran and canceling tariffs would ease fuel and household costs, and he wants low-cost housing folded into small-town Main Streets rather than onto farms and forest land.
He says rural hospitals and clinics need protection because Medicaid covers a large share of the district, including many of its children.

people.name: Chris Henry
lines: He says he would cut the military budget, support Medicare for All, and raise wages while rejecting both broad tariffs and trade deals that override labor and environmental rules.
He proposes a federal fund for earthquake retrofits, backup power, and supplies ahead of a Cascadia earthquake.
His site says state law can end a smaller party that misses a statewide vote threshold, and that this Senate race is the Progressive Party's contest this year.

people.name: Christine Drazan
lines: She says she would order agencies to find rules and fees that raise the cost of housing, energy, food, child care, health care, and running a business, and that she would veto new tax and fee increases.
She says she would speed housing permits, expand help for first-time buyers, and make it easier to build more kinds of homes.
She says homelessness spending should be audited and shifted toward addiction recovery, mental-health treatment, and programs measured by how many people reach stable housing.

people.name: Cliff Bentz
lines: He says he will back tighter border security and finishing a border wall, and he describes himself as a right-to-life candidate who believes life begins at conception.
He opposes government-run health care and says he will direct investment toward rural Oregon while holding the federal government accountable for how it manages forests and wildfire.
He says he supports the Second Amendment and the wise use of Oregon's water and land.

people.name: David Brock Smith
lines: He says he is running to keep working on solutions for working families, their communities, and the businesses that support them.
He says the Senate needs common sense, accountability, and a stronger rural voice so people across Oregon are represented.

people.name: David Russ
lines: He says he would bring manufacturing back, ease rules on small businesses and family farms, and end subsidies and loan programs he says target non-citizens.
He wants federal public lands and control of schools, utilities, and infrastructure returned to states and local governments.
He says he would make it a federal felony to help people cross the border illegally and would shrink what he calls an oversized federal government.

people.name: Janelle Bynum
lines: She says her mission is to lower health-care and housing costs, create jobs, and make sure every child gets a good education.
Her issues list also names climate action, protecting reproductive rights, and ending homelessness.
She says she is pushing back on what she calls cruelty and chaos from the White House while working with either party on results.

people.name: Jeff Merkley
lines: He says his daily work is to create opportunity for working families.
He says he is trying to stop the corruption of democracy.
He says he is trying to tackle the climate crisis.

people.name: Maxine Dexter
lines: She says she is working to protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, and she lists universal, affordable health care, addiction and mental-health treatment, and reproductive care among her priorities.
She also names economic opportunity, climate and environmental protection, housing, gun-violence prevention, and schools.
Her issues page includes government corruption, immigration, LGBTQ protections, and safeguarding democracy.

people.name: Monique DeSpain
lines: She says she will oppose a national abortion ban and any congressional effort to limit abortion access for Oregonians, and that those decisions belong with women and their doctors.

On immigration, she calls for a secure border, removal of people she says are dangerous criminals, a one-time path to lawful status for long-settled residents who pass background checks, and a faster legal immigration system.
She also says she will defend veterans' care, back law enforcement, tie homelessness and addiction funding to results, and speed forest management and homebuilding.

people.name: Patti Adair
lines: She says she would make daily life more affordable, make permanent the exemptions from tax on tips, overtime, and Social Security, and raise the child tax credit.

She says she would fully support law enforcement, ban members of Congress from insider trading and from being paid during shutdowns, and require big technology companies to disclose how data centers affect air, water, and electricity costs.
She also lists sustainable management of natural resources, small-business growth, and putting people ahead of parties.

people.name: Suzanne Bonamici
lines: She says she will keep opposing the Trump administration, and her priorities include an economy that works for more people, support for working families, and more affordable housing.
She calls for universal health care, stronger education, more affordable college, reproductive rights, and a response to climate change that builds a clean-energy economy.
She also lists protecting Social Security, small businesses, gun-violence prevention, voting rights, LGBTQIA+ rights, and a fairer immigration system.

people.name: Tina Kotek
lines: She says her plan is to make life more affordable and create more economic opportunity.
She says she wants every student to succeed.
She says she would defend what makes Oregon distinct while continuing work on homelessness and schools.

people.name: Val Hoyle
lines: She says people who work should be able to find a union job, buy a home, and start a family in Oregon, and she highlights paid sick leave, a higher minimum wage, apprenticeships, and the PRO Act.

She supports universal preschool, a cap on child-care costs, paid family and medical leave, lower prescription prices, and restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits while still pushing for universal health care.
Her campaign also points to reproductive health care, protecting vote-by-mail, and a shift toward cleaner energy.

people.name: Alan Bradstock
lines: He calls for higher wages, support for small businesses, and an economy that is not limited to the wealthy and well-connected.
He also says health care should be affordable and accessible and that medical debt should end, and that no one should be above the law.

people.name: Aurora Stuski
lines: She says she will work to lower costs for families and make it easier for small businesses to operate.
She also says she will back law enforcement, secure the border, and push for more transparent government.

people.name: Beth Farnham
lines: She says she would defend reproductive freedom, public education, gun safety, universal health care, and immigration reform.
She also lists affordability and the environment, and says climate change requires action to protect agriculture and communities.

people.name: Bob Brooks
lines: He says that as a union president he pressed politicians for higher wages, better health care, and stronger benefits.
His issues page lists affordability, health care, a higher minimum wage, stronger unions, housing costs, and ending corruption.

people.name: Bob Harvie
lines: He says families deserve a fair shot to earn a living, afford a home, raise children, and retire with dignity.
He describes the race as a chance to send someone to Congress who will fight for a better deal for working people.

people.name: Brendan Boyle
lines: He says his work on the Budget Committee is aimed at a federal budget that expands opportunity.
On Ways and Means, he says he wants tax and social policy that matches the priorities of working families.
He says the Blue Collar Caucus he co-founded in 2016 looks at wage stagnation, job insecurity, trade, offshoring, and careers in manufacturing and the building trades.

people.name: Brian Fitzpatrick
lines: He says that on his first day in office he proposed congressional term limits, no pay if Congress misses a budget, and a requirement to balance the budget.
He highlights a law he wrote to give law enforcement more resources to stop drugs at the border.
He says he wants people with serious terminal illnesses to have access to treatments that might save their lives, and that institutions should serve the public rather than career officials.

people.name: Chris Deluzio
lines: He says he is fighting powerful interests he argues have taken the American Dream away from working people.
Before Congress he says he worked on voting rights and election security, and he helped University of Pittsburgh faculty win a union with the United Steelworkers.

people.name: Chris Rabb
lines: His platform calls for housing people can afford, a living wage, and Medicare for All.
He also says he will fight for food security, clean air and water, and a foreign policy that prioritizes peace.

people.name: Chrissy Houlahan
lines: She says her work in Congress is aimed at the cost of living for families in Chester County and the district.
Through the BIOTech Caucus she says she is working to grow jobs tied to biotechnology.

people.name: Dan Meuser
lines: He says his priorities are an America First agenda, border security, the economy, and energy.
He says his committee work is aimed at oversight of the financial system and support for small business.

people.name: Dennis Mahoney
lines: He argues government should make work pay and should help families stay stable.
He says housing, transportation, child care, health care, food, education, and employment have to be treated as one system rather than separate programs.

people.name: Glenn Thompson
lines: He says his Agriculture Committee work is about supporting the people who produce food, fiber, and energy.
On Education and the Workforce he says he works on education from early learning through retirement.

people.name: Guy Reschenthaler
lines: His issues page says national security is personal because he prosecuted terrorists in Iraq, and that he supports a strong defense.
He says cutting regulation in Harrisburg and Washington is how the region creates jobs, and he lists immigration, security, jobs, and taxes among his priorities.

people.name: James Hayes
lines: He says he wants less regulation, a return of good-paying union jobs, support for law enforcement, and accountability for repeat violent offenders.
He also supports school choice, an all-of-the-above energy strategy, standing with allies including Israel, and reining in federal spending.

people.name: Janelle Stelson
lines: She says she wants to lower utility, health care, and housing costs and support small businesses and farms.
She says she will protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid and defend abortion rights.

people.name: Jessica Arriaga
lines: She says public safety, the cost of living, and career and technical education are the issues she hears about most.
She argues health care should put patients first and that the city needs practical results rather than partisan fights.

people.name: John Joyce
lines: He says he is working to strengthen the economy and make health care more affordable.
He also says he will defend constitutional rights.

people.name: Josh Shapiro
lines: His campaign says that as governor he has worked on jobs and money in people's pockets, law enforcement and community groups for public safety, education funding, and protecting freedoms.
The site says Pennsylvania has hired hundreds of new officers and created thousands of jobs, and that children can get free breakfast and more mental-health counselors in school.
It says high-school graduates have more paths through work, apprenticeships, or college, and that he and Lieutenant Governor Austin Davis are running to continue that work.

people.name: Justin Wagner
lines: He says housing, health care, power, and food costs are pushing working families into poverty, and that he would fight for affordability, local veterans, and labor.
He also says every school needs the tools to prepare the next generation, the justice system should be fair, and the environment should stay safe for future children.

people.name: Ken Krawchuk
lines: He says he would veto tax increases, use the line-item veto, phase out the personal income tax, and abolish property taxes.
He says he would end the state's monopoly on schooling and privatize public schools because too many students are behind in reading and math.
His listed program also says he would eliminate parole for violent criminals, pardon nonviolent drug offenders, and decriminalize marijuana.

people.name: Lloyd Smucker
lines: He says he wants to cut taxes, protect retirement, and spend taxpayer dollars more carefully.
He also lists lower health care costs, American energy, and support for small businesses and family farms.

people.name: Madeleine Dean
lines: She says she will keep working to expand access to health care and to reduce gun violence.
She also lists clean water and the climate, ethical governance, and infrastructure among her priorities.

people.name: Marty Young
lines: His platform focuses on making family life affordable, fixing health care, protecting public safety, strengthening energy security, and supporting the military.
He says his Young Americans Plan would extend real coverage to children up to age 23 and to expectant mothers, and that he wants to create jobs, secure the border, and cut waste.

people.name: Mary Gay Scanlon
lines: Her office says her priorities are voting rights, access to justice, education, economic growth in the region, gun safety, women's rights, and ending hunger.
She says her main goal is protecting and improving the lives of children, families, veterans, and seniors.

people.name: Mike Kelly
lines: He says he favors fiscal responsibility, smaller government, and pro-growth tax reform.
His campaign says businesses, not government, create jobs, and lists the economy, tax reform, energy, veterans, and education among his issues.

people.name: Nancy Mannion
lines: She says her first priority is affordable, high-quality health care, including removing cost barriers to treatment and medicine.
She also calls for stronger public education and workforce training, help for Lancaster and York farmers, and federal support so local farmers can supply fresh food to area pantries.

people.name: Nick Manganaro
lines: He says he would work across the aisle on a path to balance the budget, oppose new entitlement expansions that widen the deficit, and demand oversight of federal spending.
He also calls for an all-of-the-above energy policy, less regulation, and equal treatment under the law, free association, and free speech.

people.name: Paige Cognetti
lines: She says she would ban congressional stock trading, refuse corporate PAC money, and audit the federal government for waste, fraud, and abuse with a scalpel.
She says she would break up monopolies that hurt small businesses, make it easier to join a union, cap credit-card swipe fees, and fight for paid family leave and affordable child care.
She says she would reshore manufacturing, use targeted tariffs, and block data-center projects in northeastern Pennsylvania that do not follow local rules or supply their own energy.

people.name: Rachel Wallace
lines: She says she is focused on fixing health care, lowering the cost of living, and keeping promises to veterans and farmers.
Her priorities page also lists raising wages and rooting out government corruption and fraud.

people.name: Ray Bilger
lines: He says a strong economy should be judged by whether a paycheck covers groceries, a family can afford a home, and young people can find work without leaving, and he wants more local hiring in manufacturing, health care, cybersecurity, and related fields.
He says no one should have to choose between a doctor and a mortgage, and he wants lower drug costs, protection for Medicare and Medicaid, and stronger rural hospitals.

people.name: Rob Bresnahan Jr.
lines: He says he supports securing the border, stopping wasteful spending, cutting taxes, and backing law enforcement against fentanyl.
He says he will protect Social Security and Medicare without raising the retirement age or cutting benefits, and that he wants more jobs in the region.

people.name: Ryan Mackenzie
lines: His campaign says he is focused on seniors and Medicare, lowering costs, and banning members of Congress from trading stocks.
He says his committee work is aimed at protecting workers and the district's interests on education, foreign affairs, and homeland security.

people.name: Stacy Garrity
lines: Her Turn Around PA plan says she would lift a ban on new drilling sites and call a special session to speed energy permits, pipelines, and power plants.
The same plan says she would make daily costs more affordable, reduce property taxes for families and seniors, and restore fairness and transparency in state government.
She says she would roll back costly mandates and pause or reform renewable-energy and efficiency mandates so the state can produce more energy.

people.name: Summer Lee
lines: She supports automatic voter registration, early and mail voting, and an end to the Citizens United ruling, and she says she will not trade individual stocks while in office.
She supports Medicare for All, a higher minimum wage, and the PRO Act so workers can form unions.
She says a shift to clean energy should come with union jobs and training, and that employers should not be allowed to pay disabled workers a subminimum wage.

people.name: Tony Guy
lines: He says he will back law enforcement, fund and finish a border wall, deport people he calls criminal immigrants, and stop fentanyl trafficking.
He also wants pro-growth policies for small business, manufacturing, natural gas, and agriculture, and less federal regulation and spending.

people.name: Aaron Guckian
lines: He says he would expand housing, reduce construction barriers, and lower utility and health-care costs.
He says the campaign would invest in public schools, teacher support, and vocational and technical programs tied to local employers.
He says he would expand training and incentives so the state has more primary-care doctors and dentists, and he calls for targeted tax relief and less wasteful spending.

people.name: Alan Gordon
lines: He says he would apply the same law and the same evidence standard to political allies and opponents, and seek an outside review when the office has a conflict.
He says he would defend religious liberty, conscience, lawful self-defense, and other constitutional rights.
He says he would focus prosecution on dangerous offenders while confronting trafficking, exploitation, and domestic violence.

people.name: C. Reynolds
lines: The site contrasts Rhode Island's state budget with New Hampshire's and says Rhode Islanders pay far more per person for government.
It frames the campaign as returning money to residents under the banner of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.

people.name: Gabe Amo
lines: A seniors plan on his campaign site says protecting Social Security and Medicare is a top priority, including work on the Social Security 2100 Act.
The plan says he would lower the Medicare eligibility age to 60 and defend Medicare drug-price negotiation and the insulin cap.
It also calls for more home and long-term care, fair pay for care workers, and more supportive housing for low-income seniors.

people.name: Gregg Amore
lines: He says Rhode Islanders believe in fair elections, transparent government, and a democracy that works for everyone.
He says he will keep building on work to expand access to the ballot and to stand up for residents when those rights are threatened.

people.name: Helena Foulkes
lines: She says she would create good-paying jobs and make Rhode Island more affordable, and she criticizes the state's handling of housing and the Washington Bridge.
She says she would push back against federal funding cuts aimed at states like Rhode Island.
Her plans page lists health care, jobs, child care and transportation, career and technical education, and a housing program called Rhode Home.

people.name: Jack Reed
lines: He says he voted against the Iraq War, opposes the Iran war, and is using his Senate vote to stop that war and other military operations he calls unnecessary.
He says he wants housing, education, health care, and environmental spending paid for by higher taxes on billionaires and changes to the tax system.
He says he has worked to bring federal money to Rhode Island for housing, coastal research, Coast Guard ships, Quonset jobs, the airport, roads, and transit.

people.name: Jasjit Gotra
lines: He says he would cut waste, fully fund teacher and firefighter pensions, and make the state easier for businesses.
He says he would end the state tax on Social Security within two years.
His listed plans include cutting energy costs, teaching artificial intelligence in every high school by 2028, capping out-of-pocket health costs, and building 20,000 housing units in four years.

people.name: Kellie Keenan
lines: She says she would lower everyday costs and energy bills, offer tax relief for working families and seniors, and make housing more affordable.
She says she would cut red tape for small businesses, expand workforce training, invest in community health centers, and support the ocean economy.
She says she supports a parental bill of rights, curriculum transparency, school choice, stronger public safety, and secure borders.

people.name: Kenneth Block
lines: He says the state budget is about $15 billion and that residents are not getting services that match what they pay.
He points to the Washington Bridge and large technology projects as examples of agencies repeating mistakes.
He says his focus is accountability, fixing broken processes, and results for residents.

people.name: Kimberly Ahern
lines: She says that as attorney general she would put the criminal unit first and prosecute violent offenders, including murder, sexual assault, domestic violence, and trafficking.
She says she would expand diversion so people with mental illness or addiction can get treatment while communities stay safe.

people.name: Michael Bahry
lines: His campaign videos argue that Congress needs term limits and regular turnover.
Other videos call the war in Gaza a tragedy and argue for peace rather than more bombing in Gaza and in the Russia-Ukraine war.

people.name: Raymond McKay
lines: His Right Direction program says it would restore constitutional promises and the rights of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
He says he would apply common-sense answers so the country does not waste current and future opportunities.
He says the campaign is meant to secure freedom, values, and prosperity for Rhode Islanders and other Americans.

people.name: Sabina Matos
lines: She says she is pushing legislation to stop grocery price gouging and to bring more grocery stores into neighborhoods that need them.
She says she has fought for affordable housing since her time on the Providence City Council.
She says she will defend reproductive freedom and the right to vote, and that every Rhode Islander should feel safe at home.

people.name: Seth Magaziner
lines: He says he ran to fight for working people and has introduced bills to lower drug prices, guarantee paid time off, and invest in career and technical education.
He says he is committed to protecting Social Security and Medicare, protecting abortion rights, and banning lawmakers from trading stocks.

people.name: Victor Mellor
lines: He says his housing plan would speed homebuilding, empower local trades, and send federal housing funds to working families, first-time buyers, and veterans.
He says he would work to bring investment home for ports, manufacturers, and skilled trades so Rhode Island has good-paying jobs from entry level to executive level.
He says elections should be easy to vote in and hard to cheat, with accurate voter rolls and open processes.

people.name: Alan Wilson
lines: He highlights child-predator prosecutions, a larger Internet Crimes Against Children task force, and the state's human-trafficking task force.
He says he has gone to court against policies of the Obama and Biden administrations, including what he calls a transgender agenda.
He says he backs President Trump on immigration enforcement and election integrity.

people.name: Annie Andrews
lines: She says families are struggling with grocery prices, child care, and the cost of health care, and her platform treats health care as a right.
Her listed plans include tackling debt and congressional perks, cutting taxes, lowering premiums, protecting rural hospitals, and reversing Medicaid cuts.
The platform also lists strong schools and affordable child care, reproductive freedom, political corruption, and an end to gun violence.

people.name: Courtney McClain
lines: She says her Upstate First agenda would expand health care, build affordable homes, manage rapid growth, invest in small businesses, and stop data centers from coming into local communities.
She says she would fight for stronger schools, fair wages, safer communities, the power of every vote, and veterans.
She says she is committed to a more affordable and inclusive future for Greenville and Spartanburg.

people.name: Darline Graham
lines: She says she would make the Trump tax cuts permanent, cut waste and fraud, and back workforce training, the skilled trades, and work requirements for able-bodied adults.
She says she supports finishing a border wall, ending catch-and-release, and opposing amnesty and taxpayer-funded benefits for people here illegally.
She says she opposes taxpayer funding of abortion, supports voter identification and current voter rolls, and opposes gun registries and red-flag confiscation.

people.name: David Stumbo
lines: He says he would defend the Constitution, religious liberty, parental rights, and what he calls the sanctity of life of the unborn.
He says he has prosecuted people in the country illegally, murderers, rapists, domestic abusers, and drug dealers, and that he would keep doing that work on the first day in office.
He says he supports law enforcement, health-care freedom, lower taxes, and a more transparent government.

people.name: Eunice Lehmacher
lines: She says there is no excuse for a lapse in health-insurance funding, for what she calls the reckless brutality of masked, untrained ICE agents, or for tariffs she says have cost households more than a thousand dollars.
She also says there is no excuse for delays releasing the Epstein files or for sabotage of close alliances.
She says she would advocate for vulnerable people, protect the Upstate's natural beauty, and help families and small businesses thrive.

people.name: Jason Belton
lines: The site says the campaign takes no corporate PAC money.
It says contributions pay for community events and voter outreach in every South Carolina county.

people.name: Jenny Costa Honeycutt
lines: She says she would put the Lowcountry first, stand with law enforcement, and secure the border against fentanyl and people she calls criminal illegal aliens.
She says she would fight wasteful spending, balance the budget, and defend the Constitution, including free speech, religious liberty, and the Second Amendment.
She says she would protect the unborn, keep men out of women's sports, lower family costs, and press for veterans' health care, benefits, jobs, and housing with less red tape.

people.name: Jermaine Johnson
lines: He says he would expand the number of families who owe no income tax rather than eliminate the tax, because he says ending it would mainly help the wealthiest, and he says he would work with cities to cut property taxes.
He says he would let cities fix roads with transportation-department money, raise law-enforcement pay, and fund more rural hospitals and trade schools.
He says he would audit public education, protect reproductive decisions for patients and doctors, and legalize medical marijuana while putting recreational use to a statewide vote.

people.name: Jim Clyburn
lines: He says his 10-20-30 formula sends at least 10 percent of certain funds to communities where 20 percent or more of people have lived in poverty for 30 years.
He points to his Rural Energy Savings Program, which lets rural electric cooperatives lend for home energy efficiency, and to a broadband bill funded in the 2021 infrastructure law.

His biography says he has worked to make America's greatness accessible and affordable, including preserving historic buildings at historically Black colleges and creating heritage corridors and parks.

people.name: Joe Wilson
lines: He says he promotes a strong national defense and peace through strength.
He says he is working to create jobs and to limit the size and scope of the federal government.
He says his commitments also cover the economy and veterans' services.

people.name: John Vincent
lines: He says he would work to pass a war-powers measure on the war in Iran and to end tariffs he says are making life more expensive for farmers and small businesses.
He says he would remove the Social Security income cap to extend solvency, and he names veterans bills he would push, including the Major Richard Star Act.
He says he would introduce an All American Healthcare Act for low-cost optional insurance and a plan to bring federal spending under control without adding to the debt.

people.name: Kasie Whitener
lines: She says she would simplify the tax code, return to actual budgets, and cut federal spending across agencies.
She says she would separate health insurance from employment and remove barriers that keep people from starting medical practices.
She says she wants a balanced-budget amendment, no new foreign wars, and no new federal abortion laws or new limits on the Second Amendment.

people.name: Mallory Dittmer
lines: She says voters she met are unhappy with divisive politics, high costs, unreliable health care, attacks on public education, and congressional gridlock.
She says she will fight for practical solutions through conversation and collaboration, and that she will not bend her values to party or special interests.
She says she advocates legislation to make it easier for independents to vote and run for office.

people.name: Mark Hammond
lines: He says Business One Stop has made it easier for businesses to expand in the state.
He credits the High Growth Small Business Job Creation Act with drawing angel investment into early-stage, high-growth companies.
He says oversight of charities is part of why the state ranks in the top five nationally for charitable giving.

people.name: Michael Addison
lines: He says the state needs a governor who combines health-care knowledge with environmental accountability.
He says prosperity has to start with people who are most vulnerable, including help with jobs and housing distress.

people.name: Nancy Lacore
lines: She says she would lower housing, health-care, child-care, and tariff-driven costs, restore enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies, and reverse Medicaid cuts.
She says the border should be secure and immigration cases decided faster, and that ICE officers should follow due process, wear body cameras, and show their faces.
She says she would write women's reproductive freedom into law, ban offshore drilling on the East Coast, and overturn Citizens United and congressional stock trading.

people.name: Richard Hricik
lines: He says the attorney general should answer to the public and the rule of law, not to donors, parties, or special interests.
He says he would go after violent crime and also corporations, insurers, and officials he says put profit or power above people.
He names flock cameras, data centers, and polluters as targets, along with consumer fraud and corruption.

people.name: Russell Fry
lines: He says that as a state legislator he fought for lower taxes, less government, and pro-Second Amendment legislation.
He says government decisions fall hardest on families living paycheck to paycheck, and that he wants to leave the country better than he found it.

people.name: Sheri Biggs
lines: She says she would build the wall, stop illegal immigration and drugs, and replace catch-and-release with what she calls stop-and-deport.
She says she would fight wasteful spending and demand accountability for tax dollars, and she would defend the sanctity of life.
She says veterans should receive the honor, dignity, and care the country promised them.

people.name: Walid Hakim
lines: His listed platform objectives are a 100-year plan, education reform, law-and-order reform, and land reform.
The site says the Green Party campaign is meant to widen the debate in a state long dominated by one party.

people.name: Wes Climer
lines: He says he has led fights to cut taxes, block wasteful spending, and shrink the power of unelected bureaucrats, including a ban on secret budget spending and more than $2 billion in tax cuts.
He says he championed constitutional carry, medical freedom during COVID, school choice, and the toughest fake-meat rules in the nation to protect agriculture.
He says he blocked a legislative pay raise in court, secured road funding for York County, and backed property-tax exemptions for veterans.

people.name: William Timmons
lines: He says he ran for office to make a difference and entered Congress in 2019 to bring real reform to Washington.
He says he represents Upstate residents on the Financial Services Committee, including its Digital Assets Subcommittee.
He says he chairs the Oversight Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs and serves on the Delivering on Government Efficiency Subcommittee.

people.name: Zyon Khalifa
lines: He says communities thrive when young people have real options, and that safer communities come from opportunity.
He says he would expand workforce training, apprenticeships, and technical education, and strengthen small-town economies.
He says he would keep opportunity in South Carolina through small-business growth and local economic development.

people.name: Brian Bengs
lines: He says he wants a constitutional amendment to ban unlimited corporate political spending that he traces to the Citizens United decision.
He says local communities should be able to refuse a new data center, and that he will not take data-center money.
He says he supports term limits for Congress and that he would not vote to continue what he calls an unnecessary war with Iran.

people.name: Heather Baxter
lines: She says she would push secure and transparent elections and restore trust in how votes are run.
She says she would give small businesses easier access to office resources and cut red tape through what she calls SD DOGE.
She says she would improve customer service in the secretary of state's office.

people.name: Lance Russell
lines: He says tough-on-crime policies work.
He says his daily work is meant to protect the people of South Dakota.

people.name: Larry Rhoden
lines: He says his mission is to keep South Dakota strong, safe, and free, with less government and less red tape.
He says his legislative record focused on low taxes, strong property rights, and personal freedom.
He says he would stand up for law enforcement and for property rights, and keep the state open for business.

people.name: Marty Jackley
lines: The campaign says the job in Congress is to keep South Dakota safe, and it points to three years as U.S. attorney and three elections as attorney general.
The site highlights an A+ NRA rating and endorsements that include the NRA-PVF and South Dakota Right to Life.

people.name: Mike Rounds
lines: He says he stands with an America First agenda and with President Trump, and that he will back policies that put South Dakota and the country first.
He says that as a member of the Armed Services Committee he works to keep the military the best in the world.
He says he supports local control of education, wants to eliminate the U.S. Department of Education, and supports the Second Amendment.

people.name: Tamara Lesnar
lines: She says she would make voting places easier to reach, curb what she calls double taxation, and build a statewide database of ballot-initiative signatures.
She says she would file lawsuits against laws she believes violate the Bill of Rights.
She criticizes sharing voter lists with federal agencies and giving the Postal Service a role in deciding who receives an absentee ballot.

people.name: Terrence Davis
lines: He says he trusts South Dakota's election system and will protect it.
His stated standard is that every vote is counted and every voice is heard.

people.name: Andrew Gerena
lines: He says government should keep life safe, affordable, peaceful, healthy, and fair, with personal liberty as the minimum.
He says tax money should not go mainly to regime-change wars or to tax breaks for corporations that have not shown loyalty to the public.
He says candidates, including himself, have a duty to serve the public rather than foreign governments or corporations.

people.name: Anna Golladay
lines: She says workers deserve wages that cover the bills and the freedom to organize, and that rural counties need funded hospitals, schools, and infrastructure.
She says she takes no corporate PAC money and wants fair elections and fair maps.
She says she would protect reproductive freedom and LGBTQ+ people, treat health care as a human right, and fund Oak Ridge's science without sacrificing the land.

people.name: Bill Hagerty
lines: He says he is running to keep fighting for lower taxes, energy independence, secure borders, and the rule of law.
He says his Senate work has included securing the southern border, supporting small businesses, and strengthening national security.
He says he will keep pushing an America First agenda and treat the Chinese Communist Party as a serious adversary.

people.name: Catherine Whitson
lines: She says she would lower costs, seek high-paying jobs, back local small businesses, and promote cleaner energy, safe water, and recycling.
On health care, she says she would cut prescription prices, protect rural hospitals, and use existing law to help people who do not have group coverage.
She says she would boost public-school funding and vocational training, support private and home schooling, and push for safe, affordable housing and child, adult, and elder care.

people.name: Charlie Hatcher
lines: He says he would fight inflationary spending and rules that raise energy and business costs, and let families keep more of what they earn.
He says food security is national security and that he would protect farmers from foreign disease threats and dependence on other countries for food.
He says he would enforce immigration law, defend the Second Amendment for law-abiding owners, and make constituent service a priority.

people.name: Chaz Molder
lines: He says he would ban stock trading by members of Congress and restore trust through transparency and accountability.
He says he would lower the cost of health care, housing, and groceries, and stand up for the right to organize.
He says affordable health care is a basic right and that rural hospitals need support so they can stay open.

people.name: Chuck Fleischmann
lines: He says massive federal spending meant to stem unemployment is counterproductive, and that the tax system does not support the growth the economy needs.
He says the country's founding values still matter to him, and that environmentally safe energy exploration should be part of energy policy.

people.name: Darden Copeland
lines: He says too many politicians are serving billionaires while cutting safety nets, including expanded Medicaid, Medicare, health-care premiums, student loans, and food assistance.
He says his career has been about protecting the working and middle class, including work on solar farms, affordable housing, rural hospitals, and transit funding.

people.name: Dave Seeman
lines: He says he would end the state grocery tax, close corporate tax loopholes, cancel a large share of medical debt, and phase in a livable minimum wage with 12 weeks of family leave.
He says he would end private-school vouchers, cover child care for household incomes under $99,000, and put a community health center in every county.
He calls for a 24-month pause on new data centers, open primaries, fairer districts, and ranked ballots in a future governor's race.

people.name: David Hatley
lines: He says the state should help pay for water, sewer, and roads when a city sets aside part of a new development for lower-priced homes and speeds approvals, and that Tennessee should drop energy-code changes that raise the price of a starter home.

He says he would pause new data-center approvals until the state writes rules, end tax breaks for them, and send at least half of a data center's new tax revenue to cut property taxes for homeowners in the host county.
He says he would create an elected independent state auditor and post disclosable contracts, grants, and payments within 30 days.

people.name: David Kustoff
lines: He says public safety is his top priority and points to his work prosecuting public corruption, violent crime, and drugs.
He says teachers do not need national mandates, that he would secure the border and stop drug trafficking, and that he supports legal immigration for people who follow the rules.
He says life begins at conception, that people have a right to keep and bear arms, and that he is working on a farm bill for the district's agriculture.

people.name: David Sutman Jr.
lines: He says groceries, housing, and fuel are crushing working families, and that he will focus on practical ways to cut those everyday costs.
He says he would push term limits, clearer spending records, and performance standards for elected officials.
He says he answers to Tennessee rather than to either party, and that he will support constitutional rights and the rule of law.

people.name: Diana Harshbarger
lines: She says she would finish the border wall, end catch-and-release, restore Remain in Mexico, and defund sanctuary cities.
She says she will defend the Second Amendment, support term limits, and treat the opioid crisis with border enforcement, treatment funding, and accountability.
Drawing on her pharmacy work, she says health-care choices should stay with patients, drug prices should come down, and the country should not rely on China for medicines.

people.name: Heidi Kuhn
lines: She says data centers should not get a blank check.
She says communities deserve a say in whether and where data centers are built, and in how much water and power they use.

people.name: Jeremy Hearn
lines: He lists his priorities as defending the Constitution, clarifying history, and restoring what he calls equality for people.
He says he would draft an Equal Earnings Act and use assets at Fort Knox toward legislation and the national debt.
He says he wants economic alternatives to war and protection of what he calls American human freedom.

people.name: Jerri Green
lines: She says she will expand paid family and medical leave, support collective bargaining, and invest in small businesses, especially in underserved areas.
She says public schools should be fully funded, with respected teachers and without what she calls censorship and political interference.
She says the state should expand Medicaid, especially in rural Tennessee, and she supports background checks, red-flag laws, and gun locks.

people.name: Johnny Garrett
lines: He says he would work with the president on that agenda, including deportations and securing the southern border.
He says he would fight inflation, seek lower taxes, and defend the Second Amendment.
He also lists keeping men out of women's sports, standing with Israel, backing police, protecting what he calls the sanctity of life, and supporting farmers.

people.name: Justin Pearson
lines: He says he would guarantee jobs, raise the minimum wage to a living wage, pass the PRO Act, and make billionaires and large corporations pay more.
He supports Medicare for All, rural hospitals, and the veterans' health system, and he wants permits to carry, a ban on assault rifles, and background checks.
He says he would pause large data-center construction, overturn Citizens United, and ban members of Congress from trading stock.

people.name: Kristi Burke
lines: She says health care should be a right and that workers should be empowered.
She says people should have the freedom to live with integrity, and that the campaign relies on grassroots donations rather than corporate PAC money.

people.name: Lauren Pinkston
lines: She says she would eliminate the grocery tax, cap property taxes, and make it possible to own a home.
On schools, she says she would end vouchers, reduce testing, limit screens, and add 50,000 child-care slots.
She says she would close health-care deserts, challenge middlemen who raise costs, and allow no new data centers until the state sets the rules.

people.name: Marsha Blackburn
lines: She says she will keep taxes and prices low and cut spending and regulation she calls unnecessary so more companies move to Tennessee.
She says she will help Tennessee-grown small businesses expand at home while the state recruits outside employers.
She says she will work with businesses on workforce gaps, including training, and commit to filling them.

people.name: Matt Van Epps
lines: He says he would cut red tape, bring manufacturing back, unleash American energy, and set rules for crypto and artificial intelligence that protect privacy.
He says he would reform the VA so veterans get the care and benefits they earned, finish the border wall, and stop fentanyl trafficking.
He says he would protect farmers from overregulation and foreign land purchases and expand rural health care.

people.name: Michaela Barnett
lines: She says gas, groceries, infrastructure, and rent are squeezing East Tennessee, and that both parties' insiders are waiting the problems out.
She wants to limit corporate political spending, overturn Citizens United, ban congressional stock trading, and require independent redistricting commissions.
She also calls for term limits, a lobbying ban after members leave office, and age limits for Congress and the presidency.

people.name: Mike Croley
lines: He organizes the campaign around affordability, accountability, and accessibility, including lower everyday costs and easier access to health care, voting, and veterans' services.
He says he is not taking corporate PAC money and wants government to serve families rather than a powerful few.
He says public officials, agencies, and corporations should be transparent and accountable.

people.name: Misam Abidi
lines: He says Tennessee exists in its workers, parents, entrepreneurs, and students, and that government should support those people rather than overpower them.
He says the campaign's mission is to restore a balance in which citizens can build wealth, protect their rights, and live meaningful lives.

people.name: Robert Jones
lines: He says he would seek an Accountability Act so constituents can be polled on major issues and officials must explain votes that go against that result.

On daily costs, he says communities should buy food together, use simpler construction to make housing cheaper, and rethink a health system that charges cash patients and insured patients very different prices.
He says he supports the Second Amendment for law-abiding people, wants an open debate about modern limits, and says immigration enforcement should use due process.

people.name: Robert Vick
lines: He says his schooling background is meant to guide how the state spends on teachers and on student results.
He says Tennessee needs community mental-health systems that can handle a crisis and support students.
He says the state budget should be managed within the state's means.

people.name: Scott DesJarlais
lines: He supports a constitutional amendment requiring a balanced budget, and he says people and businesses should keep more of their money.
He says health coverage should compete across state lines, with tort reform and health savings accounts, and that he would repeal the Affordable Care Act.
He says the military must stay a top priority and that energy policy should use domestic oil, gas, nuclear, coal, hydroelectric power, and renewables.

people.name: Tim Burchett
lines: He says members of Congress should not trade stocks, and he supports term limits because long tenure ties politicians to special interests.
He says the federal government already taxes and spends too much, and that regulations once put his mulch company out of business.
He says he is pro-life, a gun owner who expanded gun rights in the legislature, and that veterans and American security should come first.

people.name: Victor Scoggin
lines: He says he would fund law enforcement, restore gun rights and voting rights to people with nonviolent felony convictions, and change bail and plea practice.
He lists property-tax reform, English as the only official language, and keeping lobbyists out of health-care decisions.
He says he opposes a Duck River dam at Columbia and opposes new data centers, and he wants campaign spending limits and term limits.

people.name: Victoria Broderick
lines: She says her SAFE plan covers community safety, including rural hospitals and gun violence, and bringing down everyday costs, including pre-K and a path to homeownership.
She says she would protect privacy, keep the federal government out of personal decisions, secure the border with a fair immigration process, and end federal marijuana penalties.
She also says corporate taxes should encourage American investment and that data centers should be accountable to communities.

people.name: Wendell Jackson
lines: He says he wants health care for everyone, covering both mental and physical health, with the details still to come and with people placed ahead of profit.
He says secure housing should be a priority so people can thrive rather than only get by.
He says he would push job growth, workforce training, and incentives for businesses that hire and train local workers.

people.name: Yoshi Matthews
lines: She says independent leadership should put hardworking Tennesseans first, with practical steps to strengthen the economy and widen opportunity.
She describes a reparations proposal as a fair, lawful, and limited Tennessee-based solution.
She says she wants to protect seniors from losing their homes to property taxes.

people.name: Adam Bauman
lines: He says El Paso property taxes are too high because of school budgets and bonds, and that he would work with local leaders to make them more affordable.
He says he would help local and small businesses get the resources they need.
He says a secure border should stop criminals and drugs, and that veterans and seniors should get care and Social Security without raising the age for benefits.

people.name: Alex Mealer
lines: She says she would ban members of Congress from trading individual stocks, seek term limits, cut taxes and regulations, and lower the cost of living.
She says she would keep boys out of girls' sports and locker rooms, secure the border, and back law enforcement.
She says she would push flood projects around Lake Houston and expand oil and gas so energy stays affordable.

people.name: Alexander Hale
lines: He says he would champion Houston energy companies rather than subsidize competitors, and go after housing, insurance, health-care, and electricity costs Washington controls.
He says Houston's crime rate needs federal help for local police, and that he would cut spending he calls wasteful.
He says state and local governments should handle problems they understand better than federal agencies.

people.name: Angela Rodriguez Prilliman
lines: She says she would seek universal health care and universal child care, paid for by taxes on billionaires.
She also lists voting rights, full funding for public schools, and getting billionaire money out of politics.
She says Congress should protect AI whistleblowers, set liability and testing rules, and restrict AI companions for children.

people.name: Anthony Cristo
lines: He says real tax relief requires cutting spending, and that property-tax plans without spending cuts only move the bill somewhere else.
He says he opposes taxpayer-funded welfare and supports immigrants who come to Texas to work.
He says Texas should legalize marijuana and end what he calls the lieutenant governor's war on drugs.

people.name: Arthur DiBianca
lines: He says the market, not the state, should choose the energy mix, with no subsidies or mandates that pick winners among oil, gas, wind, solar, or nuclear.
He says mineral and surface owners should be protected from eminent-domain abuse, and that disputes with energy developers should be settled by voluntary agreements.
He says operators should plug wells and clean sites through bonding and insurance priced to their risk, rather than through taxpayer bailouts.

people.name: August Pfluger
lines: He says Republicans delivered border-wall money, support for immigration enforcement, and tax cuts that include no tax on tips, overtime, and Social Security.
He says he helped secure billions in border reimbursements for states such as Texas and will keep defending conservative Texas values and national security.

people.name: Beth Van Duyne
lines: She says she is running in the 24th District so her children have the same opportunities she had, and she warns about socialism, the border, and hostile nations.
She says she is a conservative who has fought government corruption, supported removing criminal noncitizens from North Texas, and backed growth and the Constitution.

people.name: Bo French
lines: He says the Railroad Commission oversees oil and gas plus uranium, coal, and salt, and that the seat should be held by a conservative who will back the president.
He says he will end diversity, equity, and inclusion programs, regulation he calls overbearing, and influence from radical Islam and the Chinese Communist Party in Texas oil.
He says he will enforce the Legislature's ban on hostile foreign ownership of land in order to protect the Texas oil industry.

people.name: Bobby Pulido
lines: He says he would challenge corporations raising prices, cut red tape for small businesses, and back apprenticeships and higher-wage jobs that stay in South Texas.
He says farmers and ranchers need fair markets and open trade, and that tariffs are raising costs.
He says the border should stay secure and violent criminals should be removed, without raids that he argues hurt local workers and businesses.

people.name: Brandon Gill
lines: He says that in Congress he has worked to stop a large tax increase, secure the southern border, and end funding for projects he calls leftist.
He says he is running again so children can live in a better Texas and a better America, alongside an America First agenda.

people.name: Brandon Herrera
lines: He says he would take practical steps to secure the southern border and improve support for veterans and their families.
He says he would seek national concealed-carry reciprocity, pledge no new taxes, cut waste, and back the REINS Act.

people.name: Brian Babin
lines: He says securing the border, including support for a border wall, is his top immigration priority.
He says he is running to keep the country safe, strong, and economically secure for his children and grandchildren.

people.name: Caitlin Rourk
lines: She says she would lower costs, restore government accountability, and expand access to health care.
She says she would strengthen public schools and child care, set rules for communities facing artificial intelligence, and fix immigration.
She says foreign policy and national security should be practical rather than driven by headlines.

people.name: Carlos De La Cruz
lines: He says he would keep securing the border, give Border Patrol more support, and welcome legal immigration.
He says he would lower costs for working families, expand Texas energy, and vote to ban members of Congress from trading stocks.

people.name: Casey Shepard
lines: He says Congress should be able to check the executive branch, and that courts should stay independent enough to review those decisions.
He says he would fully fund SNAP and school meals, restore Medicaid and Medicare support, and expand the health-care workforce.
He says tax incentives and rental aid should produce affordable homes, and that tariffs are raising the price of food and building materials.

people.name: Chelsey Hockett
lines: She says she would end tariffs she argues raise prices, enact Medicare for All, and create universal child care.
She says the minimum wage should start at $25 and be tied to the cost of living, and that Social Security should keep up with prices.
She says billionaires and corporations should pay more so public schools, Title I, special education, and Head Start are fully funded.

people.name: Chris Gober
lines: He says he would make life affordable, secure the border against cartels, and stop what he calls the weaponization of government against conservatives.
He says he would grow defense and technology jobs in Austin and the Brazos Valley so the country outcompetes China.
He says rural communities need fewer regulations, nearby health care, and data-center rules that do not drain water or raise electric rates.

people.name: Christian Menefee
lines: He says he would seek Medicare for All, protect public schools and abortion rights, and make daily life more affordable.
He lists workers' rights, jobs, gun-violence prevention, immigration, veterans, and criminal-justice reform among his priorities.
He says he went to court against voting restrictions, pollution in Black and Latino neighborhoods, and disaster price gouging.

people.name: Claire Reynolds
lines: She says wages have not kept up with prices and that nobody should go bankrupt over a broken hip or cancer.
She supports moving toward single-payer coverage like Medicare, a strong border with a faster legal immigration process, and abortion that is safe, legal, and rare.
She says Texas needs both oil and gas and renewable energy jobs to stay competitive.

people.name: Colin Allred
lines: He says he is running to lower costs and stop politicians from rigging the economy against people who work hard.
He says his earlier service included work on voting rights and on VA care in North Texas.

people.name: Craig Goldman
lines: He says his first bill signed into law rolled back regulations he argues would have cost Americans billions, and that he voted to extend the 2017 tax cuts.
He says he supported the Laken Riley Act so immigration authorities detain people in the country illegally who are accused of theft or assault.
He says border security is the federal government's first duty and that he backed more defense spending to keep building the F-35.

people.name: Dan Barrios
lines: He says he would confront rising grocery and housing costs by strengthening consumer protections.
He says nobody should be left without affordable medical care, and he would oppose extremism and defend the Constitution.

people.name: Dan Patrick
lines: He says he fights to protect liberty, lower property and business taxes, create jobs, and grow the economy.
He says he wants a stronger electric grid through more reliable thermal power and a high-quality education for every student.
He says he works to secure the border, support law enforcement, and protect life, religious freedom, and the Second Amendment.

people.name: Danny Minton
lines: He says health care is a right and points to Medicare and the VA as models for care that costs less and covers more people.
He says he would protect public schools from what he calls billionaire voucher schemes, and he wants Congress to vote before troops are sent into lasting wars.
He says immigration policy should combine a secure border with basic dignity, and that small businesses should come ahead of Wall Street.

people.name: Dione Sims
lines: She says real freedom means families can afford to live, communities have a voice, and government answers to the people.
She says she will be fair in what she decides and stand up for the rights of people who are suffering and in need.

people.name: Edgardo Baez
lines: He says he would defend constitutional rights, reject socialism, and protect freedoms.
He says he would stimulate local business, attract investment, and champion tax changes that help neighborhoods.

people.name: Eric Flores
lines: He says he would lower the cost of living, oppose spending that feeds inflation, and fund roads, ports, broadband, and water supplies.
He says he would shorten VA waits, protect seniors' earned benefits, and back South Texas farmers, ranchers, and small businesses.

people.name: Evan Hunt
lines: He says he would put mission ahead of party, defend constitutional limits and the rule of law, and seek a government that works for the whole district.
He says he wants more opportunity and less hardship for North Texas families, and solutions that give every family a voice.

people.name: Everett Jackson
lines: He says real change comes from the ground up and that he has advocated for economic justice.
He says he is fighting for working families because he has lived their struggles.

people.name: Frederick Haynes III
lines: He says Congress has too long centered policymaking on corporate interests and political convenience.
He says the district has a history of servant-leaders and needs that kind of representation again.

people.name: Gina Hinojosa
lines: She says she will save Texas public schools.
She says she will put money back in Texans' pockets.
She says she will end what she calls Greg Abbott's corruption so families can reach the American dream.

people.name: Greg Abbott
lines: He says new data centers are being paused and must show they will pay their own way, supply their own power, reuse their own water, reduce electricity costs, and avoid disturbing neighborhoods.
He says the state made bail tougher, backed law enforcement, and focused on violent repeat offenders.

people.name: Greg Casar
lines: He says he would lower costs for working families, make billionaires pay more, and guarantee health care.
He says he backs restoring abortion rights, the PRO Act, Medicare for All, and union jobs in clean energy, and stronger rules on artificial intelligence.

people.name: Henry Cuellar
lines: He says education is the key that opens the door to opportunity for every child.
He says his Appropriations work, including as ranking member of the Homeland Security Subcommittee, is meant to strengthen national security while delivering results for South Texas.
He says a bipartisan reputation keeps him at the table fighting for Texas families no matter which party is in power.

people.name: Jace Yarbrough
lines: He says he would back immigration enforcement and oppose amnesty, and keep legal immigration from being used to push down wages.
He says he would seek national concealed-carry reciprocity and repeal of the National Firearms Act.

people.name: Jake Ellzey
lines: He says he will defend gun ownership, opposes leaving families unarmed at home, and supports a legal right to life.
He says Congress should finish a border wall, back Border Patrol, and stop projects he says seize private land, including a proposed high-speed rail.
He says he serves on Appropriations and Small Business and advocates for veterans, small firms, and taxpayers.

people.name: James Talarico
lines: He says he has led a fight against billionaire donors and politicians he calls puppets.
He says he is running for the Senate to take that fight against corruption to Washington and return power to working people.

people.name: Jason Pearce
lines: He says he knows what it is like to live paycheck to paycheck and to choose among rent, food, and health insurance.
He says leadership should be about service, lifting people up, telling the truth, and making sure no one gets left behind.

people.name: Jessica Hart Steinmann
lines: She says she would put Texas and American workers ahead of what she calls global elites, secure the border, and defend the Constitution.
She says she has fought diversity programs in higher education, represented service members who challenged a COVID vaccine mandate, and sued to keep boys out of girls' sports.
She says parents, not government, should direct how children are raised, and that she led federal work against human trafficking.

people.name: Joaquin Castro
lines: He says he wants to build what he calls an infrastructure of opportunity: strong public schools and universities, a sound health-care system, and good jobs.
His biography says that as a state legislator he helped restore funding for health care and education and worked on mental health, teen pregnancy, and juvenile justice.
He says he created a college tour for students with few resources and founded SA READS, a San Antonio literacy campaign.

people.name: John Carter
lines: His issues page lists border security, protecting the homeland, care for veterans, lower taxes and a stronger economy, the Second Amendment, and protecting children.
He says he treats Central Texas as home and comes back after votes rather than staying in Washington.

people.name: Johnny Garcia
lines: He says he would lower everyday costs, end tariffs that raise prices, and stop members of Congress from trading stocks.
He says he would secure the border, focus immigration enforcement on criminals, keep police funded, and reverse health-care cuts.

people.name: Jon Bonck
lines: He says he would finish the border wall, protect life from conception, and put parents ahead of school ideology.
He says he would defend the Second Amendment and religious liberty, cut spending on foreign wars, and reject vaccine mandates.

people.name: Jon Rosenthal
lines: He says Texas families need a commissioner who will not bend to the companies being regulated while energy bills climb.
He says that in the House he pushed weatherization rules for gas infrastructure after the 2021 grid failure and fought utilities passing the cost of their own failures on to families.
He says the commission has bent to special interests while energy bills rise, and that engineering judgment should replace that pattern.

people.name: Justin Early
lines: He says his priorities are affordability, responsible technology and AI, and defending democracy.
He says families are squeezed by the cost of living and unaffordable health care, and that he is not a career politician.

people.name: Katy Padilla Stout
lines: She says the cost of living comes from the current administration's economic policies, and that the tax code should help the middle class rather than cut taxes for billionaires while food aid is debated.
She says she would expand Medicare toward coverage for everyone and treat gun ownership as a right that still allows commonsense limits.

people.name: Keith Self
lines: He says he voted to restart border-wall construction, offered a bill to use seized cartel money on border security, and wants the federal government to repay Texas for its border spending.
He says he cut the county property-tax rate, opposes stopgap federal budgets, and wants lower taxes, less spending, and energy permitting that expands American production.
He says he started a caucus to stop what he calls the spread of Sharia law in Texas and the country.

people.name: Ken Paxton
lines: He says he will push tax cuts, border security, deportations, an end to what he calls the weaponization of government, and less federal spending.
He says he will take on large drug and food companies, seek more transparency in food and health care, and side with a Make America Healthy Again effort.
He says he will defend gun rights and laws against abortion, oppose transgender participation in girls' sports, and support a clear legal framework for crypto, including the CLARITY Act.

people.name: Kevin Burge
lines: He says he would fast-track affordable housing, crack down on corporate landlords, raise the minimum wage, and expand Medicaid.
He says he supports Medicare for All, restoring abortion rights, tuition-free public college, and rules so data centers recycle water and limit pollution.

people.name: Kevin McCormick
lines: He says his first bills would expand city bus fleets, invest in rural family-farm greenhouses and hemp, and change elections to ranked-choice voting, one statewide primary, and a nonpartisan redistricting commission.
He says he would appraise property by rent or lease value instead of comparable sales and drop exemptions he calls special-interest favors.
He says he favors a moratorium on data centers with strict limits on their electricity and water, and legal THC with rules to protect the public.

people.name: Kristin Hook
lines: She says she would lower costs, fight corruption, and stop AI data centers from taking local water and electricity.
She says billionaires should pay more, health care and public schools should be expanded, abortion rights restored, and the border secured.

people.name: Kyle Rable
lines: He says he would pass fair-pricing rules, limit corporate purchases of single-family homes, and offer tax credits for first-time buyers.
He says he would fund child-care training and facilities, curb presidential tariff power, and bring back manufacturing jobs.
He says legal paths to citizenship should expand because immigrants are part of West Texas communities.

people.name: Lance Gooden
lines: He says people are tired of Washington deal-making and of growing calls for socialism.
He says another term would be used to protect what he calls God-given freedoms.

people.name: Laura Jones
lines: She says the minimum wage should rise and be tied to the cost of living so a full-time worker can cover housing, utilities, and food.
She supports Medicare for All, including cutting out insurance middlemen and negotiating drug and medical prices.
She says taxes should fall for most households and rise for billionaires and large corporations.

people.name: Lauren Peña
lines: She says she would audit agencies, expose fraud, cut federal spending she ties to inflation, and cut regulations she says are raising energy costs.
She says she would defend parental rights and school choice, restore law-enforcement funding, and make veterans' care a priority.
She says her first bill would be the SAFE NIGHTS Act to fight human trafficking, and that she would press to release the Epstein files.

people.name: Leticia Gutierrez
lines: She says her priorities are lower costs, good jobs, strong public schools, affordable health care, and secure retirements.
She says she is for industry and jobs without blank checks for billionaires, and for safe neighborhoods, secure borders, and equal justice.
She says she opposes wars of choice and corporate handouts, and wants government to answer to families rather than the highest bidder.

people.name: Lizzie Fletcher
lines: She says the district's values are inclusion, innovation, and collaboration, and that those should produce progress and opportunity.
She says she looks for common-sense solutions for Houstonians rather than slogans, including on energy and health policy.

people.name: Mark Nair
lines: He says tariffs should be set by Congress rather than a president, and that he wants wages people can live on.
He says government should stop using artificial intelligence for facial recognition and social-media surveillance until privacy rules exist, and that workers should know when AI affects their jobs.
He says health care should put people ahead of insurers and corporate profits.

people.name: Mark Teixeira
lines: He says he would secure the border, deport people here illegally, and go after cartels.
He says he would cut federal spending, expand oil, gas, and nuclear production, and defend parental rights, the Second Amendment, and the unborn.

people.name: Marquette Greene-Scott
lines: She says she is running because Congress is broken and she will judge issues by what is best for the district rather than by party.
She says her focus is creating jobs, improving infrastructure, and protecting essential rights.

people.name: Martha Fierro
lines: She says health care should get more affordable through competition and patient choice rather than government mandates, and she supports school choice and parental rights.
She says she would cut federal spending, back Texas oil and gas, and support Border Patrol against illegal crossings and trafficking.

people.name: Mayes Middleton
lines: He says as attorney general he will sue sanctuary cities, enforce federal border and deportation orders, and fight human trafficking.
He says he will defend laws protecting unborn children, keep males out of women's sports and private spaces, and enforce voter-identification and citizenship rules for voting.
He says he will go after waste, fraud, and abuse, enforce the open-records law, and protect oil and gas jobs from activists he calls far left.

people.name: Melissa McDonough
lines: She says she would protect Social Security, fund public schools, make tuition more affordable, and support renewable energy and flood control.
She says she supports responsible gun ownership, letting women make their own medical decisions, Medicare for All, and more effective border management.

people.name: Michael Cloud
lines: He says the border needs a wall and a response to cartels and trafficking, and that cutting regulation and simplifying the tax code would help small businesses.
