He says federal spending is on a path to ruin and he has filed bills to improve cost estimates and to sunset federal agencies.

people.name: Monica De La Cruz
lines: She says she would finish border infrastructure, end catch-and-release, restore Remain in Mexico, and support E-Verify and more immigration judges.
She says she would cut farm regulations, oppose tariffs that block farm exports, protect Medicare and Social Security, and lower taxes on families and small businesses.
She supports oil and gas jobs, nuclear power, and a balanced-budget amendment, and rejects what she calls Green New Deal policies.

people.name: Nathan Johnson
lines: He says he will defend individual rights, go to court against federal actions he calls illegal, and investigate public corruption without regard to party.
He says he will enforce consumer-protection and competition laws against price gouging, scams, and unfair competition.
He says he will work with local district attorneys on identity theft, cybercrime, Medicaid fraud, and human trafficking, and help secure the border without tactics he says violate the Constitution.

people.name: Nathaniel Moran
lines: He says his politics come from Christian faith, family, and a duty to defend liberty and the Constitution.
He highlights his work on the Ways and Means Committee, which covers taxes, trade, Social Security, and Medicare, and on a House committee focused on the Chinese Communist Party.

people.name: Pat Dixon
lines: He says shrinking government to its proper size means a person may do anything that does not harm someone else.
He says voters should not be limited to two choices when the office is this important.
He says he will not publish a long list of promises, because future crises are unpredictable and his Libertarian principles are what make his positions predictable.

people.name: Pat Fallon
lines: He says he championed a border crackdown, a ban on sanctuary cities, and protection of Texas historical monuments.
He says he co-authored legislation to restrict abortion, backed a permanent ban on a state income tax, and supported limits on future property taxes.
He says he will defend the Second and Tenth Amendments.

people.name: Patrick Gillespie
lines: He says he would protect human life from fertilization to natural death, limit government to enumerated powers, and support parents' choice of schools.
He says immigrants should be vetted, illegal crossings stopped, existing gun laws enforced, and federal spending brought back to a balanced budget.

people.name: Pete Sessions
lines: He says a conservative agenda should use capitalism and the rule of law to put more money in Americans' pockets and create jobs.
He says infrastructure has to keep up with Texas population growth, and that he spends time in the district when he is not voting.
He says the country should lead with moral character and invest in a purpose-driven life for young people and families.

people.name: Randy Weber
lines: He describes himself as conservative, opposed to abortion, opposed to socialism, and a Second Amendment supporter.
He says that in the Texas House he wrote a human-trafficking law that trained police and protected minor victims.

people.name: Rhonda Hart
lines: She says she opposes school vouchers and would invest more in public schools, including pay for teachers and support staff.
She says she believes in climate change, wants serious investment in solar and wind, and would protect natural resources while recognizing the role of energy in southeast Texas.
She says health care should not be tied to a paycheck, and she says she worked to pass the Kimberly Vaughan safe-storage law and will keep fighting gun violence.

people.name: Roger Williams
lines: He says his priorities are lower taxes, less government, cutting spending, defending the border, listening to generals, the Tenth Amendment, and standing with Israel.
He says that as a business owner he opposes taxes and regulation that hurt small businesses, and that he chairs the House Small Business Committee.

people.name: Ronny Jackson
lines: He says his focus is national security, support for farmers and ranchers, and keeping the country strong and free.
The campaign describes that work as defending Texas families in Congress.

people.name: Shaun Finnie
lines: He says he would apply business budgeting to government, remove tariffs, and tackle the federal debt so younger people are not stuck with it.
He says he would protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid for the middle class, leave reproductive decisions to women, and invest in public schools and medical research.

people.name: Steve Toth
lines: He says that as an appropriations member he steered billions toward border barriers and security, and that he will keep pushing Congress to stop traffickers and cartels.
He says he led efforts to remove critical race theory and diversity programs from Texas classrooms and universities, and that he will defend the Second Amendment without red-flag laws.

people.name: Steven Shook
lines: He says he would create jobs, protect Social Security and Medicare, and make health care affordable.
He says he would support local businesses, defend educational opportunity, and improve local infrastructure.

people.name: Sylvia Garcia
lines: She says she is focused on defending democracy, lowering costs, and making housing more affordable.
She says she is standing up for women's rights, an economy that works for more than those at the top, and a more compassionate immigration policy.

people.name: Tano Tijerina
lines: He says the border should be secured and immigration should happen legally, and that as county judge he lowered property taxes five times in ten years.
He says he would lower taxes for working families and small businesses, cut federal regulation, and stop wasteful spending.

people.name: Tanya Lloyd
lines: She says rural hospitals are closing and she would seek single-payer health care, restore reproductive rights, and fund rural schools.
She says she would support family farmers, protect water and land, and create jobs in clean energy and sustainable agriculture.

people.name: Ted Brown
lines: He says he will never vote to raise taxes and wants the federal income tax repealed and the IRS abolished, with nothing put in their place.

people.name: Teresa Fox
lines: She wants federal spending restrained and naval readiness funded through the workforce rather than through more bureaucracy.
She calls for police staffing in rural communities, Title IX rules she says would protect fair competition and privacy, and health care for rural areas.
She supports congressional term limits.

people.name: Teresa Fox
lines: She wants federal spending restrained and naval readiness funded through the workforce rather than through more bureaucracy.
She calls for police staffing in rural communities, Title IX rules she says would protect fair competition and privacy, and health care for rural areas.
She supports congressional term limits.

people.name: Ace Parsi
lines: He says the campaign is values-driven and is trying to reclaim affordability, care, and empowerment.
He says he wants to reclaim what it means to be human, kind, and empowered in an age of technology, political spectacle, and concentrated control.
He says he is fighting for a future where people rise together when government steps back from its commitments.

people.name: Carol Miller
lines: Her campaign says she is pro-life, pro-jobs, pro-energy, and for lower taxes.
The site says taxes, spending, and regulation from Washington hurt West Virginia families and businesses.
It says she has worked to lower taxes, create jobs, protect energy industries, and secure the border.

people.name: Rachel Fetty Anderson
lines: She says family farmers should be shielded from foreign takeovers of land and from rules that punish them for choosing methods other than those of large agribusiness.
She wants a moratorium on hyperscale data centers and local control over their zoning and taxes.

She says Social Security should be preserved, including by ending the wage cap on the Social Security tax, and that U.S. military force should be reserved for self-defense with Congress declaring war.

people.name: Riley Moore
lines: He says that as treasurer he divested state funds from BlackRock over its support for ESG policies and helped other states push back on those policies.
He says he also helped pass and administer the Hope Scholarship and Jumpstart Savings programs.

people.name: Shelley Moore Capito
lines: She says her Senate work focuses on the opioid crisis, broadband, and public infrastructure, and on rolling back rules such as California's electric-vehicle mandate.
The campaign says she is running again as a champion of tax cuts, border security, and the Second Amendment.
It says her earlier work in the Legislature and the House centered on education, job training, transportation, and federal funding for highways and bridges.

people.name: Vince George
lines: He says the minimum wage has stayed at $8.75, jobs have disappeared, hospitals are closing, and more families are struggling to put food on the table.
He says the state's members of Congress voted for cuts to SNAP, Medicaid, Medicare, and veterans' benefits, and that the biggest cuts take effect after this election.

people.name: Andrew Beck
lines: He says he would bring practical leadership aimed at lower costs, good-paying jobs, and better health care.
He says protecting fair elections and democratic institutions is the issue that makes progress on jobs, health care, and education possible.
He says women must be able to make their own reproductive-health decisions and that Congress should secure that right.

people.name: Brad Smith
lines: He supports a higher minimum wage, apprenticeships, prevailing wage, project labor agreements, and the right to organize, plus training through tech schools, college, and trades.
He says health care should protect people with pre-existing conditions and stay close to home, and he wants transparency before large data centers are built.
As a gun owner, he supports background checks, red-flag laws, and secure storage, and he also calls for fair milk prices, farm broadband, reproductive freedom, and LGBTQ+ protections.

people.name: Bryan Steil
lines: He says he is cutting wasteful spending to lower prices, securing the border against fentanyl and human trafficking, and working with local law enforcement.
He says he will protect Social Security and Medicare, including their solvency, and work to lower prescription prices for seniors.
He also says he is working so service members, their families, and veterans get mental-health care and the benefits they earned.

people.name: David Crowley
lines: He says he would take a storefront-revitalization program statewide, tie infrastructure spending to local hiring and labor standards, and expand apprenticeships in the trades and health care.
He proposes more affordable housing, universal early childhood education, and closing the state's broadband gap.
He says he would protect voting rights and push for nonpartisan redistricting.

people.name: Derrick Van Orden
lines: He says life should be protected, drawing on friends lost in training and combat.
He says the rights in the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution should not be infringed.
He says people do better when government gets out of the way and they can decide what to do with their own money.

people.name: Eric Toney
lines: He says he would back police, keep violent offenders off the street, and put public safety ahead of politics.
He says he would go after cartels and dealers tied to fentanyl and meth.
He says he would modernize the state crime labs and clear the testing backlog.

people.name: Fred Clark
lines: He says data centers and artificial intelligence need public oversight and guardrails, and he supports women's decisions on reproductive care, including contraception.
He says the border should be secure and criminals deported, while people here legally keep their rights.
He says health care costs too much for the access Americans get, and that constitutional guarantees are at risk if leaders do not uphold them.

people.name: Glenn Grothman
lines: He says he is fighting to protect manufacturing jobs, expand technical education, reform welfare, secure the border, and cut federal spending.
He says he sponsored a bill to limit welfare benefits such as Medicaid and Medicare to U.S. citizens so the safety net is not compromised.

people.name: Gwen Moore
lines: The campaign calls her a champion for working Wisconsinites and a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus.
It says she has been a champion for protecting Social Security and Medicare and an advocate for low-income communities.
It says she is a voice against what it calls an assault on democracy.

people.name: Jay Schroeder
lines: He says Wisconsin should move election administration from the Wisconsin Elections Commission to the secretary of state, by legislation or by referendum.
He says voters can hold an elected secretary accountable for how elections are run in a way they cannot hold an appointed commission.
He says the office should also stand for transparency in public records and in the land funds it oversees.

people.name: JoCasta Zamarripa
lines: She is using the campaign to call for state investment in affordable child care, housing, and relief on grocery costs.
She says the secretary of state sits on the Board of Commissioners of Public Lands and that she would protect the trust funds and land that support public schools and libraries.
She says she would push the state to fund public schools so districts rely less on local referenda.

people.name: Josh Kaul
lines: He says the department has investigated homicides, sexual assaults, internet crimes against children, and drug trafficking, and has sought money from companies tied to the opioid epidemic.
He says he supports wider background checks on firearm transfers and more funding for crime-victim services and school safety.
He says he is pro-choice, points to a Wisconsin Supreme Court ruling on an old abortion law, and says the office has joined cases against federal funding cuts and weaker environmental rules.

people.name: Mark Pocan
lines: He says he uses private-sector and public-sector experience to promote job growth and support families in south-central Wisconsin.
He is chair emeritus of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and describes himself as a progressive leader.
A campaign news note says he stopped taking corporate PAC money for his reelection.

people.name: Michael Alfonso
lines: He says he would cut spending and red tape so young families can buy homes, ease rules on farms, and back school choice and homeschooling.
He says he is fully opposed to abortion and assisted suicide, would ban members of Congress from trading stocks, and would defend the Second Amendment, including constitutional carry.
He says immigration policy, including H-1B visas, should serve American workers, and that he would return power to the states and stop spending he calls wasteful foreign aid.

people.name: Mitchell Berman
lines: He says he will lower costs for working families, make health care more affordable, and protect programs that feed children.
He says he will stop giveaways to corporations and billionaires and fight corruption in Washington.
He says he is running for families rather than for billionaires and big corporations.

people.name: Pete Karas
lines: He says the secretary of state's limited duties make this a race where a vote can send a statewide message.
He says electing a third-party candidate would push for political reform and an end to what he calls the two parties' hold on elections.

people.name: Rebecca Cooke
lines: She says she is running to lower costs and expand opportunity for working people and retirees, especially in rural areas, rather than for the ultra-wealthy.
She says she would ban stock trading by members of Congress and the White House, overturn Citizens United, and enforce congressional term limits.
She says she would fully fund law enforcement to keep communities safe and protect the border.

people.name: Rick Crosson
lines: He says the campaign is focused on affordability, which he describes as helping families meet their needs without constant financial stress.
He says accountability means leaders who show up, listen, and act transparently.
He says results means real improvements in people's lives, and that he wants leadership that brings people together.

people.name: Scott Fitzgerald
lines: He says he is working with President Trump to secure the border, stop illegal drugs and illegal immigration, and end what he calls reckless spending.
He says he will help small businesses, support law enforcement as the son and father of officers, and defend the right to life and the Second Amendment.
He says he is pushing back on socialism and on bureaucracies he says are out of control.

people.name: Tim Rogers
lines: He says schools, graduation rates, and a justice system he calls uneven have declined, and that he wants justice applied equally.
He says aging lead water lines and poor drinking water need action, not more talk.
He says he will stand up for the district on taxes and representation and try to restore neighborhood quality of life.

people.name: Tom Tiffany
lines: He says he has balanced budgets and worked on border security, and that he is running so Wisconsin families can still own a business and raise children.
He says he will stand up to unelected bureaucrats and fight for farmers and other workers.
He argues that another four years of the current leadership in Madison would raise taxes and shrink opportunity.

people.name: Tony Wied
lines: He says illegal immigration surged under the Biden administration and that the border still has to be secured against crime and human trafficking.
He says he will cut federal spending, get government out of the way of American energy, and keep the military strong.
He says he will protect farmers and other agricultural producers by reducing regulations so they can succeed.

people.name: Chuck Gray
lines: His campaign says he will protect coal, oil, and gas jobs, oppose what he calls woke wind projects and ESG rules, and fight inflation with lower taxes and less spending.
The site says he sponsored Wyoming's voter ID law, required proof of citizenship to register, and banned ranked-choice voting and foreign funding of elections.
It says he supports securing the border, the Second Amendment, and pro-life policies, and opposes taxpayer-funded abortion.

people.name: Eric Barlow
lines: He says his legislative work has centered on Wyoming energy independence, rural health access, and water infrastructure.
He says he is running to offer leadership rooted in service, and that the campaign is counting on Wyoming residents rather than special-interest money.

people.name: Harriet Hageman
lines: She says she will defend speech, gun rights, and private property, and that she wants voter identification and an end to mailing ballots to people who did not request them.
She says she will fight tax increases, cut federal spending, and defend oil, gas, and coal production.
She says federal land agencies have mismanaged forests and that she wants multiple-use rules that answer to the people who live with those decisions.

people.name: James Byrd
lines: He says he will try to lower energy costs by backing domestic production, cutting red tape, and ending foreign wars he says are driving prices up.
He says he will keep public lands public and open for hunting, fishing, grazing, and recreation, rather than selling them.

people.name: Kenneth Casner
lines: He says his first issue is free and open elections: a person should be able to file and run without having to join a party.
He says health care is the main reason young people leave, and he wants a statewide system that connects rural clinics.
He says he wants small business to grow, and he wants property tax ended for people once they turn 65.

people.name: Lisa Kinney
lines: She says public lands should stay public, and she would work with local communities to keep access open rather than sell or transfer the land.
She says she would restore Affordable Care Act subsidies, keep the rural-hospital funding she says is set to end, and work toward health coverage for everyone.
She says she would cut tariffs, raise taxes on the wealthy, lower taxes for people making under $100,000, and help first-time buyers and renters with housing.

people.name: Rebecca Bextel
lines: She says she would defend gun rights, religious liberty, private property, and parents' authority over their children's education, and veto bills she says infringe on those freedoms.
She says she would take Wyoming out of the federal refugee resettlement program and end policies that let people without legal status get a Wyoming driver's license.
She says she would defend coal, oil, natural gas, uranium, and critical-mineral jobs, and fight property-tax bills that rise faster than a family can pay.

people.name: Robert Short
lines: He says he would use the office against sham corporations and people who misuse privacy laws to disadvantage Wyoming businesses.
He says fair elections depend on county clerks and local volunteers, and that he would act quickly if the process goes wrong.
He says he would investigate securities violations, including cryptocurrency scams, and refer criminal matters to the proper authorities.

people.name: Tamara Trujillo
lines: She says elections should be secure and open to U.S. citizens, and that county clerks need the tools and a shared system to do that work.
She supports hand counts as a second check on machine totals and supports mail ballots. She opposes ballot drop boxes and absentee voting for anyone who asks.
She says Wyoming's easy business filings bring in money but also fraud, and she wants a company's owners identified when it registers.
